issues.title: Cosmetic provider polish: leading-BOM W123, and namespace eval selectionRange spans the whole body
issues.body:
Two small provider items from the #1122 audits, neither fixed in #1212.

**1. Leading U+FEFF produces `W123 Unknown command 'set'`.** A file starting with a UTF-8 BOM gets its first command name glued to the BOM. Harmless for VS Code (which strips the BOM before sending didOpen text) but visible to non-stripping clients and CLI analysis of BOM'd files. Deliberately skipped in the line-ending fixes because it is *not* byte-length preserving, so it can't ride the `normalise_lone_cr` boundary: the lexer and CST must agree on skipping U+FEFF at offset 0, the lexer is shared with the VM's eval path (where a leading BOM in a string is ordinary data), and the correct behaviour is dialect-dependent (Tcl 9 `source` skips a leading BOM; 8.6 does not). Fix shape: skip-at-offset-0 in the file-analysis entry only, gated per dialect, with position math tests proving columns on line 0 stay client-correct.

**2. `namespace eval` symbols use a full-body `selectionRange`.** Every other symbol kind narrows `selectionRange` to the name token; namespaces return `selectionRange == range` (probe: `::myns` at `13:22–19:0` for both). Harmless for sticky scroll (same start line) but wrong per the LSP contract ("the range that should be selected and revealed when this symbol is being picked") — clicking the namespace in the outline selects the whole body instead of the name. Fix in `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/document_symbols.rs` (~`:436-449`): use the namespace-name token span, as `proc_symbol` does.

issues.title: False W210 on a braced data argument: `puts {set y 1; return $y}` reports read-before-set
issues.body:
## Problem

A **braced** word performs no `$` or `[` substitution at all, so its contents are inert text at the call site. The SSA use scan nonetheless harvests `$var` references from the word's de-braced text, which produces a false `W210 read before it is set` on any command carrying brace-shaped data.

## Minimal repro

```tcl
puts {
    set y 1
    return $y
}
```

Emits:

```
W210: Variable 'y' is read before it is set
```

There is no read at all here — and even if the word were evaluated, `y` is set two lines above the `$y`.

Even smaller, with no write anywhere:

```tcl
puts {$y}
```

## Oracle

tclsh 9.0.4 and 8.6.16 agree that a braced word is literal:

```tcl
% puts {$y}
$y
% puts {
    set y 1
    return $y
}

    set y 1
    return $y
```

Neither reads a variable named `y`; `puts {$y}` succeeds with `y` undefined.

## Where it comes from

`tcl_compiler::ssa::scan_command_words` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/ssa.rs`) scans **every** non-`Body` argument word with `VarReferenceScanner::scan_word` over the word's de-braced text:

```rust
for (idx, arg) in args.iter().enumerate() {
    if body_indices.contains(&idx) || name_role_braced.contains(&idx) {
        continue;
    }
    vars_found.extend(scanner.scan_word(arg, registry));
}
```

The one existing carve-out — `name_role_braced`, added for #1078 — covers only braced words in `ArgRole::VarWrite` / `ArgRole::VarRead` positions (`unset {$n}`). A braced word at a position the registry gives **no** role is still scanned.

## Why the obvious fixes do not work

Both were implemented and measured against the suite, then reverted:

1. **Skip the scan for a braced word at a role-less position.** Removes every false positive — but `analyser::diagnostics::tests::w220_braced_literal_arg_is_not_a_read` documents a *deliberate* policy that a braced mention conservatively keeps a variable alive, because the word may be evaluated later (`after 100 {incr x}`, a deferred callback, an unknown definer). With the scan skipped, `set a(k) 1; …; puts {$a(k)}` starts reporting `W211 Variable 'a(k)' is set but never used`.

2. **Record the word's names as `safe_on_uninit` self-initialising `defs` on the call.** Keeps the liveness read and suppresses W210 — but a `defs` entry is a genuine SSA definition, so it kills the preceding store. `optimiser::manager::tests::braced_word_is_never_propagated` regresses:

   ```
   left:  "\nputs {$x}\nputs $x\n"
   right: "set x 42\nputs {$x}\nputs 42\n"
   ```

   i.e. `set x 42` is deleted. A miscompile, not a diagnostic wobble.

## What a fix needs

Two consumers of the same use want opposite conservatism:

| Consumer | Assumption it needs about a braced word |
|---|---|
| liveness / dead-store (W211, W220, store elimination) | it *may* be evaluated → keep the use |
| read-before-set (W210) | it *may not* be evaluated, or may be evaluated in a frame that binds the name → do not claim the read |

So the SSA use set needs a **classified** use — a *speculative* read carried by an unevaluated braced word, distinct from a definite one — with the W210 emitter ignoring speculative uses while the liveness passes keep honouring them. That is a change to `uses_of` / `DefUseChain`, not a filter at either end.

## Relationship to other issues

- #1142 frames the same asymmetry as an *un-hooked definer* problem; measurement on `c79f4d1a3` shows it is not definer-specific — `puts` reproduces it — so this is the general form. #1142's OptProc half is already closed by its idx 90 fix.
- #1078 fixed the narrow name-role case (`unset {$n}`) with the same underlying diagnosis.

## Tests to pin

- **TP:** `puts {$y}` and `puts {set y 1; return $y}` emit no W210; an invented command's braced body likewise.
- **FP guard:** `expr {$a + $b}` still reads `a` and `b` (a braced `Expr` really does substitute); `lsort -command {cmp $x}` keeps its read.
- **TN:** `puts "$y"` (quoted, genuinely substituted, `y` unset) still fires W210.
- **Regression:** `w220_braced_literal_arg_is_not_a_read` and `braced_word_is_never_propagated` must both stay green — they are the two guard rails that rule out the shortcut fixes.

issues.title: `is_dynamic_word` on a reconstructed braced word: `namespace path {$ns ::a}` is skipped entirely
issues.body:
Braces suppress substitution, so in `namespace path {$ns ::a}` tclsh reads `$ns` as a *literal* namespace name — the word is not dynamic in any sense.

`Analyser::handle_namespace_path_command` (and, by the same pattern, other handlers that gate on the word's reconstructed text) tests `crate::naming::is_dynamic_word(&args[1])`. `args[1]` for a braced word is its content with the braces already stripped, so the scan finds `$` and the whole command is skipped: neither the `namespace_paths` entry nor the per-element `NamespaceRef`s are recorded. Consequences:

- bare-command resolution inside that namespace loses the path tier for the rest of the file;
- navigation on the element abstains (recorded as a documented limit by `tn_a_braced_path_word_that_looks_dynamic_is_still_skipped` in `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/namespace_symbol.rs`).

Wrong direction only — a miss, never a wrong span — which is why it was left as-is while landing #1113 item 2.

Fix direction: the dynamic test should consult the word's token kind rather than re-scanning reconstructed text. A `TokenType::Str` word never substitutes, so it is literal by construction; the text scan is only correct for `Esc` / quoted words. Worth auditing the other `is_dynamic_word(&args[N])` call sites for the same shape at the same time.

issues.title: Cross-document namespace navigation does not answer implicit parents
issues.body:
Follow-up residual from #1113 item 1.

The implicit-parent answer — `namespace eval ::p::q::r {}` really creates `::p::q`, so navigation on a `::p::q` reference answers with the *covering prefix* of the deeper written name, and hover words it "implicitly created by" rather than "declared by" — is implemented in the in-document tier (`tcl_lsp_core::namespace_symbol::namespace_implicit_parent_spans`, `NamespaceFacts::implicit_declarations`), and `definition()` falls back to it when nothing declares the cell outright.

The server's cross-document tier does not:

- `Backend::namespace_declaration_locations` merges local declaration spans with `index.namespace_declarations_qualified(cell, …)`, which matches the exact qualified name only. A namespace implicitly created by a deeper `namespace eval` in *another* file still answers nothing.
- `Backend::namespace_hover` folds index rows into `NamespaceFacts` by `declares` alone, so `implicit_declarations` stays at the local count and a sibling file's implicit site is invisible to the hover wording.

Needs a workspace-index query for "declaring rows whose qualified name is a strict descendant of CELL", plus the covering-prefix computation run against that row's own document text (the prefix span is a sub-range of the written name word, so it needs the text, not just the span).

issues.title: W210 false-fires again on a `dict update` value-var: `fp_depth::bug_dict_update_value_var` is red
issues.body:
`rust/tcl-compiler/tests/fp_depth.rs::bug_dict_update_value_var::dict_update_known_key_value_var_should_be_silent` fails:

```
proc f {} { set d {k 5}; dict update d k v { puts $v } }
```

emits `W210` on the read of `$v`. tclsh binds `v` to `5` inside the body (`info exists v` → 1 on 8.6 and 9.0), and the key-aware suppression in `analyser/diagnostics/helpers.rs::harvest_dict_with_suppression` was added precisely to keep this silent — the sibling controls (`dict update` on an empty dict fires; the `dict with` analogue stays silent) still pass, so only the key-present `dict update` path regressed.

Reproduced on `91f209c11` ("Merge rust: full 12-PR series (#1219-#1229, #1235) landed") with no other changes applied. The harvester resolves the dict's value through the SSA/SCCP version read by the `dict update` statement, falling back to a same-block literal `set`; the failing shape is a **proc body**, which is what #1123 / #1235 ("Per-item/whole-file analysis parity") reworked in the same merge — a plausible first place to look, since a per-item pass that no longer carries the same-block `AssignConst` (or a different SSA version at that statement) would drop the key harvest and leave the value-var unsuppressed.

Not investigated further — found while running the crate suite for unrelated work.

issues.title: Audit the remaining `is_dynamic_word(&args[N])` call sites for the reconstructed-braced-word miss
issues.body:
Follow-up to #1245, which fixed the one call site that issue named.

`crate::naming::is_dynamic_word` scans a word's *reconstructed* text for `$` / `[`. For a brace-quoted word the IR stores its content with the braces already stripped, so the scan reports "dynamic" for a word Tcl never substitutes — and the caller then abstains from a command it could have recorded exactly. #1245 fixed `handle_namespace_path_command` by consulting the token kind (`naming::word_is_dynamic(text, braced_literal)`); roughly thirty other call sites have the same shape and were not touched:

```
rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/commands.rs   ~7 sites
rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs   ~4 sites
rust/tcl-compiler/src/unit_scope.rs          ~7 sites
rust/tcl-compiler/src/command_binding.rs     ~7 sites
rust/tcl-compiler/src/alias.rs               ~3 sites
rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/method_barrier.rs  2 sites
```

Not all of them are wrong: a site whose word is a *command name* or a bare identifier can never legitimately be brace-quoted with a `$` in it, and some sites already have the token in hand and check it (`analyser/handlers.rs:331` gates on `tok.kind == TokenType::Esc`, `var_refs.rs:110` on `!braced_literal`). The audit is to classify each site — token available / token not available / bracing impossible — and convert the ones that can be reached with a braced word.

Wrong direction only in every case: a miss (the command is skipped and nothing is recorded), never a wrong span or a false diagnostic. `naming::word_is_dynamic` already exists as the shared answer.

issues.title: W210 false positive: a `$var` inside a braced `foreach` / `lmap` list word is read as a substitution
issues.body:
Found while auditing #1252.

A brace-quoted `foreach` / `lmap` value word substitutes nothing, so a `$name` inside it is a literal list element. The analyser harvests it as a variable read anyway:

```
$ tcl diag --source 'foreach n {a $b c} { }'
<inline:1>:1:1: warning W210     Variable 'b' is read before it is set

$ tcl diag --source 'lmap n {a $b c} { }'
<inline:1>:1:1: warning W210     Variable 'b' is read before it is set

$ tcl diag --source 'proc p {} { foreach n {a $b c} { } }'
<inline:1>:1:13: warning W210     Variable 'b' is read before it is set
```

tclsh 8.6.16 / 9.0.4 disagree — the loop runs three times over the literal values `a`, `$b`, `c` and never reads `b`:

```tcl
foreach n {a $b c} { puts $n }    ;# -> a / $b / c   (b undefined throughout)
```

This is a **false positive**, not the wrong-direction miss #1252 describes: the diagnostic is emitted where nothing is read.

Scope: `foreach` / `lmap` only. `set l {a $b c}`, `lsearch {a $b c} a` and `switch` pattern lists are all clean, and a `[cmd]` in the same position (`foreach n {a [x] c} { }`) does not fire either — it is specifically the `$`-reference harvest over the value word.

Root cause: `ir::ForeachIterator` carries `list_arg: String` — the value word's *text*, braces already stripped — with no record of whether the word was brace-quoted. Every other IR word that has this problem carries the flag (`Statement::AssignConst::braced`, `Statement::Return::braced`, and the shared `CommandTokens::arg_is_braced_literal`); the `foreach` iterator is the gap, so the downstream read harvest has nothing to gate on.

Fix direction: add a `list_braced: bool` to `ForeachIterator`, populated from the value word's `TokenType::Str` at lowering (the same `CommandTokens::arg_is_braced_literal` every other site uses), and gate the variable-reference harvest over `list_arg` on it. The analyser-side sibling of this — the per-iteration literal simulation — is fixed in #1252 and already takes the flag from `arg_tokens`, so the two would end up agreeing.

Repro is one line; TP/FP/TN shape is the usual one (braced word → no read; quoted word `foreach n "a $b c" {}` → read, and must stay a read).

issues.title: `namespace path` list entries have no per-element span, so the namespace rename tier refuses instead of rewriting them
issues.body:
Residual from the namespace rename tier (#1114).

`namespace path {::a ::b}` takes a single **list** word. The `NamespacePath` analyser hook records the resolved entries on `AnalysisResult::namespace_paths` (a `HashMap<String, Vec<String>>`) with no span at all — neither for the word nor for each element — and the argument carries no `ArgRole::NamespaceName`, so the entries appear in no reference table either.

Consequences:

- **Rename** (#1114) refuses whenever any indexed document's `namespace path` names the namespace being renamed. The refusal is correct — leaving the entry behind would point the path at a namespace that no longer exists — but it is a refusal where an edit is possible.
- **Find-references / go-to-definition** on a namespace do not report path entries at all: `namespace path {::mypkg}` is a real reference to `::mypkg` and answers nothing.

Fix shape: record the path word's span plus a per-entry sub-span (the element's byte range inside the list word, which needs the list parse, not just the word text) on the `namespace_paths` record, and lift them into `WorkspaceNamespaceRef`-shaped rows so the existing namespace tiers pick them up with no new resolution rule. The rename tier then rewrites the entry's own segment through `namespace_rename::written_cell_segment` like every other spelling, and the `namespace path` refusal arm can be deleted.

Note the entries are resolved names: a relative entry roots against the namespace the `namespace path` runs in, which the hook already does — the span work is what is missing, not the resolution.

issues.title: Dynamic variable-name provenance stops at the written word — no per-site constant-value record survives analysis
issues.body:
Residual from the per-site provenance work on #1093.

`rename_safety::namespace_variable_rename_hazard` now asks, per site, whether a dynamic variable-name word *can spell* the cell being renamed. The bound it uses is the word's own text: a substitution can evaluate to anything, but the literal characters around it cannot change, so `dynamic_names::dynamic_variable_word_can_spell` treats the word as a pattern (`::other::$n` cannot reach `::ns::v`; `${p}_count` cannot spell `v`).

What it cannot do is consult the *value* set. The obvious case:

```tcl
namespace eval ::ns {
    variable v 1
    proc p {} { set n other ; set $n 2 }   ;# `$n` is provably `other`, never `v`
}
```

still refuses a rename of `::ns::v`, because a bare `$n` is a lone wildcard textually.

The analyser knows this while it walks — `Scope::lookup_dominating_const_string` is exactly the fact, and it is already what `namespace eval $ns` uses to decide whether a computed namespace target is recorded (#1113 item 3). But it is analyser *state*: nothing per-site survives into `AnalysisResult`, and `rename_safety` is a post-analysis consumer, so it has nothing to read.

Fix shape: record the sites the way #1113 item 3 records namespace targets — a per-site table on `AnalysisResult` for registry `ArgRole::VarWrite` / `VarRead` words that `names_a_dynamic_variable`, carrying the span and the dominating-constant resolution (`Some(value)` / `None` when branch-dependent or parameter-fed). The gate then refuses only where the resolution is `None` *and* the textual pattern admits the cell. Abstain-toward-refuse is unchanged; this shrinks the abstention set a second time.

The same table would let the namespace rename tier (#1114) narrow its computed-namespace-word refusal the same way, since both consult the same predicate today.

issues.title: A member arrived via a cross-file `renamemethod` is missing from workspace member enumeration (completion / outline)
issues.body:
Residual from #1167.

The arrival channel now works for *resolution*: a `renamemethod old new` in a cross-file `oo::define` stub records the destination on the tombstone, and `WorkspaceIndex::dispatch_chain` re-keys the defining record's member so `new` resolves — go-to-definition, references and rename all reach it, and `method_family_qnames` counts the arrival as a definition.

What still reads the raw table is **enumeration**. `WorkspaceClass::methods` is built additively from each record's own declarations, so the defining record still lists `old` and the stub lists nothing. Anything that lists a class's members rather than resolving one name against them therefore shows the pre-rename name:

```tcl
# a.tcl
oo::class create C { method old {} { … } }
# b.tcl
oo::define C { renamemethod old new }
# c.tcl
set c [C new]
$c <TAB>          ;# offers `old`, not `new`
```

(tclsh 8.6.14: `info class methods ::C` after sourcing both is `new`, and `[::C new] old` errors `unknown method "old"`.)

Fix shape: apply the arrival re-key where the table is *read as a list*, not only where a single name is resolved — either a `WorkspaceClass::effective_methods()` that folds the class's records' retractions and arrivals once, or the same fold materialised at index-build time. The dispatch chain should then read that fold too, so one place decides what the class's member set is.

Same unordered-cross-file caveat as the tombstone channel it extends (#1116's source graph is the eventual foundation).

issues.title: Thread HeadIdentityMap through the seven remaining raw-head-text consumers
issues.body:
Follow-up from #1185.

That issue made semantic tokens and inlay hints resolve a command head's **effective identity** through `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/head_identity.rs` — an offset-keyed `HeadIdentityMap` built from one top-level segmentation, fed by `namespace import`, `interp alias`, `rename`, and built-in-shadowing `proc`, with which commands mutate the table coming from `CommandTableEffect` rather than any spelled command name.

Seven other consumers still resolve **raw head text** and therefore silently disagree with those two once a command has been rebound:

- folding
- formatting
- minify
- the declaration scan
- `interprocedural.rs`
- param-trait inference
- the iRules object-ref walker

`HeadIdentityMap` is the shared pre-pass they need. Threading it through is mechanical, but it touches seven files and their test suites, which is why it was left out of #1185's round rather than half-landed.

## Why it matters

A document that does `interp alias {} myfmt {} format` or `rename format origfmt` now gets correct semantic tokens and inlay hints, while folding, formatting and the declaration scan still treat the old spelling as authoritative. That is an internal inconsistency, and the formatting one is user-visible: a rebound command can be formatted under the grammar of the command it no longer is.

## Acceptance

- Each of the seven consumers resolves its head through `HeadIdentityMap` rather than raw text.
- A `Rebound` head — one whose binding cannot be proven — abstains in each consumer rather than falling back to the written spelling.
- Tests per consumer covering: the aliased form, the renamed form, a built-in shadowed by a user `proc`, and a dynamic binding that must abstain.
- The leading-`::` spellings behave identically to the bare ones, as `qualified_*_classify_like_the_bare_form` already pins for the two consumers that are done.

## Related residuals in the same area

- **snit `installhull ?using TYPE?`** is not modelled. It binds the implicit `hull`, so it has no `name_at` and needs a new `HandleClassSource`-style variant rather than another `HandleBindingSpec` row.
- **Chained bindings do not compose.** `interp alias {} a {} format; rename a b` leaves `b` unresolved rather than resolving to `format`. Currently a documented abstention.
- **`class_is_configurable`** still compares `metaclass == "oo::configurable"`. That is a class identity rather than one of the command-grammar layouts #1185 enumerated, so it was deliberately out of scope, but it is the same "matched by spelling" shape.

issues.title: Cross-file TclOO metaclass classes are invisible: the walk has no workspace class index
issues.body:
Residual from the #1019 tclOO cluster (audit findings idx 96/97).

Classes created through a **locally-defined TclOO metaclass** — `::tk::Megawidget create Name Supers Body` — are recognised when the metaclass is declared in the **same file**: `handle_oo_class_command::user_metaclass_of_command` plus `ManufacturerLayout` resolve the class, its members, and `next` through a 3-hop chain, verified against tclsh 9.0.4.

**Cross-file, the analyser abstains entirely.** The walk is per-file, and `X create Name Supers Body` is indistinguishable from `interp create` or `image create` without knowing that `X` is a metaclass. So when the metaclass lives in another file — which is the real shape in Tk's `library/iconlist.tcl`, and the shape the original audit reported — nothing is recorded and nothing is diagnosed.

This is currently a **deliberate, documented, tested abstention** (`analyser.rs::a_metaclass_defined_in_another_file_abstains_rather_than_guessing`, plus a section in `docs/design/tcloo-mro-lattice.md`). It abstains rather than guessing, which is correct behaviour — but it means real Tk gets nothing from the LSP for these widget classes.

## What closing it needs

The analyser must consult a **workspace class index during the walk**. The cross-document command-resolution lattice builds one, but only *after* the fact, so it is not available at the point the `X create …` call has to be classified. Options worth weighing:

- a cheap pre-pass that collects metaclass declarations workspace-wide before per-file walks, keyed by qualified name;
- promoting metaclass declarations into the existing workspace index and making the walk able to query it, accepting the ordering constraint that introduces;
- deferring classification of unrecognised `X create …` shapes and resolving them in a later pass once the index exists.

Whichever is chosen, the abstention must remain for a genuinely dynamic metaclass name — the current behaviour is right when nothing can be proven, and the fix should narrow it, not remove it.

## Note

One part of the original finding has already dissolved: `references` at `CreateHull` is now at **parity** with the literal `oo::class` control (both return the declaration only). The audit's contrast there was against a baseline that has since changed.

issues.title: Record literal foreach-installed member names once MethodDef can say "signature unknown"
issues.body:
Residual from the #1019 tclOO cluster (audit finding idx 53).

A class whose members are installed reflectively — `constructor {*}[info class constructor …]` plus a `foreach {method …}` installer loop — now correctly marks its member set as a **lower bound** (`ClassDef::member_set_incomplete`, set by `Analyser::member_declaration_is_opaque`), so `$obj options` no longer draws a false W308 on a call tclsh actually executes.

What is still missing: for a **literal** installer such as `foreach m {alpha beta gamma} { method $m {args} {…} }`, the member *names* are statically knowable, but they are deliberately not recorded.

## Why they were not recorded

`MethodDef` has no "signature unknown" state. Recording `alpha`/`beta`/`gamma` would require inventing a parameter list, and an empty one is a fabrication that arity-shaped consumers (E003, signature help, inlay hints) would then treat as authoritative. Abstaining entirely was the honest option available at the time.

## What would close it

Give `MethodDef` a `params_computed`-style flag, mirroring what `ProcDef` already carries. Then the installer's member names can be recorded honestly — visible to the outline, hover, go-to-definition and completion — while every arity-shaped consumer sees that the signature is unknown and abstains rather than checking against a fabricated one.

## Acceptance

- A literal `foreach`-installed member appears in `documentSymbol`, resolves for definition/hover, and is offered in completion.
- Arity diagnostics (E002/E003/E005) abstain for it rather than validating against an invented parameter list.
- A **computed** member name (`method $someVar …` where the value cannot be folded) still leaves the member set incomplete and still abstains, exactly as today.
- The W308 abstention from the current fix stays green — the class surface remains a lower bound even once some names are known.

issues.title: Renaming an ensemble -map target corrupts the dispatch by rewriting the subcommand word
issues.body:
## The hazard

`rename_proc` uses the same `invocation_references_proc` rule as find-references. So renaming a proc that is an ensemble `-map` **target** also rewrites the **subcommand word** at the dispatch site:

```tcl
namespace ensemble create -command ::app::widget -map {show ::app::widget::Show}
proc ::app::widget::Show {} { ... }
puts [::app::widget show]
```

Renaming `::app::widget::Show` → `Display` rewrites `show` → `Display` in the dispatch, producing `::app::widget Display`, which is not a valid subcommand — the `-map` key is an arbitrary name with no required relationship to its target. The rename silently breaks working code.

This is the same failure family as the rename hazards fixed in #1019 (idx 79's untargeted member rename, idx 89's alias-shadowed proc): an edit that looks complete and changes what the program does.

## Why a blanket exclusion is wrong

With `-subcommands` rather than `-map`, the subcommand word **is** the target's tail:

```tcl
namespace ensemble create -command ::app::widget -subcommands {alpha}
proc ::app::widget::alpha {} { ... }
```

Here renaming `alpha` → `beta` **should** rewrite the dispatch word, because the ensemble derives the subcommand from the proc name. Excluding ensemble dispatch sites from rename would break this case.

The two shapes need distinguishing, which means `ensemble_subcommand_targets` has to carry provenance (`-map` versus `-subcommands`) and rename has to gate on it:

- `-map` provenance → rename the target's declaration and its other references, leave the subcommand word alone. If the user's intent was to rename the *subcommand*, that is an edit to the `-map` value, which is a different operation.
- `-subcommands` provenance → current behaviour is correct; rewrite the dispatch word with the declaration.
- Anything dynamic → abstain, consistent with the `-map` built via `[list …]` case, which already records no mapping and leaves the dispatch unattributed.

## History and current exposure

The hazard shipped with the idx 106 fix, for ensembles created in a **lexically nested** shape. PR (pending) for #1019 idx 85 extends the same recording mechanism to the **qualified-proc-homed** shape, which widens the set of affected documents — it does not introduce the mechanism.

The idx 85 work deliberately did not touch `rename.rs` (another change was active in that file) and deliberately did not add a test pinning the current behaviour, since the current behaviour is the bug.

## Acceptance

- `ensemble_subcommand_targets` records provenance.
- Rename gates on it: `-map` targets do not rewrite the subcommand word; `-subcommands` targets do.
- A dynamic map continues to abstain.
- Tests at unit and e2e tier for both provenances in both directions, and — following the precedent set by idx 79 — validate by applying the emitted `WorkspaceEdit` and running the result under `tclsh8.6` and `tclsh9.0`, proving the program still behaves identically.

issues.title: A class made by a cross-file metaclass that was itself made by another file's metaclass resolves to nothing from a call site
issues.body:
## Summary

A class manufactured by a metaclass that was **itself manufactured by another file's metaclass** is not resolvable from a call site in a third file. Its members come back empty.

This is the residual recorded in the #1276 work ("a metaclass itself manufactured by a third file's metaclass resolves only on the next sync round — it converges, it is not a fixpoint"). It was documented in the design notes but never tracked, and it reproduces deterministically, so here it is with the isolation.

## Oracle

Valid Tcl; both interpreters agree.

```tcl
namespace eval ::MC {}
oo::class create ::MC::MetaA { superclass oo::class }
::MC::MetaA create ::MC::MetaB { superclass oo::class }
::MC::MetaB create ::MC::Widget { method go {} { return went } }
set w [::MC::Widget new]
puts [$w go]
```

```
tclsh8.6 (8.6.14) → went
tclsh9.0 (9.0.4)  → went
```

So `::MC::Widget` genuinely has `go`, reached through two levels of metaclass.

## Isolation

Same call shape in every case — `set w [::X::Widget new]` then `puts [$w go]` — with go-to-definition on `go`:

| Case | Layout | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| plain `oo::class` | class in file 1, call in file 2 | **1 location** ✓ |
| 2-level metaclass | `MetaA` in file 1, `Widget` in file 2, call in file 3 | **1 location** ✓ |
| 3-level metaclass, single file | `MetaA`+`MetaB`+`Widget` all in file 1, call in file 2 | **1 location** ✓ |
| **3-level metaclass, cross-file** | `MetaA`, `MetaB`, `Widget` each in its own file, call in a fourth | **0 locations** ✗ |

Neither variable alone breaks it. Chain depth is fine on its own (row 3), and cross-file metaclass resolution is fine on its own (row 2 — that is what #1276 fixed). It is the combination: the *intermediate* metaclass living in a different file from the metaclass that made it.

Deterministic — 2/2 runs, and unchanged whether or not the intermediate file (`b_meta.tcl`) is explicitly opened.

## Partial resolution makes it easy to miss

`documentSymbol` on the file declaring `Widget` **does** report it correctly:

```
=== Symbol Definitions (2 symbols) ===
  Class Widget MC::MetaB (line 1)
    Method go () (line 2)
```

So the class is known where it is written — it is the cross-file member lookup from a *call site* that comes back empty. Anyone checking the outline would conclude this works.

## Reproduction

Three files plus a caller:

```tcl
# a_meta.tcl
namespace eval ::MC {}
oo::class create ::MC::MetaA { superclass oo::class }

# b_meta.tcl
::MC::MetaA create ::MC::MetaB { superclass oo::class }

# c_use.tcl
::MC::MetaB create ::MC::Widget { method go {} { return went } }

# d_call.tcl
set w [::MC::Widget new]
puts [$w go]
```

```bash
python3 .claude/skills/lsp-client/lsp_client.py \
  --also-open a_meta.tcl --also-open b_meta.tcl --also-open c_use.tcl \
  definition d_call.tcl 1 10
```

→ `=== Definition (0 locations) ===`

Swap `b_meta.tcl`'s contents into `a_meta.tcl` (making it a 2-level chain) and the same command returns 1 location.

Verified on `rust` @ 3ccb3fe91, which includes #1276.

## Note on the "converges on the next sync round" claim

The design note says this resolves on a later sync round. That is plausible from the implementation — the workspace class-factory index is published per round, so a factory whose own class only became known this round cannot yet have been used to derive the next one — but the probe above waits for the workspace scan barrier and still gets nothing, so I could not demonstrate the convergence from outside. Worth confirming before relying on it: if it does not in fact converge, the impact is larger than the note implies.

issues.title: `refresh_source_rehoming_locked` never converges for a document `source`d from the global namespace, dropping every `WorkspaceIndex` `Derived` memo on every navigation request
issues.body:
`Backend::refresh_source_rehoming_locked` (`rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs:11560-11627`) never reaches its early return on **any** workspace that `source`s a file from the global namespace — which is the ordinary way to write Tcl, not an edge case. No rename is required, unlike #1298; a plain workspace scan is enough.

Each unconverged pass re-analyses and re-indexes the affected documents, which bumps the `WorkspaceIndex` generation, which drops **every** `Derived` memo on the index. So the whole #1152 memoisation effort is defeated on every navigation request, and the `settled_invocations` view is rebuilt from scratch each time.

Found while fixing #1297 against the #1181 corpus: it is what remained after #1297's stated cause was fixed, and it is the larger of the two effects.

## Root cause — a representation mismatch inside one function

The work queue and the result store disagree about how "no rehoming needed" is spelled.

Queue side (`:11571`):

```rust
for (uri, seeds) in &desired {
    let seeds: Vec<String> = seeds.iter().cloned().collect();
    if recorded.get(uri) != Some(&seeds) {
        work.push((uri.clone(), seeds));
    }
}
```

Store side (`:11620`), after each work item has been re-analysed and re-indexed:

```rust
if seeds == ["::".to_owned()] {
    self.rehomed_source_seeds.lock().await.remove(&uri_s);   // <-- removes
} else {
    self.rehomed_source_seeds.lock().await.insert(uri_s, seeds);
}
```

For a document whose **desired** seed set is exactly `["::"]` — it is `source`d, but only ever from the global namespace — the work item runs and then *removes* the entry instead of recording it. On the next round `recorded.get(uri)` is `None`, which `!= Some(&["::"])`, so the identical document is queued again. Forever.

`work` is therefore never empty, the `return` at `:11583` is never reached, and all four rounds always run, re-analysing and re-indexing on each one.

## Measurements

Release `tcl-lsp-server`, branch `rust` @ `af164d9` plus the #1297 `tcl-lsp-core` fix, Linux x86-64. Corpus: the eight `georgtree` repos from #1181 under one workspace root (113 `.tcl` files), `SpiceGenTcl` @ `b6ee79b5`, `tcl_tools` @ `6be5470f`. Instrumented the round loop and the settled-invocations memo, then issued 12 `textDocument/references` requests plus one `codeLens/resolve`:

```
[probe] rehoming round 0
[probe] rehoming work=4 first=Some(("file:///.../corpus/tcl_tools/test/rfutil.test", ["::"]))
[probe] rehoming round 1
[probe] rehoming work=4 first=Some(("file:///.../corpus/tcl_tools/test/rfutil.test", ["::"]))
[probe] rehoming round 2
[probe] rehoming work=4 first=Some(("file:///.../corpus/tcl_tools/test/rfutil.test", ["::"]))
[probe] rehoming round 3
[probe] rehoming work=4 first=Some(("file:///.../corpus/tcl_tools/test/gnuplotutil.test", ["::"]))
[probe] settled_invocations(follow_links=true) rebuild 1.00191666s
```

…and that whole block repeats identically for **every** subsequent request. The queued seeds are `["::"]` on every item, which is exactly the shape above. Four `.test` files under `tcl_tools/test/` are re-analysed and re-indexed four rounds deep on every navigation request, forever.

The memo rebuild is the user-visible cost: `settled_invocations(follow_links=true)` was rebuilt on all 13 requests at ~1.0 s each. For scale, the `follow_links=false` variant of the same view costs 5.7 ms.

`refresh_source_rehoming` is entered via `rehomed_index_guard` from ten request paths (`:6004`, `:6082`, `:6134`, `:6183`, `:6544`, `:6961`, `:6977`, `:7265`, `:8011`, `:8217`) — references, definition, hover, rename, call hierarchy — and the gate serialises them, so this is a per-request cost on every navigation feature, under a shared lock.

## Relationship to #1297 and #1298

- **#1297** reported `references` / `codeLens/resolve` at 26 s and blamed the `RunOrder::alternatives` fast path. That cause is real and fixing it takes the corpus from 29.0 s to 1.46 s. The residual 1.4 s *on every request* is this bug — with the memo working, requests after the first should be nearly free.
- **#1298** is the same non-convergence reached by a different route (a rename stranding an entry that no cleanup path can reach). Same function, same consequence class, and both want the same invariant written down.

## Minimal repro

```tcl
# a.tcl
source b.tcl
```
```tcl
# b.tcl
proc helper {} {}
```

Open the workspace, then issue any two navigation requests (`textDocument/references`, `definition`, `hover`, …). The second request re-runs all four rehoming rounds instead of early-returning, and re-indexes `b.tcl` again. Contrast with `namespace eval ::ns { source b.tcl }`, which records a `::ns` seed and does converge.

## Suggested shape

Give "no rehoming needed" one canonical representation. Making the queue side agree with the store side's convention — a desired seed set of exactly `["::"]` means "not recorded", filtered out of `desired` before both loops — converges, and the reverse direction still works: a document recorded as `["::ns"]` whose desired set becomes `["::"]` is then absent from the filtered `desired`, so the existing `recorded` loop queues the standalone restore, re-indexes, removes and converges. A document never recorded whose desired set is `["::"]` produces no work, which is correct — the index already holds its standalone analysis from the workspace scan.

The invariant worth stating at the declaration of `rehomed_source_seeds` is that it holds **exactly** the documents whose indexed analysis is re-homed away from the standalone view.

## Regression guards worth having

- Convergence: `a.tcl` with a top-level `source b.tcl`; one `refresh_source_rehoming_locked` call, then assert a second call performs no work. Currently the second call does four rounds.
- The consequence, which is the part with user impact: assert the `WorkspaceIndex` generation is **stable** across two consecutive no-op refreshes, so the `Derived` memos survive. That assertion ties this to #1297 and is the one that would have caught it.
- Mixed shape (`namespace eval ::ns { source b.tcl }` alongside a top-level `source c.tcl`) reaches a fixed point with the re-homed document keeping its `::ns` seed.
- Transition: a document re-homed to `::ns` whose `source` site later moves to global scope ends up standalone, entry removed, and converges.

issues.title: The workspace import-conflict gate does not know about registry builtins: a wildcard `namespace import` binds a name real Tcl refuses to import, giving find-references a false positive on every builtin the source namespace exports
issues.body:
`WorkspaceIndex::defines_command` (`rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/workspace_index.rs:2111-2125`) is the "already exists" side of the non-`-force` `namespace import` conflict rule, and it asks only whether the **workspace** defines a proc or class at that qualified name. It has no idea that `::set`, `::if`, `::puts` or `::tcl::mathop::+` already exist because the *registry* says they do.

Real Tcl refuses such an import outright. So a bare call to a builtin is filed as a reference to — and resolves to — a proc it never reaches.

The single-document tier already gets this right: `definition::resolve_called_proc` (`rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs:3737`) computes `has_builtin` from `ctx.registry` and gates on it. The workspace tier is the one that drifted, which is exactly the kind of two-tier disagreement `exported_at_import_site` / `alias_live_at` / `load_order` were centralised to prevent.

Found while fixing #1297; not a perf issue, so filing separately rather than widening that change.

## Oracle

`tclsh 9.0.4` (built from `core-9-0-4`) and `tclsh 8.6.14`, byte-identical:

```tcl
namespace eval ::Foo { proc set {a b} {return SHADOW}; namespace export set }
namespace import ::Foo::*
#  -> can't import command "set": already exists
namespace origin ::set
#  -> ::set          (the builtin; nothing was installed)

namespace import -force ::Foo::*
namespace origin ::set
#  -> ::Foo::set     (`-force` does replace it)
```

It is not special to the global namespace — the rule is about the target namespace's command table, whatever is in it:

```tcl
namespace eval ::Bar { proc + {a b} {return BAR}; namespace export + }
namespace eval ::tcl::mathop { namespace import ::Bar::* }
#  -> can't import command "+": already exists
```

…and a name that is *not* a builtin still binds normally, which is the behaviour that must not regress:

```tcl
namespace eval ::Baz { proc nonbuiltin {} {return OK}; namespace export nonbuiltin }
namespace import ::Baz::*
namespace origin ::nonbuiltin
#  -> ::Baz::nonbuiltin
```

## Failing test

Drop this into `workspace_index.rs`'s test module — it passes today, and it should not:

```rust
#[test]
fn wildcard_import_must_not_bind_a_name_the_registry_already_defines() {
    let a = analyse(
        "namespace eval ::Foo {\n    proc set {a b} { return SHADOW }\n    namespace export set\n}\n",
    );
    let b = analyse("namespace import ::Foo::*\nset x 1\n");
    let index = WorkspaceIndex::from_documents([("file:///a.tcl", &a), ("file:///b.tcl", &b)]);
    // Real Tcl refused the import, so `set x 1` reaches the builtin and is
    // not a reference to `::Foo::set` at all.
    assert!(index.linked_invocations_of("::Foo::set", "").is_empty());
}
```

Observed (with `analyse` pinned to `tcl9.0`):

```
linked_invocations_of(::Foo::set) = [("file:///b.tcl", "set", 26)]
```

`set x 1` in `b.tcl` is filed as a reference to `::Foo::set`.

## Why it happens

In `WorkspaceIndex::import_hop` (`:3898`) the filter chain is:

```rust
.filter(|row| tcl_syntax::glob::string_match(&row.imp.tail_pattern, word))
.filter(|row| row.exported.covers(word))
.filter(|row| {
    row.imp.forced
        || !(self.defines_command(&tcl_syntax::naming::qualify(ns, word))
            || wci.conflicting_alias_at(ns, &row.imp.source_ns, word, row.site()))
})
```

For `ns = "::"`, `word = "set"`: the `*` pattern matches, `::Foo` really does export `set`, `defines_command("::set")` is false (no *workspace* proc is named `::set`), and no other import conflicts — so the import is treated as installed and the call resolves to `::Foo::set`. The `row.imp.forced` short-circuit is correct and should stay; only the unforced branch is wrong.

## Impact

`linked_invocations_of` backs `textDocument/references`, the reference-count code lenses, and (per #1158) the definition/rename path. The blast radius is proportional to how many builtin names the source namespace exports, so a `namespace export *` next to a proc named after any builtin poisons every bare call of that builtin in the whole workspace. The most likely real-world shapes are the common helper names that are also builtins — `set`, `append`, `split`, `join`, `format`, `time`, `trace`, `load`, `open`, `close`, `read`, `after`, `update`, `variable`, `error`, `info` — and `namespace import ::tcl::mathop::*`, which the #1181 corpus does use.

## Why the fix is registry data, not a name list

Which commands exist is exactly what `tcl-registry` is the source of truth for, and it is dialect- and version-dependent (a Tcl 9 builtin may not be an 8.4 one; iRules and the EDA dialects have their own surfaces). A hardcoded name list in the consumer would be the anti-pattern `AGENTS.md` calls out. The predicate wanted is "does a command exist at this qualified name", answered as `workspace-defined ∪ registry-declared`, evaluated against the importing document's dialect.

## Why it is not a one-line fix

`WorkspaceIndex` has no registry and no dialect. `add_document(uri, &AnalysisResult)` does not carry one — `dialect()` lives on the analyser state (`tcl-compiler/src/analyser/state.rs:1095`), not on `AnalysisResult` — so there is nothing to look up `registry_for_dialect` with. Options, roughly in increasing blast radius:

1. **A workspace-level setter on the index**, mirroring the existing `set_source_resolver` / `SourceResolver` precedent (`:1621`, `:1637`). Smallest change and follows a pattern already there, but assumes one dialect per workspace, which is wrong for a mixed workspace (iRules + Tcl in one folder).
2. **Record the dialect per document** at `add_document` time. Correct for mixed workspaces; changes a public API with many call sites.
3. **Put the dialect on `AnalysisResult`.** Most faithful — the analyser already knows it — but the widest blast radius, in the compiler crate.

(2) or (3) is the right answer if mixed-dialect workspaces matter here; (1) is defensible as a first step if they do not.

## Related surfaces worth covering in the same change

- The **exact**-import twin: `live_command_links` (`:2061`) applies its own "already holds" test for `namespace import ::src::p` and has the same blind spot.
- `workspace_command_exists_for_call` (`:3711`) already takes a `has_builtin` flag *from its caller* (`tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs:6852` computes `registry.get(...).is_some()`), which is a third place the same fact is plumbed a fourth way. Worth unifying onto one predicate while fixing this.
- A `rename ::set {}` recorded in the index genuinely deletes the builtin and would then let the import succeed. The index already records `command_deletions`, so the honest predicate is "exists *at the import's position*", not merely "exists" — the same timeline treatment the export gate already gets.

## Suggested test matrix

- **TP** — source namespace exports a builtin name, unforced import: the bare call is *not* a reference to the exported proc (the assertion above).
- **TN** — same shape with `-force`: the call *is* a reference to the exported proc (`namespace origin` → `::Foo::set`, oracle above).
- **TN** — source exports a non-builtin name: still binds, unchanged.
- **FP guard** — a *sub*-namespace target (`namespace eval ::Bar { namespace import ::Foo::* }` where `::Bar::set` is not a builtin): must still bind, because only `::` holds the builtin.
- **Ensemble/`::tcl` surface** — importing into `::tcl::mathop` over `+`.
- **Dialect sensitivity** — a name that is a builtin in one supported dialect/version and not another must be gated per dialect, not globally.

issues.title: A `rename`d metaclass command manufactures nothing — classes made through the new name are invisible
issues.body:
## Summary

`rename` a metaclass's command and the classes it subsequently manufactures are not recorded. The class-factory record (#1276) is keyed on the name the metaclass was *created* with; nothing carries it across a `rename`, so `NewName create Widget {…}` is treated as an unproved factory call and abstains.

Single-file, so this is unrelated to cross-file chaining or to #1296.

## Oracle

Valid Tcl — `rename` moves the class's command, and the class keeps working through its new name.

```tcl
namespace eval ::R {}
oo::class create ::R::M { superclass oo::class }
rename ::R::M ::R::Mk
::R::Mk create ::R::W { method go {} { return went } }
puts [[::R::W new] go]     ;# -> went
```

## Isolation

Go-to-definition on `go` in `puts [$w go]`, one file:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| metaclass created as `::R::Mk`, used as `::R::Mk` | **1 location** ✓ |
| metaclass created as `::R::M`, `rename`d to `::R::Mk`, used as `::R::Mk` | **0 locations** ✗ |

Only the `rename` differs.

## Reproduction

```tcl
namespace eval ::R {}
oo::class create ::R::M { superclass oo::class }
rename ::R::M ::R::Mk
::R::Mk create ::R::W { method go {} { return went } }
set w [::R::W new]
puts [$w go]
```

```bash
python3 .claude/skills/lsp-client/lsp_client.py \
  --server-dir /path/to/fixture --server-bin target/debug/tcl-lsp-server \
  definition r1.tcl 5 10
```

→ `=== Definition (0 locations) ===`. Delete the `rename` line and create the class as `::R::Mk` directly → **1 location**.

Verified on `claude/tickets-1293-1296-registry-wpvi21` at 0e49243.

## Why it matters

`rename` is a first-class Tcl mechanism and the repo already models it elsewhere — there is command-alias/rename tracking (`docs/design/contracts/command-alias-resolution.md`, `commandAliasTracking` tests). The class-factory index simply does not participate in it. The same question probably applies to `interp alias` and to a metaclass reached through an ensemble, neither of which I tested.

## Suggested direction

The factory record lives on the metaclass's `ClassDef::factory` keyed by qualified name, and `ClassFactoryIndex` is a `name -> ClassFactory` map. Rename tracking already resolves a command's current name to its original; the factory lookup (`class_factory_for_command`) should go through that same resolution rather than matching the literal head text. Per AGENTS.md this stays registry/analyser data — no special-casing `rename` by name in a consumer.

issues.title: A TclOO object created by name (`C create obj`) resolves no members — `obj badmethod` is silent where `[C new]` gives W308
issues.body:
`ClassName create objName` is the more common of TclOO's two construction forms, but the object-method dispatch resolver models only the handle form. A call on the named object binds to no class, so every member-aware feature abstains on it.

The gap is recorded in the resolver's own golden fixture table, `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/semantic_tokens.rs:8197`, under the heading "not yet modelled, but abstains safely (flip to `Resolve` when done)":

```rust
(
    "named_object", // TODO(phase-3): resolve via created_instance_commands
    "oo::class create C { method mrun {} {} }\nC create obj\nobj mrun\n",
    "mrun",
    2,
    Abstain,
),
```

The index it needs already exists and is already populated for this shape — `AnalysisResult::created_instance_commands` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/commands.rs:3560`, `:3578`, `:3615`, `:3689`) — so the residual is wiring the dispatch resolver to it, not building new analysis.

## Reproduction

Handle form, `handle.tcl`:

```tcl
oo::class create C {
    method mrun {} { return 1 }
}
set h [C new]
$h nosuchmethod
```

Named form, `named.tcl` — identical class, identical bad call:

```tcl
oo::class create C {
    method mrun {} { return 1 }
}
C create obj
obj nosuchmethod
```

```console
$ cargo run --bin tcl -- diag handle.tcl
handle.tcl:5:4: warning W308     Unknown method 'nosuchmethod' on class '::C'
diagnostics=1 across 1 input(s)

$ cargo run --bin tcl -- diag named.tcl
no diagnostics
diagnostics=0 across 1 input(s)
```

W308 is the cheapest observable, but the abstention is in the shared dispatch resolver, so the same object loses member completion, hover, go-to-definition, and the member semantic-token class.

## Relationship to the open metaclass cluster

This is the plain-class base case of the same resolver, distinct from the metaclass work in #1303 (`unknown`-dispatched constructor), #1304, #1305, and #1306. The fixture immediately below it (`snit_named_object`) already resolves, because the signature scan records snit types as classes and the handle then types normally — so the named-constructor shape is reachable, just not for `oo::class`.

issues.title: `[self] methodName` (TclOO's own self-dispatch idiom) resolves nowhere — 0 references, 0 definitions, mis-highlighted as a string
issues.body:
## Summary

TclOO's `self` command, called with no arguments to return the current object's own command name, is a completely ordinary same-object dispatch idiom: `[self] methodName` inside a method body calls another method on the same object. It is not recognised by any candidate-receiver-class resolver in the LSP, so every consumer that resolves object dispatch abstains on it — go-to-definition, find-references (and therefore the reference-count code lens), and semantic-token method classification.

Reported by @nico-robert against v2.1.16 in two comments on #1181 that look unrelated on the surface but share one root cause:
- "in version 2.1.16, the highlighting does not work correctly for certain Tcl commands (VSCode)" — the `[self] methodName` call colours as a plain string, not a method.
- "in version 2.1.16, `animTick method` shows 0 references (VSCode)" — with a full repro, reproduced below.

(A third report in the same thread, "it takes a little while to display the number of references", is a **separate, already-fixed** issue — #1297, fixed in #1308. v2.1.16 predates that fix; the pre-fix benchmark in #1297 measured 9.38–9.50s on 2.1.16, and the fixed version measures 0.43s on the first request / 0.00s cached on the same corpus. Not part of this ticket.)

## Oracle

Valid, idiomatic Tcl — `self` with no arguments returning the current object and dispatching on it is documented TclOO behaviour (`oo::object` / `self` command, Tcl 8.6+).

```tcl
oo::class create test {
    method animTick {} {
        return {}
    }
    method anim {} {
        [self] animTick
        return {}
    }
}
set t [test new]
$t anim
```

`[self] animTick` calls `test`'s `animTick` method on the current object — no different in effect from `my animTick` (which the LSP already resolves) or `$t animTick` from outside the class.

## Isolation

Same fixture, same call site (`[self] animTick` on line 6), three different resolvers:

| Provider | Result |
|---|---|
| Semantic tokens on `animTick` at 5:15 | colours as `string`, not `method` |
| Go-to-definition on `animTick` at 5:15 | **0 locations** |
| Reference-count code lens on the `animTick` declaration (1:11) | **0 references** |
| Find-references on the `animTick` declaration | 1 location — the declaration itself only, no call site |

Control, same class, dispatch via `my` instead of `[self]` on an otherwise identical body — resolves correctly on all four (not included here since it's the existing, working baseline `is_self_dispatch_keyword`/`MethodDispatchKind::SelfDispatch` covers, per #1050).

## Reproduction

```tcl
# selfref.tcl
oo::class create test {
    method animTick {} {
        return {}
    }
    method anim {} {
        [self] animTick

        return {}
    }
}

set t [test new]
$t anim
```

```bash
python3 .claude/skills/lsp-client/lsp_client.py --server-dir <fixture-dir> --server-bin target/debug/tcl-lsp-server semantic-tokens selfref.tcl
# 5:15 "animTick" classified as `string`

python3 .claude/skills/lsp-client/lsp_client.py --server-dir <fixture-dir> --server-bin target/debug/tcl-lsp-server definition selfref.tcl 5 15
# === Definition (0 locations) ===

python3 .claude/skills/lsp-client/lsp_client.py --server-dir <fixture-dir> --server-bin target/debug/tcl-lsp-server code-lens selfref.tcl
# 1:11-1:19  '0 references'  [tcl-lsp.showReferences, 3 args]
```

Deterministic, single-file, no workspace/cross-file component.

## Why it matters

`[self] methodName` isn't an exotic shape — it's the TclOO-native way to spell "call my own method", used in exactly the kind of code (widget/animation callback dispatch) `nico-robert`'s report came from. Because go-to-definition, references, and highlighting all abstain the same way, the failure reads as "this method is unused" rather than "the LSP doesn't understand this call form" — the same "partial resolution makes it easy to miss" trap #1296 recorded for the metaclass cluster.

## Suggested direction

#1050 already established the registry-driven pattern for exactly this class of problem: `tcl_registry::MethodDispatchKind` (`SelfDispatch` for `my`, `NextChain` for `next`/`nextto`), queried via `method_dispatch_keyword_in`/`is_self_dispatch_keyword` in `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs`, rather than hardcoding `"my"`/`"next"` string literals in each consumer. `self` (TclOO's own introspection command, zero-arg form) was never added to that classification — this ticket is closing that gap, not inventing a new mechanism.

Two things worth checking before choosing the exact shape of the fix:
1. Whether a `[self]`-headed command substitution can share the *same* registry lookup as the bareword `my` case (both mean "the enclosing class"), or needs a distinct `MethodDispatchKind` variant because it's syntactically a command substitution (`TokenType::Cmd`) rather than a bareword dispatch prefix.
2. `self` takes an optional first argument (`self class`, `self next`, `self object`, `self method` inside `oo::define` bodies for the sub-command forms already handled elsewhere in `semantic_tokens.rs`) — the zero-arg form (`[self]` alone, or `[self object]` explicitly) is the one that means "return my own command name and dispatch through it"; the fix must not confuse this with the already-handled `self`-as-definer-keyword shapes (`semantic_tokens.rs:3076`) or misfire on `self class`/`self next` chains.

Consumers needing the fix, all downstream of the same candidate-receiver-class resolution:
- `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/semantic_tokens.rs`'s `insert_object_method_overrides` (`TokenType::Cmd` branch — currently checks `constructor_class_of_head`/`user_constructor_class_of_head`, neither of which recognises `self`)
- The analyser/LSP go-to-definition and find-references resolvers in `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs`

Per AGENTS.md this must stay registry data — no `match cmd_name == "self"` special-casing added directly to a consumer walker; go through the same `method_dispatch_keyword_in` registry query #1050 established.

issues.title: W308 (unknown method) doesn't fire for `[self] nosuchmethod` — the analyser's own dispatch resolution doesn't know `[self]` either
`runtime/rust` diverges from C Tcl on `namespace eval` + `append` to a global, and `dict lappend` onto a non-dict silently succeeds
issues.body:
## Summary

Two `runtime/rust` divergences from C Tcl, both found by the new `runtime/rust` ↔ `tclsh` differential fuzzer arm added for #1313, and both hand-verified against `tclsh` rather than taken on the fuzzer's word.

### 1. `namespace eval` + `append` writes the wrong variable

```tcl
set i foo
namespace eval n1 { append i baz }
```

- **C Tcl:** appends to the existing **global** `i`.
- **`runtime/rust`:** creates a fresh **namespace** variable `n1::i`.

**`tcl-vm` has the same bug.** That is the significant part: it is exactly why the pre-existing `tcl-vm` ↔ `tclsh` pairing could not see it — both of this project's own backends agree with each other and disagree with C Tcl. This is precisely the blind spot #1313 was filed about, demonstrated on its first real campaign.

### 2. `dict lappend` onto a non-dict silently succeeds

`dict lappend` against a value that is not a dict should raise; `runtime/rust` accepts it silently.

## How they were found

```
tcl-fuzz --tclsh /usr/bin/tclsh8.6 --runtime-rust …/run_script \
  run --subject runtime-rust --reference tclsh --iterations 200 --seed 90000
→ total 200 | matched 192 | findings: stdout 1 | status 7
```

## Caveats — please read before triaging the rest

- **The reference oracle was `tclsh8.6`, not 9.0.** No `tclsh9.0` was available and disk ruled out building one. The two divergences above were hand-verified and are real; the **other six findings from that run are uncharacterised** and some may reflect 8.6-vs-9.0 semantics rather than `runtime/rust` bugs. They should not be treated as a bug list until re-run against 9.0.
- `runtime-rust` needs **libtommath ≥ 1.3.0** or most of `expr`/math is `cfg`'d out and the arm is mostly noise. The expected `tmp/tcl9.0.4/libtommath` was absent; v1.3.0 was cloned into gitignored `tmp/` and the step documented in the `fuzz-findings` skill.

## Suggested order

Fix (1) in both `runtime/rust` and `tcl-vm` — they share the defect, and until one of them is right the `tcl-vm` ↔ `runtime/rust` pair cannot detect it either.

issues.title: W308 never fires for bareword `my nosuchmethod` — the self-dispatch keyword is not recorded as a dispatch site at all
issues.body:
## Summary

W308 ("unknown method") does not fire for the bareword TclOO self-dispatch form:

```tcl
oo::class create test {
    method animTick {} { return {} }
    method anim {} {
        my nosuchmethod          ;# expected W308 — actual: no diagnostic
    }
}
```

Found while fixing #1324 (`[self] nosuchmethod`), verified empirically against a built server and then confirmed by code inspection. Deliberately left out of scope there, since #1324's acceptance criteria were the `[self]` / `[self object]` spellings.

This is a **wider gap than #1324 described**. `my` is the most common way to spell a same-object dispatch in TclOO — considerably more common than `[self] method` — so this is likely the larger real-world false negative of the two.

## Root cause

`record_bareword_instance_dispatch_site` is the only place a bareword command head becomes a dispatch site, and it only recognises an instance command bound by `CLASS create NAME` (the #1312 shape). It never recognises `my`, so the method word after it is never validated against the enclosing class and W308's producer is never reached.

Note the asymmetry this leaves after #1322/#1324, which is what makes it worth fixing rather than tolerating:

| Spelling | Resolves for nav/highlight | Fires W308 |
|---|---|---|
| `$obj method` | yes | yes |
| `Class create obj; obj method` | yes (#1312) | yes |
| `[self] method` / `[self object] method` | yes (#1322) | yes (#1324) |
| **`my method`** | **yes** (long-standing) | **no** |

So `my` is now the only self-dispatch spelling that navigates and highlights correctly but is never diagnosed — the inverse of the situation #1324 just fixed.

## Suggested direction

The registry already answers this without any name matching: `CommandRegistry::method_dispatch_keyword(head) == Some(MethodDispatchKind::SelfDispatch)` identifies `my` (issue #1050), and `tcl-lsp-core`'s `definition.rs` / `references.rs` / `semantic_tokens.rs` already use exactly that to resolve `my` for navigation. The analyser's dispatch-site recording needs the same query.

The enclosing-class lookup needed to validate the method word already exists too — `Analyser::enclosing_class_at_offset` was factored out in #1324 for precisely this purpose and is reusable as-is.

Per AGENTS.md this must stay a registry query; no `head == "my"` literal in the walker.

## Acceptance

Paired TP/FP tests mirroring #1324's: `my nosuchmethod` fires W308; `my animTick` (a real method) stays silent; and the existing `my`-dispatch navigation tests must keep passing.

issues.title: Diagnostics ignore the cross-file symbol index: W123 calls a workspace proc "Unknown command", and arity (E002/E003) never fires for it
issues.body:
Reported by @nico-robert on #1181 ([comment](https://github.com/bitwisecook/tcl-lsp/issues/1181#issuecomment-5221018709)) as "there is no check to see if there are too many or too few arguments in the command", on v2.1.16 / VS Code.

## The check exists and works — in one file only

nico's minimal repro **does** produce the diagnostic on current `rust` HEAD:

```tcl
proc test {a b c} {
    set result [expr {$a + $b}]
    return $result
}
test 1 2
```

```
ERROR  E002  4:0-4:8  Too few arguments for 'test': expected at least 3, got 2
```

So E002/E003 are not missing. What's missing is that they only see procs defined **in the same file**. In any real multi-file project — which is every project in the #1181 corpus, and nico's own — the proc lives elsewhere and no arity check ever happens.

## The isolation that identifies the root cause

Two files in one workspace, no `source`, nothing clever:

```tcl
# deflib.tcl
proc libtest {a b c} { return [expr {$a + $b + $c}] }
```
```tcl
# plaincaller.tcl
libtest 1 2
```

| request at `libtest` | result |
|---|---|
| `textDocument/definition` | **resolves** → `deflib.tcl 0:5-0:12` |
| `textDocument/publishDiagnostics` | **`W123 Unknown command 'libtest'`**, and no E002 |

The workspace index holds `libtest` — navigation proves it. The diagnostics path does not consult that index, so it concludes the command is unknown and, having no signature, cannot arity-check it.

This holds with the defining file **explicitly open** (`--also-open`), so it is not a scan-completion artifact.

## Why the "no arity check" symptom follows

W123 and the arity check are downstream of the same lookup. Once the command is deemed unknown there is no parameter list to compare against, so E002/E003 abstain — correctly, given their input. Fixing the lookup should restore both.

Note the second-order consequence: **W123 currently false-positives on every cross-file call in the workspace.** It is severity `hint`, which is why this has been quiet rather than loud, but on the corpus projects it will be firing on a large fraction of all call sites.

## Repro commands

```
python3 .claude/skills/lsp-client/lsp_client.py \
  --server-dir <fixture-dir> --server-bin target/debug/tcl-lsp-server \
  diagnostics <fixture-dir>/plaincaller.tcl      # → W123, no E002
python3 .claude/skills/lsp-client/lsp_client.py \
  --server-dir <fixture-dir> --server-bin target/debug/tcl-lsp-server \
  definition  <fixture-dir>/plaincaller.tcl 0 2  # → resolves
```

Per the trap documented in [this #1181 comment](https://github.com/bitwisecook/tcl-lsp/issues/1181#issuecomment-5216283434), `--server-dir` must point at the **fixture** directory, not the repo — otherwise every cross-file lookup fails for an unrelated reason and the result looks like this bug. The `definition` control above is what rules that out here: if the fixture were mis-scoped, definition would fail too, and it doesn't.

## Acceptance

- The cross-file control resolves: no W123 for `libtest`, and `libtest 1 2` reports E002.
- Arity abstains — rather than misfires — where it should: unknown commands, dynamic providers (`namespace unknown`, dynamic `namespace import`, a user `proc unknown`), `args`-tailed and defaulted parameter lists.
- A regression test for the two-file shape specifically, since the existing single-file coverage passes today and would not have caught this.

issues.title: Hover on a proc definition name returns null unless the proc is called somewhere (regressed in v2.1.1, still at HEAD)
issues.body:
Hovering a procedure's **definition name** returns nothing unless that procedure is called somewhere. Regressed in **v2.1.1** and still present at `origin/rust` `b1cacf1a9`.

This hits exported library APIs hardest: a package defines procs that its *consumers* call, so nothing in the defining file references them, and hovering any of them in their own file gives no signature and no doc comment.

Found by the cross-version benchmark (#1335) — the `nav.hover` check reports 6 results on v2.1.0 and 0 on every version after.

## Minimal repro — 4 lines, deterministic

`b.tcl`, proc never called:

```tcl
proc plainProc {a b} {
    return [expr {$a + $b}]
}
```

`c.tcl`, byte-identical plus one call site:

```tcl
proc plainProc {a b} {
    return [expr {$a + $b}]
}
plainProc 1 2
```

Hover at **line 0, character 5** (the `p` of `plainProc`, i.e. the definition name) in each:

| file | v2.1.0 | HEAD `b1cacf1a9` |
|---|---|---|
| `b.tcl` — no call site | signature + docs | **null** |
| `c.tcl` — one call site | signature + docs | signature + docs |

`b.tcl` at HEAD is **0/10 non-null** over ten fresh server launches; v2.1.0 is **10/10**. Not a race.

Driver (uses the repo's own `.claude/skills/lsp-client`, i.e. its stock `initialize` / `open_document`, so this is not an exotic client):

```python
import sys
from pathlib import Path
sys.path.insert(0, "/path/to/tcl-lsp/.claude/skills/lsp-client")
import lsp_client as L
srv, target, ln, col = sys.argv[1], Path(sys.argv[2]).resolve(), int(sys.argv[3]), int(sys.argv[4])
c = L.LspClient(str(target.parent), launch_cmd=[srv]); c.start(); L.initialize(c)
uri, _ = L.open_document(c, str(target))
r = c.send_request("textDocument/hover", {"textDocument": {"uri": uri},
    "position": {"line": ln, "character": col}}, timeout=30)
print("null" if r is None else "OK")
c.shutdown()
```

```
python3 p.py <server> b.tcl 0 5   # null on >= 2.1.1
python3 p.py <server> c.tcl 0 5   # OK
```

## Real-world case

`georgtree/tcl_tools/mathutil.tcl` (pinned in `scripts/perf/MANIFEST.toml`) defines six `namespace export`ed procs and calls none of them in-file. All six hover as `null` from v2.1.1 onward, and all six return full markdown on v2.1.0:

```
14:5 ::mathutil::trapz    '```tcl\nproc ::mathutil::trapz {args} {...}\n```\n\nDoes trapezoidal integration of '
35:5 ::mathutil::cumtrapz '```tcl\nproc ::mathutil::cumtrapz {args} {...}\n```\n\nDoes trapezoidal integration '
...
=> 6 non-null hovers          (v2.1.0)
=> 0 non-null hovers          (v2.1.1 … HEAD)
```

## Bisect

`v2.1.0` → OK, `v2.1.1` → null, and null at every version after (spot-checked 2.1.1, 2.1.5, 2.1.9, 2.1.11, 2.1.12, 2.1.14, 2.1.16 and `origin/rust` `b1cacf1a9`). The window is the 120 commits in `v2.1.0..v2.1.1`.

## What I ruled out

* **Not the workspace.** `mathutil.tcl` alone in an otherwise empty directory fails identically, as does its 10-file package. Not a scan or cross-file-index effect.
* **Not namespace qualification.** Unqualified `plainProc` fails just as readily as `::mathutil::trapz`.
* **Not the wildcard import.** `mathutil.tcl` has `namespace import ::tcl::mathop::*`; adding one to the minimal file changes nothing, and removing it does not fix it.
* **Not the client.** Reproduced with the repo's own `lsp-client` skill flow. `hover_smoke` passes at HEAD because its fixture happens to call the proc it hovers.
* **Not go-to-definition.** `textDocument/definition` returns the right target at the *same offsets* where hover returns null (`nav.definition` = 6 results on `mathutil.tcl` at HEAD). So `proc_declaration_sites` is populated and the offset is recognised as a declaration.

## Where I got to on the cause

`proc_hover_at` (`rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/hover.rs:349`) already handles this case correctly and does not depend on call sites — its first action is:

```rust
// A proc's own declaration name (`proc greet …`) is an argument of
// `proc`, so the head gate below would refuse it; it is answered here,
// mirroring how `definition()` consults `proc_declaration_sites` before
// its own call resolution.
if let Some(proc_def) = crate::definition::proc_declaration_at(analysis, cursor_offset) {
    return Some(Hover::markdown(proc_hover_text(proc_def)));
}
```

and `proc_declaration_at` (`definition.rs:1815`) is a pure span-cover test over `all_procs` / `proc_declaration_sites`, with no notion of references.

Since go-to-definition succeeds at the same offset, that data is present. So the fault is almost certainly that **`proc_hover_at` is never reached** — one of the earlier *definitive* gates in `hover_impl` (`hover.rs:583`) returns `None` first. The candidates, in the order they run, are:

1. `variable_position_hover` returning `PositionHover::Abstain` (`hover.rs:600`) — `Abstain` is an explicit `return None`.
2. `offset_is_in_parameter_list` (`hover.rs:621`).
3. `namespace_cell_at` (`hover.rs:635`) — definitive: it returns `namespace_hover_text(...).map(...)`, so a `None` text becomes a `None` hover and everything below is skipped.

Why the presence of a call site elsewhere in the file would flip any of those is the part I have not explained, and it is the thing to instrument first.

## Impact

Hover on a definition is one of the most-used LSP features, and "define a proc, hover it" is the first thing a user does. It currently works only after the proc has a caller, which is backwards: the moment you most want the signature is while writing the definition and before any call exists.

issues.title: Prove live dispatch stability in world SSA before enabling stable-call CSE
issues.body:
## Summary

Add a world-SSA proof of live-dispatch stability/absence so common-subexpression elimination (CSE) can safely reuse registry-declared stable Tcl calls and emit O105.

The semantic-diagnostics work introduces registry-owned `ResultStability`, typed `dispatch_dependencies`, and a generic GVN candidate gate. It deliberately abstains at the use site because world SSA currently versions trace, binding, namespace, alias, and interpreter-policy domains without proving their contents or the absence of observers.

## Why this is required

A call can be referentially transparent with respect to its result and still be observable through Tcl's mutable dispatch machinery. For example:

```tcl
proc observe {command operation} {
    puts "$command $operation"
}
trace add execution llength {enter leave} observe

set first  [llength $items]
set second [llength $items]
```

Eliminating the second `llength` changes the execution-trace callbacks and is unsound. Equivalent hazards exist around `rename`, `unknown`, aliases, namespace ensembles, safe/sub-interpreter policy, and dynamically installed commands.

## Required design

- Add a generic world-state contents/absence lattice for the dispatch domains named by `InvocationFacts::dispatch_dependencies`.
- Produce a typed site proof that every dependency relevant to a GVN candidate is stable and has no live observer/interceptor that would make reuse observable.
- Carry the proof through control-flow joins, loops, exceptional edges, and widening. Unknown/dynamic transitions must invalidate precision conservatively.
- Model literal add/remove/rename/alias/ensemble/interpreter transitions from registry `StateTransitionDescriptor` data. Do not match command names in the optimiser, analyser, or LSP.
- Account for execution traces and command traces separately from variable traces.
- Account for command bindings, `unknown` resolution, namespace imports/exports/ensembles, aliases, safe-interpreter hidden commands, and child-interpreter policy.
- Incorporate `ReadsVersionedWorld` domains into the GVN key before enabling versioned-world calls.
- Keep `Volatile` and unresolved/dynamic calls ineligible.
- Preserve Tcl 8.4–9.1 and dialect gates from the registry.

## Acceptance criteria

- Repeated stable, closed calls such as `llength` and `format` can emit O105 only when the site proof is complete.
- The same calls do not emit O105 when an applicable execution/command trace or mutable dispatch interceptor may be live.
- Literal removal of the last applicable trace can restore eligibility on the success edge; dynamic removal must abstain.
- Binding/alias/`unknown`/namespace/interpreter mutations invalidate only the relevant proof domains.
- Joins are sound: a trace or interceptor present on either predecessor prevents reuse after the join.
- Tests cover loops, abrupt control flow, aliases, renamed commands, namespace ensembles, safe/sub-interpreters, and dynamic `eval`/package/source barriers.
- O105 code actions remain unavailable unless the proof is strong enough for the action's advertised safety.
- Registry-sweep/architecture tests prove no command-specific consumer branches were introduced.
- Design documentation explains the lattice, invalidation rules, proof object, and conservative abstentions.

## Non-goals

- Encoding Tcl command names or trace operation names in GVN.
- Treating result purity alone as proof that a call is observationally removable.
- Re-enabling CSE with a broad “no trace seen in this file” heuristic. Workspace, package, sourced-file, and interpreter state must be represented by the proof contract.

issues.title: O102/O104/O119/O125/O130 ignore the dynamic-name barrier that O109 and SCCP consult, miscompiling any proc containing `set $name …`
issues.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. Same shape as that PR: one semantic question, two answers, only some consumers migrated — except here the unmigrated consumers emit **quick-fix-applicable rewrites**, so the divergence is a miscompile rather than a missed optimisation.

## The question

"Can an access through a computed variable name reach this variable?"

## The modern path

`crate::dynamic_names::DynamicNameBarrier` (`dynamic_names.rs:143-155`) — a typed `{writes, destroys, reads}` record, built per function by `dynamic_name_barrier` (`dynamic_names.rs:404`) and stored on every `FunctionUnit` (`compilation_unit.rs:303`, populated at `:630`). Its contract: *after a dynamic write, any name may be defined; after a dynamic read, any store may have been observed.*

Consumers that respect it:
- O109/O126/O108 elimination — `elimination.rs:446`, `if fu.dynamic_names.reads { return HashSet::new(); }`
- SCCP existence-branch folding — `sccp.rs:1152`, `:1176`, `:1198`
- analyser dataflow diagnostics — `analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs:282`, `:561`, `:1038`

## The legacy path

Four sibling passes answer the same question by hand from IR text and never read `fu.dynamic_names`:

- **O104/O130 chain fold** — `chain_fold.rs:73`, `:96-104` (`protected_vars` unions only `analyse_var_observability` + `cross_event_vars`). Worse, `classify_write` (`chain_fold.rs:241-252`) normalises the *dynamic* target word `$name` to the plain name `name`, so `chain_fold.rs:345` walks the accumulation chain straight past `set $name …`.
- **O125 code sinking** — `code_sinking.rs:57-62`, and `statement_uses_var` (`:579-584`) whose only evidence is a textual `$var` scan; it returns `false` even for `Statement::Barrier` (`:584`).
- **O102 load forwarding** — `propagation.rs:223-241`. Its doc (`:199-222`) enumerates its guards as `is_externally_mutable` + `has_intervening_barrier` and argues "a plain proc-local variable … cannot be touched by an intervening call to any other proc". A dynamic `set $name …` in the *same frame* is exactly what that argument misses.
- **O119 multi-set packing** — `pattern_recognition.rs:122-153`.

## Reproducers

Three demonstrated miscompiles on the current build (`tcl opt`):

```tcl
# 1 — O130. Returns "zzz b" before, "a b" after.
proc f {name} { set acc {}; lappend acc a; set $name zzz; lappend acc b; return $acc }
#   rewritten to: set $name zzz; set acc {a b}; return $acc

# 2 — O102 + O109. `f x` prints 2 before, 1 after.
proc f {name} { set x 1; set $name 2; puts $x }
#   rewritten to: set $name 2; puts 1

# 3 — O125. `f flag 1` prints "zzz" before, "hello" after.
proc f {name c} { set flag hello; if {$c} { set $name zzz; puts $flag } }
#   `set flag hello;` inserted immediately before `puts $flag`, after the dynamic write
```

In case 3 the paired O125 delete is separately suppressed by `manager.rs:238 drop_def_elims_resurrected_by_replacements`, so the emitted rewrite is insert-only — which is what makes it visible rather than silently correct.
