All three are surfaced in the editor as applicable quick fixes, not hints.

## Cleanup

Narrow version: a shared helper on `FunctionUnit` (`fn dynamic_barrier_blocks_value_motion(&self) -> bool`) consulted by `chain_fold::protected_vars`, `code_sinking::run`, `propagation::run_load_forwarding`, and `pattern_recognition` before emitting.

Precise version: make `chain_fold::classify_write` and `code_sinking::sinkable_assignment` return `None` for a non-literal variable word, and fold `dynamic_names.writes` into the `escaping` set built at `propagation.rs:238-241` — matching what `sccp_with_builtin_folds` already does with `trace.traced_variables`.

**This will change user-visible output:** O102/O104/O119/O125/O130 stop firing in any proc containing a computed variable name.

**Scale:** four call sites plus one shared helper; no cross-crate change.

issues.title: Variable-trace observability has three implementations; O109/O126 and O104/O130 use spelling-sensitive scans and delete stores to traced globals
issues.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. The canonical fact is `::`-canonicalised *on purpose*; two of the three consumers key on the surface spelling instead, so soundness depends on how the user wrote the variable.

## The modern path

`Module::traced_variables` + `Module::has_dynamic_variable_trace` (`ir.rs:1502`, `:1507`), populated at lowering by `populate_trace_facts` / `populate_variable_trace_facts` (`lowering/mod.rs:3427-3450`, `:3607-3633`). Registry-driven (`Traits::ESTABLISHES_VARIABLE_TRACE` + `ArgRole::VarWrite`, no hardcoded `trace` grammar), covering top level, every proc, every `body_unit`, every TclOO method — and `::`-canonicalised so a top-level `set x 5` matches `trace add variable ::x …`. The comment at `lowering/mod.rs:3618-3622` says exactly that.

The field doc at `ir.rs:1488-1501` names the intended consumers: *"the propagation optimiser (O102 load-forwarding) **and dead-store elimination** must never treat a use of one of these names as equivalent to its last literal assignment."*

Threaded as `sccp::TraceInputs` (`sccp.rs:295-314`) and consumed by SCCP (`:395-398`, `:448`), O102 (`propagation.rs:123-132`, `:238-248`), and taint (`taint.rs:2134-2135`).

## The legacy paths

Dead-store elimination never received it.

- `elimination.rs:456` builds `scope_aliases` from `scan_scope_aliases` (`:1282-1310`), a per-CFG walk inserting the trace target's **raw argument text** (`aliases.insert(t.clone())`, `:1303`). The O109/O126 gate at `:537` compares that against the chain's normalised name. `manager.rs:482` builds the same set for the O109 propagation-coupling removal, tested at `:523`.
- `chain_fold.rs:96-104` (`protected_vars`) uses `var_observability::analyse_var_observability(…).escaping_var_names()` — single-function, likewise keyed on the spelled name.
- A **third** implementation, `scan_module_traced_globals` (`elimination.rs:1322-1357`), scans the whole module but only for `::`-qualified literal targets. It lives in the optimiser; its only caller is the **analyser** (`analyser/diagnostics.rs:454-455`, feeding W211/W220 suppression). No optimiser pass calls it.

## Reproducer

```tcl
proc onw {a b c} { puts trace }
trace add variable ::g write ::onw
set g 1
set g 2
puts $g
```

`tcl opt` emits **O109 "Eliminate dead store"** and deletes `set g 1`, so the write trace fires once instead of twice. `tcl diag` on the same file emits **W220 "Assignment to 'g' is never read"**.

Change the stores to `set ::g 1` / `set ::g 2` and both correctly go silent — O109 via the unrelated `var.starts_with("::")` check at `elimination.rs:543`, W220 via `scan_module_traced_globals`. Meanwhile **O102 on the same unqualified spelling correctly abstains**. Same variable, same file, one pass sound and one not.

The list fold has the same hole:

```tcl
trace add variable ::acc write ::onw
set acc {}; lappend acc a; lappend acc b
```

folds to `set acc {a b}` under O130, dropping two write-trace callbacks — even with the `trace` call in the same scope, because `analyse_var_observability` recorded `::acc` and `chain_fold` asks about `acc`.

## Cleanup

Route the O109/O126 gate and `chain_fold::protected_vars` through the same canonicalised fact SCCP and O102 use: widen their protected set with `cu.ir_module.traced_variables` and bail on `has_dynamic_variable_trace`, normalising the chain key the way `populate_variable_trace_facts` normalises the target.

Because `Module::traced_variables` is name-keyed and scope-blind, doing that verbatim would also protect a proc-local `x` when another proc traces its own local `x`. The precision-preserving version promotes `scan_module_traced_globals`' scope filter into one module-level fact (globals-traced-anywhere ∪ this-function's-own-traces) that all four consumers — SCCP, O102, O109/O126, O104/O130 — read.

**User-visible:** O109/O126/O104/O130 and W211/W220 all lose firings around traced globals.

**Scale:** one new shared fact plus four consumer call sites; contained in `tcl-compiler`.

issues.title: `upvar`'s level word is text-sniffed in two analyser sites, losing the `upvar $lvl a b` binding — the exact failure the registry's `FrameLevelWord::ArityParity` doc warns about
issues.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. The registry descriptor exists, is documented, has migrated consumers — and two text-sniffing copies survive, reproducing verbatim the two failure rows the descriptor's own doc calls out.

## The modern path

- `FrameLevelWord::ArityParity` — `rust/tcl-registry/src/frame_effect.rs:234-253`, with the pinned tclsh 9.0.4 / 8.6.14 table and this explicit warning:

  > *"A text-sniffing consumer gets the third and fourth rows backwards: it drops a real binding for `upvar $lvl a b` (the commonest by-reference idiom of all) and invents a level for `upvar 1 b`."*

- `FrameEffectSpec::level_word_len` / `resolve` — `frame_effect.rs:344-385`.
- `commands/tcl/upvar_.rs:187` — `frame_effect: Some(UPVAR_FRAME_EFFECT)`.
- **The migrated twin:** `analyser/param_traits.rs:938-961` — `upvar_level_and_pairs` queries `registry.frame_effect("upvar")`, and its doc says the rule "lives in the registry … queried here through the spec rather than re-derived, **so this stays the one description of `upvar`'s shape** (issue #1069)". It isn't.
- Other migrated consumers: `cfg_builder/upvar_info.rs:501`, `dynamic_names.rs:658`, `tcl-lsp-core/src/semantic_tokens.rs:1669`.

## The legacy paths

- `var_scoping.rs:310-319` — `looks_like_level(head)`: true for a decimal integer, an optionally `-`-prefixed integer, or `#<digits>`. Consumed at `var_scoping.rs:133` and `:180`.
- `analyser/diagnostics/usage.rs:1554-1568` — `upvar_local_name_positions`: a *second, differently-spelled* sniff (`head.starts_with('#') || all-digits after stripping every leading '-'`), reached from `Analyser::variable_name_positions` (`usage.rs:836`).

## Reproducer

For `upvar $lvl a b` (3 words ⇒ parity says `$lvl` is the level, pair is `(a, b)`, local is `b` at index 2):

- `upvar_local_declaration_indices("upvar", ["$lvl","a","b"])` — `looks_like_level("$lvl")` false, offset 0, pair `("$lvl","a")` skipped for its `$` source, loop ends → returns `[]`. **The `b` binding is lost entirely.**
- `upvar_local_alias_indices` on the same input returns `[1]` — declaring **`a`** the local alias, the wrong word.
- `upvar_local_name_positions(["$lvl","a","b"])` returns `[1]` — also `a`.

For `upvar 1 b` (2 words ⇒ parity says no level; `1` is the *otherVar*, `b` the local at index 1): `looks_like_level("1")` is true, offset 1, no complete pair remains → `[]`.

Both rows are verbatim the two the registry doc names. `frame_effect.rs:36-38` records that three copies of the level rule had already drifted before the descriptor existed, "two of them wrong" — two are still here.

## Why it matters

`var_scoping`'s helpers are the shared home for scope-alias declarations. Wrong answers propagate to `textDocument/declaration` (`tcl-lsp-core/src/declaration.rs:39`, which navigates to `a` instead of `b`), the memory-SSA alias detector (`var_escape/handlers.rs:186`, `var_escape/cfg_propagation/handlers.rs:184`), `place_bridge.rs:156`, `cfg_builder/global_write_info.rs:388`, and dead-store elimination (`optimiser/elimination.rs:1290`). A missed `upvar $lvl a b` alias means the optimiser does not know `b` is observable in another frame — the same soundness shape as #1371. W212's name-position check flags the wrong argument.

## Cleanup

Delete `looks_like_level` and `upvar_local_name_positions`; have `upvar_local_declaration_indices` / `upvar_local_alias_indices` derive the offset from `registry.frame_effect("upvar").level_word_len(&refs)`, exactly as `param_traits::upvar_level_and_pairs` does. `var_escape/handlers.rs:168` and `cfg_propagation/handlers.rs:172` then drop their `looks_like_level` imports.

Best done together with the `optional_leading_word` wiring (filed separately) — otherwise the parity rule ends up in two registry places.

**Scale:** ~60 lines deleted, three call sites rewritten, plus fixing `var_scoping.rs:548-559` and `tests/alias_scoping.rs:444+`, which currently pin the wrong behaviour.

issues.title: IRULE6001 uses a hardcoded 13-name variable-write table that `param_traits` already deleted as redundant, silencing it for `catch`/`lassign`/`regexp`/`scan` and false-firing on `array names ::x`
issues.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. A sibling module deleted its copy of this exact table and documented the deletion; this one survived.

## The legacy path

`analyser/irules_event_checks.rs:143-152`:

```rust
fn var_write_index(cmd_name: &str) -> Option<usize> {
    match cmd_name {
        "append" | "const" | "global" | "incr" | "lappend" | "ledit" | "lpop" | "lset" | "set"
        | "unset" | "variable" => Some(0),
        "array" | "gets" => Some(1),
        _ => None,
    }
}
```

Consumed at `:170`, `:182`, `:812`, `:843`.

## The modern path

`CommandRegistry::arg_indices_for_role(cmd, &args, ArgRole::VarWrite)` — the same query the sibling module already uses. `analyser/param_traits.rs:645-656` documents removing *its* copy verbatim:

> *"The old hardcoded `var_write_index` name list was a redundant duplicate of that registry query and has been removed."*

Same query in `auto_path_eval.rs:676`, `var_scoping.rs:256`, `diagnostics/usage.rs:845`.

## Drift

The hardcoded set names 13 commands. **33 spec files** under `rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/` declare `ArgRole::VarWrite`. Live in the iRules dialect and missed: `catch`, `lassign`, `scan`, `binary scan`, `regexp`, `regsub`, `dict`, `string`, `chan`, `info`, `vwait`, `trace`, `upvar`, `namespace upvar` (`namespace_.rs:1056`), and `foreach`/`lmap` loop variables.

Conversely the two-index arm (`"array" | "gets" => Some(1)`) is unconditional, so **`array names ::x` is read as a write to `::x`**.

## Why it matters

IRULE6001 (global-variable CMP pinning) and its RULE_INIT implicit-global variant are silent for `catch {…} ::err`, `lassign $l ::a ::b`, `regexp $re $s ::m`, `scan $s $f ::v`, and `binary scan $d $f ::v` — all of which really do pin the virtual server to one TMM.

The false positive on `array names ::x` produces a code fix that rewrites a **read** into `static::x`.

## Cleanup

Replace `var_write_index` with a helper returning **all** `ArgRole::VarWrite` indices from the registry (`Vec<usize>`, not `Option<usize>`), and let `global_var_from_command` / `implicit_global_var_from_command` / the two fix-span lookups iterate them.

The special-cases at `:184-193` (`set` with one arg is a read; `unset` destroys; `array` without `set`) all disappear — `set`'s and `array`'s `arg_role_resolver`s and `unset`'s `DESTROYS_VARIABLE` already encode them.

**Scale:** ~40 lines, one module, plus IRULE6001 test cases for `catch`/`lassign`/`regexp`.

issues.title: Wire `RepeatedArgLayout::optional_leading_word` to `upvar` and collapse the four hand-rolled scope-alias layout parsers
issues.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. A registry feature was built, documented, and unit-tested for `upvar` — and then never wired to `upvar`'s spec, so the consumer had nothing to migrate to and kept its parser. Do this together with #1379.

## The dead mechanism

`rust/tcl-registry/src/repeated.rs` exists for exactly this family. Its header (`:19-38`) names `global a b c`, `variable n v n v`, `namespace upvar NS o l o l` and records that "every LSP consumer that needed one of these layouts therefore re-derived it by hand from the command's *name*" (issue #1185).

Already declared: `global_.rs:102`/`:133` (`RepeatedArgLayout::every(VarWrite, 0)`), `variable_.rs:164` (`strided(VarWrite, 0, 2)`), `namespace_.rs:1056` (`strided(VarWrite, 2, 2)`).

`repeated.rs:62-71` documents `optional_leading_word` with `upvar`'s `?level?` as its **sole motivating case**, and `repeated.rs:193-206` (`optional_leading_word_shifts_by_the_argument_count`) unit-tests it against `upvar ?level? other local` with the parity-correct answers.

**No `CommandSpec` sets the flag.** `grep -rn 'optional_leading_word' commands/` returns nothing; `upvar_.rs` declares neither `arg_roles` nor `repeated_args`.

## The surviving hand-rolled path

`var_scoping.rs:248-262` and `:285-301` — after a correctly registry-driven *recognition* step (`is_scope_alias_call`, `:210-227`, reading `Traits::CREATES_SCOPE_ALIAS` and `SubCommand::creates_scope_alias`), the *layout* is dispatched by literal name:

```rust
match canonical {
    "global"   => global_declaration_indices(args),
    "variable" => variable_declaration_indices(args),
    "upvar" | "namespace" | "namespace upvar" => upvar_local_alias_indices(canonical, args),
    _ => { /* registry ArgRole::VarWrite query */ }
}
```

The three hand-rolled parsers: `var_scoping.rs:41-47`, `:59-69`, `:119-154`/`:167-197`.

Note `diagnostics/usage.rs:832-836` documents the gap as *intentional* ("the registry deliberately omits its roles") — which is how the `ArityParity` bug in #1379 survived.

## Why it matters

Four grammars (`global`, `variable`, `upvar`, `namespace upvar`) with five consumers each are maintained in analyser code the registry can already describe as data. Adding a fifth alias-creating command — a dialect's `::ns::localise`, say — means editing `var_scoping.rs` twice, defeating the `CREATES_SCOPE_ALIAS` recognition work already done.

Fixing #1379 without this leaves the parity rule in two registry places (`frame_effect` and `repeated_args`).

## Cleanup

Add to `upvar_.rs`:

```rust
repeated_args: &[RepeatedArgLayout {
    optional_leading_word: true,
    ..RepeatedArgLayout::strided(ArgRole::VarWrite, 1, 2)
}]
```

Then collapse both `scope_alias_*_indices` match arms to a single `registry.arg_indices_for_role(command, &args, ArgRole::VarWrite)`, keeping only the two `$`-filters as post-filters over the returned indices (the observability flavour keeps a local whose *source* substitutes; the navigation flavour does not).

`global_declaration_indices` / `variable_declaration_indices` / `upvar_local_*_indices` and their duplicate callers in `place_bridge.rs`, `var_escape/handlers.rs`, `cfg_propagation/handlers.rs`, `cfg_builder/global_write_info.rs` all become one registry query.

**Scale:** one registry field addition plus ~200 lines of parser and mirrored tests deleted across six modules.

issues.title: `inline_uplevel`'s frame-reach guard is a two-name `matches!`, so bodies calling `argparse`, `tailcall`, `info level`, or `::uplevel` are inlined
issues.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. This is that PR's shape in a **rewriting** transform, so a missed frame reach is a miscompile rather than a missed optimisation.

## The legacy path

- `inline_uplevel.rs:192-198` — `statement_has_frame_reach`:
  ```rust
  Statement::Barrier { command, .. } | Statement::Call { command, .. }
      if matches!(command.as_str(), "uplevel" | "upvar")
  ```
- `inline_uplevel.rs:155` — `if cmd != "uplevel" { return None; }`; `:164` — `2 if args[0] == "1"`, a literal level-word test.

Note it reads the **surface** `command` field, not the canonical name.

## The modern path

- `CommandSpec::frame_effect` (`rust/tcl-registry/src/spec.rs:620`) and the four frame traits (`ALIASES_CALLER_FRAME`, `CURRENT_FRAME_INTROSPECTION`, `EVALUATES_IN_SHIFTED_FRAME`, `REPLACES_FRAME`, `traits.rs`). Carriers today: `uplevel_.rs:166`, `upvar_.rs:187`, `eval_.rs:82`, **`commands/argparse/command.rs:266`**, `tailcall_.rs` (`REPLACES_FRAME`), `info_.rs` (`CURRENT_FRAME_INTROSPECTION`).
- `FrameLevel::parse` / `FrameEffectSpec::resolve_for_version` (`frame_effect.rs:127`, `:395`) for the level word — already used by `var_escape/walker.rs:269` and `var_observability.rs:131`.
- `Statement::canonical_command_or_source()` (`ir.rs:1225`), whose doc says "Use from downstream dispatch sites … so a single canonical key drives every consumer".

## What it misses

`argparse` carries `FrameArgLayout::OpaqueCallerVars`, whose whole point is stated in its spec: it *"injects variables into the frame of **its own caller** under names it derives from an argument mini-language this analysis does not interpret … a consumer must widen rather than enumerate."* The guard does not see it. Nor `tailcall`, nor `info level` / `info frame`.

The surface-vs-canonical split is visible within the same crate: three diagnostics modules check both spellings — `diagnostics/helpers.rs:444` (`canonical_command.as_deref() == Some("::unset") || command == "unset"`), `diagnostics/var_command.rs:2675`, `diagnostics/dataflow.rs:1536-1537` — while `inline_uplevel.rs` checks only `command`. `uri_split.rs:66-71` documents the rule it breaks: *"the SSA / IR layer preserves the surface text — so detection helpers must accept both."* A body containing `::uplevel 1 {…}` passes the guard.

`connection_scope.rs:245` (`command == "unset"`) has the same surface-only defect.

## Consequence

`proc P {b} {uplevel 1 $b}` invoked with a body that calls `argparse`, `tailcall`, or `::uplevel` is inlined today.

## Cleanup

Thread the registry into `body_has_frame_reach` (callers already have one) and replace the `matches!` with:

```rust
registry.get(stmt.canonical_command_or_source())
    .is_some_and(|s| s.frame_effect.is_some() || s.traits.intersects(FRAME_REACH_TRAITS))
```

where `FRAME_REACH_TRAITS` is a registry-side composite constant. Replace the `cmd != "uplevel"` / `args[0] == "1"` pair with `registry.frame_effect(canonical).resolve(&refs)` and a `FrameLevel::Relative(1)` test. Fix `connection_scope.rs:245` to read `canonical_command_or_source()` at the same time.

**Scale:** ~30 lines plus a registry composite-trait constant; one inline-refusal test per missed carrier.

issues.title: Registry migration debt: hardcoded command names in the iRules, TclOO-unknown, auto_path, and Tk analyser checks
issues.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. Four consumers hold per-command knowledge that AGENTS.md requires to live in the registry. Each has a migrated sibling in the same crate — several with doc comments explicitly saying "registry facts, not command names" — so these are stragglers, not design.

Grouped because the fix is the same move four times. Split if they land separately.

---

## 1. `"when"` matched by name three times, including a third copy of the `when EVENT` grammar

**Now:** `analyser/irules_event_checks.rs:486` (`if cmd_name != "when"`, IRULE1002) and `:597`; plus `scan_when_blocks` (`:870-948`) — a byte-level `\bwhen\s+[A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]*` scan with its own `priority N` / `timing …` skip and balanced-brace body extractor, run over `self.source` from inside IRULE4003 (`:749`) — re-scanning a document the segmenter already walked.

**Should be:** `Traits::IS_EVENT_HANDLER` (`commands/irules/when.rs:72`). Migrated consumers say so explicitly — `analyser/commands.rs:1900-1909` ("Registry facts, not command names (gap-review C3). The event handler is whatever carries `IS_EVENT_HANDLER` — `when` today, but a dialect that adds another gets the same treatment without an edit here"), `tcl-lsp-core/src/completion.rs:474`, `semantic_tokens.rs:1497`. The body text is already in hand: `commands.rs:1909-1930` sets `self.current_event` and descends the registry-resolved `ArgRole::Body`.

**Drift:** `scan_when_blocks` is the *third* implementation — `tcl-registry/src/events.rs:975-1015` (`scan_when_events`) and `profiles.rs:339-368` (`scan_file_events`) are the others. They already disagree in scope: only the analyser copy handles `priority`/`timing`, only it extracts bodies, only the registry copies deduplicate. **None respects comments, quoting, or `\{`**, so a `when` in a `#` comment or a string literal produces a phantom event block. `irules_event_checks.rs:445-448` in the same file *does* use the registry (`is_irules_top_level_only`) — the file is half-migrated.

**Impact:** IRULE4003 computed off a text scan invents phantom events from commented-out code and drops unusual `timing`/`priority` spellings. IRULE1002 will never fire for a future dialect's second event-handler command.

**Cleanup:** both gates → `spec.traits.contains(Traits::IS_EVENT_HANDLER)`. Replace `scan_when_blocks` by accumulating `(event, body_text)` during the existing structural walk. ~90 lines deleted.

---

## 2. `oo.rs`'s unknown-handler analysis keys on `CHAIN_TARGETS` plus `"exec"`/`"auto_load"`

**Now:** `analyser/oo.rs:76-82` — `const CHAIN_TARGETS: &[&str] = &["_original_unknown", "_orig_unknown", "::tcl::unknown", "tcl::unknown", "original_unknown"]`, consumed by `walk_unknown_stmt` (`:1996-2003`) reading the bare `command` field.

**Should be:** `Traits::UNRESOLVED_COMMAND_HANDLER` (`commands/tcl/unknown.rs:173`), `Traits::LOADS_EXTERNAL_UNIT` (`auto_load.rs:56`), and for `exec` the `Traits::UNSAFE` + `SideEffectTarget::Process` side effect (`exec_.rs:48-56`) — resolved on `canonical_command_or_source()` (`ir.rs:1225`).

**Migrated twins, both saying so:** `unit_scope.rs:884-905` and `analyser/handlers.rs:2514-2546` — *"Which command is the handler comes from `Traits::UNRESOLVED_COMMAND_HANDLER`, **never a literal name here**"*.

**Drift:** `handlers.rs:2540-2546` derives *both* accepted spellings from the single `unknown` spec by qualifying against `::` and `::tcl`. `CHAIN_TARGETS` lists the `::tcl` pair by hand and **omits `::unknown` / `unknown` entirely** — the two modules disagree about what "the original handler" is named. `command == "exec"` also misses `::exec`.

**Impact:** `UnknownProcInfo::chains_original` / `has_exec` / `has_auto_load` gate W123 suppression for the whole file. A handler chaining via `::unknown` or shelling out via `::exec` reads as self-contained, and **every unresolved command in the document gets a spurious W123**.

**Cleanup:** resolve via registry traits. The irreducible residue — the *user-chosen* saved names `_original_unknown` / `_orig_unknown` / `original_unknown`, which no registry can know — shrinks to a three-name convention list with a comment saying why it cannot move. ~25 lines.

---

## 3. `auto_path_eval::collect_writes` re-implements `set`/`variable`/`namespace eval` layouts

**Now:** `auto_path_eval.rs:503-545` — `match words[0].as_str() { "set" if len == 3 => …, "variable" if len >= 2 => …, "namespace" if len == 4 && words[1] == "eval" => … }`, with the `variable` arm open-coding the name/value stride at `:510-537`. Plus `:1091-1113`, a mini constant evaluator hardcoding `info script`, `file dirname`, `file normalize`, `file join`.

**Should be:** `variable`'s stride is registry data (`variable_.rs:164`); `set`'s write index comes from its `arg_role_resolver`; `namespace eval`'s body is `ArgRole::Body` + `ArgRole::NamespaceName` (`namespace_.rs:785`) with `Traits::DECLARES_NAMESPACE`. For the folder half, `CommandSpec::const_fold` / `const_fold_versioned` (`spec.rs:735`, `:740`) — 40 specs already carry one; `file` carries none.

**Drift within one module:** `auto_path_eval.rs:660-690` (`poison_mutated_variables`) reads `arg_indices_for_role(head, &args, ArgRole::VarWrite)` and cites AGENTS.md for doing so. So the two halves disagree about how to find a variable write — a write recorded by one is invisible to the other for anything outside the three-name list (`array set`, `dict set`, `lappend`, `append`, a stub-declared setter).

**Impact:** `auto_path` constant resolution decides which `source`d / `package require`d units the workspace model can follow. A missed `lappend dir …` loses a whole file from the index — definitions, references, and completion inside it.

**Cleanup:** three `match` arms → role queries; move `file dirname`/`normalize`/`join` into `const_fold` fns on the `file` subcommand specs beside the existing `fold_join`/`fold_split`. ~80 lines plus three small registry fns.

---

## 4. `tk_checks::GEOMETRY_COMMANDS` is a hardcoded three-name set

**Now:** `analyser/tk_checks.rs:140` — `const GEOMETRY_COMMANDS: &[&str] = &["pack", "grid", "place"]`, consumed by `is_geometry_command` at `:167`.

**Should be:** no registry field carries this yet — it needs one. The specs exist (`commands/tk/{pack,grid,place}.rs`) and the surrounding module already resolves everything else from the registry: `TK_PACKAGE` (`tk_checks.rs:148`) is documented as "the single source of truth for both halves of the gate", and `is_widget_command` reads `CommandSpec::required_package`.

**Impact:** TK1001 (conflicting geometry managers on one parent) is silent for any manager outside the three core names — notably `ttk::` megawidget managers and vendor Tk forks — and adding one means editing the analyser rather than the spec pack.

**Cleanup:** add `Traits::TK_GEOMETRY_MANAGER` to `traits.rs`'s `declare_traits!`, set it on the three Tk specs, replace `is_geometry_command` with a `spec.traits.contains(...)` check. One trait, three spec edits, ~8 lines.

---

## Explicitly not included

`alias.rs:201-223` (`expr_alias_names` matching the literal `"expr"`) is real debt but is **already documented as tracked** at the call site, with the intended replacement named (`Traits::EXPR_CONCATENATES_ARGS`) and the blocker stated (the registry-less `dispatch_lowering_hook` signature). Noted here so it isn't re-found; not counted as a new finding.

`analyser/commands.rs:154-160` (`orphaned_keyword_parent`) maps `else`/`elseif`/`then` → `if` and `on`/`trap`/`finally` → `try`. The forward facts are registry data, but no reverse keyword→parent index exists and the table has not drifted. Worth folding into any future `ArgRole::Keyword` index; not a defect today.

issues.title: Replace `UnknownWorld` for procedure bodies with the workspace/package/sourced-file entry contract, so the redundancy family can emit again
issues.body:
Follow-up named in #1371's own body, filed so it is not lost when that PR merges. Parent: #1364.

## The situation #1371 leaves behind

#1371 makes the dispatch-stability proof the only classifier the redundancy family uses, which is the correct architecture — but the entry state is a typed contract that currently has only two values: `PristineRegistryWorld` for a unit's top-level script, and `UnknownWorld` (fails closed) for procedure, method, and body units.

Widening is absorbing, so an `UnknownWorld` unit can never produce a proof. Real Tcl keeps its reusable calls inside procedure bodies. The measured consequence on the pinned #1181 corpus:

| Code | Before | After |
|---|---|---:|
| O100 (SCCP, untouched) | 47 | 47 |
| O105 | 8 | **0** |
| O106 | 24 | **0** |

The redundancy family emits nothing. #1371 is explicit that this trades 32 findings of unknown soundness for 0 findings of proven soundness — a good trade, but the endpoint is meant to be *sound and useful*, not sound and silent.

## What this issue is

Give procedure, method, and body units a real entry assumption instead of `UnknownWorld`: the workspace, package, sourced-file, and interpreter state represented through the proof contract, as #1364 specifies. That is the difference between a sound-but-silent optimiser and a better one.

## Why it should not wait indefinitely

While every O105/O106 is suppressed, the redundancy family has no live output — so regressions in it are undetectable by the corpus run, and `fp_opt_03` (rewritten by #1371 to assert the abstention, with the restoring work recorded at the assertion) is the only pin on the intended future behaviour.

Two audit findings also land on these same entry points and are worth sequencing against this work:
- #1385 — PRE and LICM use raw CFG reachability rather than `SccpResult::executable_blocks`, and re-derive the loop forest `loops.rs` owns. Same two functions.
- #1392 — the interprocedural purity summary never reaches GVN, so a proc proved `pure: true` yields no CSE. That is the other half of "why does the redundancy family find nothing", and it is independent of the world proof.

## Known blocker recorded in #1371

**TclOO:** `oo::class create` is a script-kind callback barrier widening every domain, so top-level proofs die at the first class definition. The blocker is the missing object-identity ↔ private-namespace reverse mapping, also behind three documented abstentions in `world_state_ssa.rs`. Worth its own issue if this one is picked up without it.

issues.title: Tracking: legacy duplication and half-completed migration audit (follow-on from #1371)
issues.body:
#1371 found the optimiser's redundancy family answering one semantic question — "can Tcl's mutable dispatch machinery observe this call site?" — in two places: a legacy command-string classifier (`traced_commands` + `has_dynamic_trace`) and a modern typed per-site proof. GVN was migrated; PRE and LICM were silently left on the legacy path, which was unsound.

This tracks a six-scope audit for the same shape elsewhere: **a shared authority exists, most consumers adopt it, one or two do not, and nothing detects the stragglers.**

Scopes: optimiser/dataflow, analyser/registry compliance, lowering/codegen/IR, LSP feature layer, runtime/VM parity, tooling/editor catalogues. 27 findings; 14 are reproduced user-visible defects.

---

## Reproduced defects

| Issue | Defect | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| #1374 | O102/O104/O119/O125/O130 ignore the dynamic-name barrier O109 and SCCP consult | 3 miscompiles; quick-fix-applicable in-editor |
| #1375 | Five lowerers gate body words on `arg_single`, not the shared kind predicate | `while {1} $body` panics `tcl compwasm` |
| #1376 | WASM emitter re-slices source, strips a closer the span excludes | `while {${x}}` emits `${x` (od-confirmed) |
| #1377 | Trace observability: 3 impls, rewriting ones spelling-sensitive | O109 deletes a store to a traced global; W220 false-fires |
| #1378 | `switch` clause layout hand-rolled ×3 vs `CaseListSpec::invocation` | False W123; find-references drops `my` sites |
| #1379 | `upvar` level text-sniffed vs `FrameLevelWord::ArityParity` | Loses the `upvar $lvl a b` binding |
| #1380 | `{*}` barrier: 9 hardcoded names vs 17 hook IDs | W210 false positive on `lmap {*}$spec` |
| #1381 | IRULE6001's 13-name table vs 33 `VarWrite` specs | Silent for `catch`/`lassign`/`regexp`; false-fires on `array names ::x` |
| #1382 | `entier`/`int`/`wide` VM↔runtime divergence | `expr {entier(1e300)}` errors on one engine |
| #1383 | `file` partial port: 17 of 31 subcommands missing | `file mtime` unknown in runtime; gate reports green |
| #1384 | `format` reimplemented instead of shared `tcl_cmd_core::format` | `format %#d 42` → `"0d42"` vs `"42"` |
| #1385 | PRE/LICM use raw reachability, not `executable_blocks` | O106 hoist offered inside an O112-deleted block |
| #1386 | Hover's 6 detectors hardcode names, ignore arg index | `regsub … {x.y}` hovers as "Regex pattern" |
| #1387 | LSP `diagramData` reimplements `tcl-diagram` | VS Code `/diagram` and JetBrains action degraded |

## Cleanup

| Issue | Scope |
|---|---|
| #1388 | Wire `optional_leading_word`; collapse four scope-alias parsers (pair with #1379) |
| #1389 | `inline_uplevel` frame-reach guard misses `argparse`/`tailcall`/`::uplevel` |
| #1390 | Registry migration debt: iRules `when`, TclOO unknown, auto_path, Tk geometry |
| #1391 | W231/W201 byte-scan for facts the segmenter and taint lattice hold |
| #1392 | Dead optimiser machinery: unwired purity oracle; `cross_event_vars` never populated |
| #1393 | Lowerer span hardening: adopt the #1325 guard; drop the dialect-blind tokeniser |
| #1394 | Dialect catalogue duplicated 10+ places, ungated, already drifted |

## Carried forward

From #890 (being closed — 166 commits behind, conflicted, cheaper to redo):

| Issue | Item |
|---|---|
| #1395 | Shared `first_positional_index` — five hand-rolled copies |
| #1396 | Audit↔registry drift guard — **the gap it found was fixed; the guard never landed** |
| #1397 | `Diagnostic` builder — ~130 literals (lowest priority; closing is a fine outcome) |

From #1371's own body:

| Issue | Item |
|---|---|
| #1398 | Replace `UnknownWorld` for procedure bodies — the work that makes the proof useful |
| #1399 | `bench.py` has no outer deadline |

---

## What the audit says beyond the individual findings

**1. Nothing detects an unmigrated consumer.** Every finding here was found by a human-directed read, not by a gate. The registry migrations that *are* complete stayed complete by luck and diligence. Worth considering: an architecture test in the shape of #1371's own (which scans production regions against every registered command name), generalised — it would have caught #1381, #1390, and parts of #1380 mechanically.

**2. Three findings are contradicted by their own doc comments.** `param_traits.rs:938` claims to be "the one description" of `upvar`'s shape (#1379); `switch_arm_bodies` claims it "can never disagree" with its migrated twin (#1378); `codegen/structured.rs:50` claims "no caller yet" while a panic backtrace shows the caller (#1376). A doc comment asserting uniqueness is a signal to check, not evidence.

**3. Gate holes cluster.** #1383 (presence-not-completeness), #1394 (no gate at all), #1396 (guard never landed) are one theme: the drift gates cover generated artefacts well and hand-written duplication not at all.

**4. Stale "not wired up yet" comments keep dead-by-belief code alive.** #1391's `path_concat` is the clearest case — a text matcher survives *because* a comment says the registry path does not work, and it has worked for some time. `place_bridge.rs`'s "No consumer is wired yet" header is stale the same way (three production consumers) though harmless.

## Method note

Six parallel agents, each required to cite `file:line` on both sides of a duplication and to verify by reading rather than suspicion. Four of six additionally reproduced their findings against a locally built `tcl`. Each was briefed on AGENTS.md's documented carve-outs — the lowering fallback-to-generic-call pattern and the irreducible analyser-local OO semantics — and declined to report them, which is why the positives here should be taken as real rather than pattern-matched.

Verified-clean subsystems are recorded in the individual issues rather than repeated here; notable ones include the segmenter's completed CST migration, `oo_body.rs`'s command-name-free `MemberKind` walker, the shared `tcl_cmd_core` command families, and the LSP feature-toggle contract.

issues.title: safe_on_uninit is never lifted from the registry into the IR, so W210's self-init suppression is dead
issues.body:
Found during a documentation audit, while checking whether a documented `REGISTRY.is_safe_on_uninit(...)` API existed (it does not). The three endpoints of this data path all exist; the middle link does not.

## The path, as it should work

1. **Registry declares it.** `CommandSpec.safe_on_uninit: Option<DialectSet>` (`rust/tcl-registry/src/spec.rs:732`) and the same field on `SubCommand` (`:2120`). Eight specs set it — exactly the commands that legitimately self-initialise an undefined variable: `lappend_.rs`, `append_.rs`, `dict.rs`, `incr_.rs`.
2. **IR carries it.** `Statement::Call { safe_on_uninit: bool, .. }` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/ir.rs`).
3. **The analyser consumes it.** `use_site_safe_initialises` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs:2588`:

```rust
Some(Statement::Call { safe_on_uninit, defs, .. }) =>
    *safe_on_uninit && defs.iter().any(|d| d == var),
```

called from the W210 read-before-set walk at `dataflow.rs:1297` under the comment *"A use site that itself safely initialises the variable (`safe_on_uninit` calls like `lappend`/`dict set`, or an `incr` of its own target) is not read-before-set."*

## The break

**Every construction site of `Statement::Call` in the compiler writes the literal `false`.** Nothing lifts the registry's `Option<DialectSet>` into the IR bool. Grep across `rust/tcl-compiler/src/` finds `safe_on_uninit: false` in `lowering/mod.rs`, `lowering/structured.rs`, `lowering/hooks/incr.rs`, and `gvn.rs` (many sites), and the only `true` in the whole workspace is a test fixture at `type_infer.rs:1835`.

So `use_site_safe_initialises` can never return `true` through its `Statement::Call` arm.

## User-visible effect

`incr` is fine — it has its own arm (`Statement::Incr`) that does not read the field. But `lappend`, `append`, and `dict set` all lower to `Statement::Call`, so W210 (read before set) should fire on the ordinary Tcl idiom of building a value from nothing:

```tcl
proc collect {items} {
    foreach i $items {
        lappend out $i      ;# `out` is undefined on the first pass — legal Tcl
    }
    return $out
}
```

Worth confirming against the real analyser before fixing: there are earlier `continue` branches in that walk, so another suppression may be masking it in practice. If it *is* masked, the field and its consumer are dead weight and should be removed rather than repaired.

## Fix

Lift the spec value at lowering time — resolve `safe_on_uninit` for the command (and subcommand, since `dict set` needs the `SubCommand` field) against the unit's dialect, and set the IR bool accordingly. `dict.rs:845` already propagates `sub.safe_on_uninit` within the registry, so the resolution shape exists.

issues.title: Three compiler integrations are declared but never wired: memory-SSA aliasing, dataflow alias/clobber edges, and execution-intent
issues.body:
Found while rewriting the CFG/SSA/core-analysis design docs against the source. In each case the documentation described a consumer that does not exist, which is how these surfaced — the design docs were the only thing asserting the integration had happened.

All three verified by whole-tree grep.

## 1. `MemorySsaFunction::may_alias` / `aliases_for` have no production caller

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/memory_ssa.rs:335` and `:346`. Their only exercise is `rust/tcl-compiler/tests/alias_scoping.rs`.

`memory-ssa.md` documented GVN (O105), LICM (O106), DSE (O109), and taint analysis as consumers of `may_alias` and `alias_sets`. **None of them reference memory-SSA at all** — `gvn.rs` never mentions it. The real consumers are O127 store-to-load forwarding (via `aliased_names()` and `statement_has_wildcard_aliasing`) and the graph/explorer payloads.

Given that the alias machinery is built, tested, and then not consulted by the passes that would most benefit, this reads as an intended integration that never landed rather than deliberate public API. Note also that `FunctionUnit::memory_ssa` is `None` unless `with_memory_ssa` is called, so even the wiring that exists is opt-in.

## 2. `EdgeKind::Alias` and `EdgeKind::Clobber` are never constructed

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/dataflow_graph.rs:42` declares four edge kinds. `extract_function_dataflow` constructs only `Direct` (`:146`) and `Phi` (`:167`); the sole other mentions are `as_str()` round-trip assertions in the module's own tests (`:477`, `:478`).

So the emitted JSON schema advertises two edge kinds no payload can contain. A consumer written against the documented schema — the `tcl dataflow` verb's wire dict, the LSP graph request, the explorer view — would be handling cases that cannot occur.

Either the alias and clobber edges are the unlanded half of item 1, or the variants should go.

## 3. `execution_intent` is an orphan module

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/execution_intent.rs` defines `FunctionExecutionIntent` and friends, and `lib.rs:109` exports it. **That export is the only reference in the entire workspace** — no producer, no consumer.

`docs/design/compiler/execution-intent-model.md` documents it as a fact category passes should read instead of re-parsing command-substitution text. `cfg-ssa-fact-model.md` listed it as consumable; it is now marked as defined but not consumable, rather than silently dropped, because the design intent may still be wanted.

## Ask

For each: confirm dead and remove, or say what it is for and wire it. Both answers let the docs stop hedging — they currently have to describe a capability that exists as a type but not as behaviour.

## Related

Same family as #1406 (`FunctionAnalysis` declared but only default-constructed in its own tests). The pattern across all four is a data structure landing without its consumer, and the design docs then describing the consumer as though it exists.

issues.title: WASM runtime: rename destroys an occupied destination, does not re-home a proc, and interp advertises four unreachable subcommands
issues.body:
Seven C-conformance defects in `runtime/rust/`, all found while rewriting `docs/design/runtime/` against the source. The bytecode VM gets several of these right, which makes the divergence easy to check against.

Ordered worst first.

## 1. `rename` silently destroys an occupied destination

`runtime/rust/src/namespace.rs:207` — `Namespaces::rename` removes the source and inserts at the destination with no occupancy check.

C Tcl refuses, leaving **both** commands intact: `can't rename to "X": command already exists`. The VM implements exactly that, and says why in a comment (`rust/tcl-vm/src/command.rs:439-444`):

```rust
// Tcl rejects a rename onto an existing command (leaving both intact), so
// check the destination before removing the source.
```

The tree-walker instead binds the source over the destination and loses the destination's command. Silent data loss, and the two engines disagree.

## 2. `rename` does not re-home a proc across namespaces

`runtime/rust/src/interp.rs:1193` — `Command::Proc(Rc<ProcDef>)` keeps its definition-time `ns` and `fqn` through a cross-namespace rename, so `namespace current` inside the body reports the *old* namespace.

C's `TclRenameCommand` updates `nsPtr`. The VM re-homes explicitly at `command.rs:489-506`, citing test `proc-3.4`.

## 3. `interp` advertises four subcommands it cannot dispatch

`runtime/rust/src/cmd_alias.rs:171` — the fallthrough emits the verbatim tclsh option list, including `cancel`, `share`, `target`, and `transfer`. None has a match arm, so `interp target {} foo` reports `bad option "target"` **while naming `target` as valid**.

## 4. Wrong verb on the delete form of `rename`

`cmd_alias.rs:63` — `rename nosuch ""` reports `can't rename "nosuch": command doesn't exist`. C words the delete form `can't delete`. The VM gets this right (`command.rs:452-459`).

## 5. `invokehidden`'s option flags are parsed and discarded

`cmd_alias.rs:450-462` — `-global` and `-namespace ns` advance the argument index and do nothing else. No evaluation context is established, and C's mutual-exclusion rejection (`cannot use -global option and -namespace option together`) is absent, so both can be passed together and silently ignored.

## 6. `hide` / `expose` misses are silent

`cmd_alias.rs:432-437` — hiding a non-existent command, exposing a non-hidden one, or naming an unresolvable child path all return an empty result where C raises. `expose` additionally overwrites an occupied destination rather than refusing, which is the same defect as item 1 on the other table.

## 7. Inconsistent error shape between the two `interp` entry points

`interp.rs:5111` — `$child <unknown>` reports `interp subcommand "X" is not supported in this runtime`, while `interp <unknown>` reports the tclsh `bad option` list. Same class of mistake, two different messages, one of which is not a Tcl error shape at all.

---

## Also: three doc comments in `runtime/rust/` that contradict their own code

These were the *source* of several false claims in the design docs, so they will regenerate the problem if left:

- `cmd_alias.rs:28` — "Single-interp scope only … Child interpreters + cross-interp aliases are deferred." Both ship.
- `cmd_alias.rs:75` — "Other `interp` subcommands (`create`, `eval`, `hide`, …) need child-interp infrastructure and trap here." They have arms.
- `interp.rs:452` — "`Builtin` and the `Alias` redirect today; `Proc { params, body }` … are the next variants." The enum has eight variants.

## And one missing test asset

`tests/external/backend_constraints.tcl` is referenced by both test harnesses' documented workflow and does not exist — nor does `tests/external/`, nor any of the constraint names (`notWasm`, `bytecodeRuntime`, `wasiPreview1`, …) anywhere in the tree. The `TCL_BACKEND_CONSTRAINTS` hook *is* wired in both harnesses, so the plumbing is there and the overlay is not: every backend currently reports capability gaps as failures rather than skips.

issues.title: command_segment_on_line's expand-selection semicolon scan ignores {}/[] nesting, truncating the selection mid-word
issues.body:
Found by the cross-surface centralisation audit following #1419's numeral-parser precedent (sibling of the #1371/#1400 legacy-duplication audit). The selection-range provider's "command segment" link widens outward using a private semicolon scan that has no awareness of brace, bracket, or quote nesting, even though the same file already computes proper CST-based spans for the enclosing-body links a little further down the same chain.

## The private semicolon scan

`command_segment_on_line` in `rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/selection_range.rs:275` is wired into the outward-growing selection-range chain at `selection_range.rs:122`. Its own doc admits the limitation: "**Single-line only.** Continuation lines, embedded `[…]` / `{…}` token nesting, and full segmenter semantics are not handled." (`selection_range.rs:271`). The left scan (`selection_range.rs:280`) walks backward for the nearest `;` with a bare character comparison and no nesting state; the right scan (`selection_range.rs:287`) does the same walking forward.

## The available alternative

The same file already resolves enclosing-body links from the segmenter's `SegmentedCommand` / CST spans a few sections later in the same selection-range chain, so the information needed to make this nesting-aware is already computed nearby — `command_segment_on_line` just doesn't use it.

## Divergence

```tcl
foo {a; b} c
```
```
Cursor inside the braced word "a; b" (on the "a").

command_segment_on_line returns the span "foo {a" — a syntactically
broken substring that cuts through an open brace, because the ';'
inside {a; b} is literal data, not a command separator.
```

## Why it matters

Requesting "expand selection" at a cursor inside a braced or bracketed word that contains a literal `;` grows the selection to a substring that crosses an unmatched delimiter, instead of the enclosing command segment — a selection an editor then can't safely operate on (comment-out, wrap, delete) without corrupting the source.

## Cleanup

Resolve the command-segment link from `segment_commands` / the CST's command span containing the cursor — already computed below for the enclosing-body links — instead of the private semicolon scan.

**Scale:** small — one function in one file, with the replacement data already computed nearby in the same chain.

issues.title: `dict` in `tcl-vm` never collapses duplicate keys: two local `dict_pairs` copies do first-match lookup where `ValueOps::dict_pairs` (and C Tcl) take the last value
issues.body:
Found by the cross-surface centralisation audit following #1419's numeral-parser precedent (sibling of the #1371/#1400 legacy-duplication audit). The VM's dict opcodes and mutating subcommands parse dict pairs with two private, non-collapsing copies of the shared `ValueOps::dict_pairs` seam, so duplicate keys survive instead of collapsing to the last value.

## Implementation A (shared, correct)

`tcl_syntax::value::ValueOps::dict_pairs` (`rust/tcl-syntax/src/value.rs:273`) is documented as the canonical `Tcl_DictObjFirst` order — "first-occurrence position, last value winning on a duplicate key" — and is explicitly "correct for any value model (the VM's list-backed dict and the WASM runtime's `TclDict`)". Its dedup loop keeps the first-seen position but overwrites the value on a repeat key: `pairs[pos].1 = chunk[1].clone(); // last value wins, keep position` (`value.rs:288`). `tcl_cmd_core::dict::dispatch_canon` routes the *pure* dict subcommands (`get`/`keys`/`values`/`size`/`exists`/`merge`/`filter`/`replace`/`remove`) through this seam (`rust/tcl-vm/src/cmd_dict.rs:218`), and `runtime/rust/src/dict.rs:192` independently collapses the same way for the WASM runtime's native dict.

## Implementation B (private, divergent)

`rust/tcl-vm/src/exec.rs:472` carries a second `fn dict_pairs` for the bytecode opcodes — a bare `chunks_exact(2)` with no dedup at all — and `Op::DICT_GET` looks a key up with `ps.iter().find(...)` (`exec.rs:2789`), so the *first* occurrence wins. `dict_set_path` (`exec.rs:507`) writes into the first matching slot via `ps.iter_mut().find(...)`, leaving any later duplicate untouched. `rust/tcl-vm/src/cmd_dict.rs:60` carries the same non-deduping `chunks_exact(2)` as `pub(crate) fn pairs`, with `lookup` (`cmd_dict.rs:81`) doing the same first-match `find`. Only the *mutating* subcommands (`set`/`unset`/`incr`/`append`/`lappend`/`for`/`map`/`update`/`with`) fall through to this local copy — `dispatch_canon`'s pure arms don't.

## Divergence

```tcl
set d {a 1 a 2}
dict set d a 9
dict get $d a
```

- tclsh 8.6/9.0: `d` becomes `a 9` (dict set collapses on write); `dict get` returns `9`.
- tcl-vm: `dict_set_path` writes only the first slot, giving `a 9 a 2`; `dict get` then runs through `dispatch_canon` → `ValueOps::dict_pairs` (last-wins) and returns `2` — the value that was just overwritten.
- The same value run through the compiled `Op::DICT_GET` opcode (first-wins) returns `1` instead.
- `dict size {a 1 a 2}` is `1` in tclsh, in `runtime/rust`, and via `dispatch_canon`, but `dict update`/`dict with` (`Op::DICT_UPDATE_START`/`DICT_RECOMBINE_IMM`) see two entries.

## Why it matters

A dict literal or a dict built by mutation with a duplicate key gives a different `dict get` result depending on which of three code paths in the same VM answers the query — interpreted mutating subcommands, interpreted pure subcommands, and compiled opcodes all disagree with each other, not just with tclsh.

## Relationship to open issues

#1419's doc-note that `dictRecombine*` ignore the key path is the same opcode family (`Op::DICT_RECOMBINE_IMM`) but a different defect — that note is about the nested key *path* being dropped; this is about duplicate-key collapse and first-vs-last lookup in the `dict_pairs` primitive those opcodes are built on. Shape-adjacent to #1382 (tcl-vm vs runtime/rust numeric divergence) but a different utility.

## Cleanup

Delete both VM-local `dict_pairs`/`pairs` copies and route `exec.rs`'s dict opcodes and `cmd_dict.rs`'s mutating arms through `tcl_syntax::value::ValueOps::dict_pairs` plus `tcl_cmd_core::dict::{lookup, upsert}`, which are already generic over `ValueOps` and already implemented for `Vm`. The dead legacy `get`/`keys`/`values`/`size`/`merge`/`exists`/`create` arms in `cmd_dict.rs` — unreachable behind `dispatch_canon` — should go with them.

**Scale:** medium — touches `exec.rs`'s opcode handlers and `cmd_dict.rs`'s mutating arms, a well-trodden migration path since the pure-subcommand half already made the same move.

issues.title: tcl-vm `set_var` rolls the variable back when a write trace errors — contract and runtime/rust keep the stored value (C's `TclObjCallVarTraces`)
issues.body:
Found by the cross-surface centralisation audit following #1419's numeral-parser precedent (sibling of the #1371/#1400 legacy-duplication audit). The repository's own trace contract states the mutation is independent of the trace outcome; one of the two engines contradicts both the contract and C.

## The contract's promise

`docs/design/contracts/variable-trace-dispatch-and-introspection.md:67` states: "the value is stored before write traces run (… its error reshapes the result, it does not un-store the value)". The rule is restated explicitly at line 74: "never gate the mutation on the trace's success." `runtime/rust` implements exactly this — its `var_set` (`runtime/rust/src/interp.rs:2198`) stores first, then fires the write trace, and on error just returns `VarError::TraceError` without touching the stored value, with a comment (`interp.rs:2209`) that spells out the intent: "A write trace errored: the value is set, but the command fails (C's `TclObjCallVarTraces`)".

## What actually exists

`Vm::set_var` (`rust/tcl-vm/src/interp.rs:4222`) snapshots the old value purely for rollback (`let old = self.get_var(name);`, `interp.rs:4233`), stores the new value, fires the write trace, and on a callback error restores the old value (`self.write_scalar_raw(name, o);`, `interp.rs:4237`) — or, if the variable didn't exist before the write, deletes the just-created cell entirely (`f.locals.remove(&nm);`, `interp.rs:4241`). The module doc in `cmd_trace.rs` even documents this rollback as intended behaviour, directly contradicting the contract doc.

## Divergence

```tcl
set v 0
trace add variable v write {error boom;#}
catch {set v 1}
set v
# tclsh, runtime/rust: 1
# tcl-vm:               0
```

```tcl
trace add variable w write {error boom;#}
catch {set w 1}
info exists w
# tclsh, runtime/rust: 1   (the fresh variable was created and kept)
# tcl-vm:               0   (the just-created cell was deleted)
```

## Why it matters

Any script using a write trace for validation-with-side-effect (a common pattern — reject and log, but still record the attempted value) observes a different post-`catch` state depending on engine, and on the VM a previously-nonexistent variable can vanish again after a failed write, which `info exists` and downstream code will not expect.

## Relationship to open issues

#1377 is the optimiser's variable-trace *observability* classifiers (O109/O126/O104/O130 source scans), a static-analysis concern distinct from this runtime firing-semantics defect; no open issue covers runtime write-trace mutation gating.

## Cleanup

Delete the rollback in `Vm::set_var` (and the parallel array-element path): store, fire, and on error only wrap the result, matching `runtime/rust` and the contract. Fix the `cmd_trace.rs` module doc, and pin the post-error value in both engines' suites plus a differential-fuzz vector.

**Scale:** small

issues.title: Trace callback ordering hand-derived per engine per kind: runtime/rust fires variable traces registration-order, tcl-vm fires element-before-array and `enter`/command traces oldest-first — each diverging from C's order somewhere
issues.body:
Found by the cross-surface centralisation audit following #1419's numeral-parser precedent (sibling of the #1371/#1400 legacy-duplication audit). The trace contract pins one observable firing order; nothing in the tree shares the loop that would enforce it, so each engine gets a different subset of trace kinds right.

## The contract's promise

`docs/design/contracts/variable-trace-dispatch-and-introspection.md:32` states rule 1: whole-array traces fire before element traces, and within a list, ordering is newest-first (LIFO) — "Ordering is observable." C prepends trace records and walks head-to-tail, with an explicit reverse scan only for `leave`.

## What actually exists — three independent derivations

`runtime/rust`'s `fire_var_trace_resolved` (`runtime/rust/src/interp.rs:2606`) collects matches with a forward `.iter()` over the registration-ordered Vec — oldest-first, array and element interleaved rather than array-first. The same file's exec-`enter` loop (`interp.rs:2745`) gets the direction right and documents why: "C fires `enter` newest-first (the trace list is prepended; the loop walks it head→tail)... iterate reversed", using `.rev()` — the compensation the variable-trace loop above it lacks. `tcl-vm`'s `fire_var_traces_inner` (`rust/tcl-vm/src/interp.rs:3575`) lists the element-specific key first and pushes the whole-array key second — inverted versus C's array-first rule — while getting the within-list order right (`traces.iter().rev()`, `interp.rs:3584`). `tcl-vm`'s execution `enter` traces (`rust/tcl-vm/src/exec.rs:3097`) iterate forward — oldest-first, diverging from both C and from `runtime/rust`'s own (correct) exec-enter loop.

## Divergence

```tcl
trace add variable v write {lappend ::log 1;#}
trace add variable v write {lappend ::log 2;#}
set v x
# tclsh, tcl-vm:  log is "2 1"  (newest-first)
# runtime/rust:    log is "1 2"  (registration order)
```

```tcl
proc p {} {}
trace add execution p enter {cb 1}
trace add execution p enter {cb 2}
p
# tclsh, runtime/rust: cb 2 fires first
# tcl-vm:               cb 1 fires first
```

```tcl
set a(k) 0
trace add variable a(k) write {lappend ::log E;#}
trace add variable a write {lappend ::log W;#}
set a(k) 1
# tclsh:       log is "W E"  (array always before element)
# tcl-vm:       log is "E W"
# runtime/rust: registration order
```

## Why it matters

Multiple traces registered on the same variable or command are an ordinary pattern (logging plus validation, or layered instrumentation), and the fire order is part of the observable contract, not an implementation detail — a script relying on tclsh's documented LIFO/array-first order gets silently different behaviour on either engine, and the two engines disagree with each other as well as with tclsh.

## Relationship to open issues

#1377 covers the optimiser's three observability scans, a static-analysis concern, not runtime dispatch order. #1412 is runtime rename-table bugs, unrelated. `docs/design/runtime/trace-implementation.md:80` already records the registration-order scan as an as-built fact, but no issue tracks it as a contract violation.

## Cleanup

Centralise the per-kind firing plan (scan direction per op, array-before-element grouping, stop-on-first-read/write-error) in `tcl-cmd-core::trace` — an order-selecting iterator adapter both engines drive their own storage through — and add tclsh-pinned multi-trace ordering vectors to both suites and the differential fuzzer.

**Scale:** medium

issues.title: `namespace origin` in tcl-vm returns the *caller's* qualification, never the import source or the resolved command — and `namespace which -variable` answers with proc locals
issues.body:
Found by the cross-surface centralisation audit following #1419's numeral-parser precedent (sibling of the #1371/#1400 legacy-duplication audit). tcl-vm hand-rolls `namespace origin` and `namespace which -variable` instead of routing them through a shared resolution core, and both give wrong answers.

## tcl-vm's hand-rolled `origin` and `which -variable`

`rust/tcl-vm/src/cmd_namespace.rs`'s `namespace` dispatch routes `current`/`qualifiers`/`tail`/`exists`/`parent`/`children`/`which -command` through the shared `tcl_cmd_core::namespace` cores, but the very next arm hand-rolls `origin` (`cmd_namespace.rs:182-191`) as `vm.qualify_name(name)` (`:188`) — a bare current-namespace prefix, not a resolution and not an import walk. Its own comment claims "we do not track import provenance", yet the VM *does* keep `imported_commands: HashMap<String, String>` (`rust/tcl-vm/src/interp.rs:457`, canonical key → origin FQN), already used by `namespace forget`. `namespace which -variable` (`cmd_namespace.rs:172-177`) is hand-rolled the same way: the gate is `vm.exists_var(&name)` (`:173`), which follows call-frame locals, so a proc-local variable answers a namespace-variable query.

## The WASM runtime's separate, correct implementation

`runtime/rust/src/namespace.rs`'s `Namespaces::command_origin` (`:488`) follows `Command::Imported { source }` chains (bounded 64 hops) after resolving via `which_command`, and `which_variable` (`:470`) consults only namespace variable tables — `Tcl_FindNamespaceVar` semantics — ignoring proc-local links entirely. Neither of these routes through a shared core either: `rust/tcl-cmd-core/src/namespace.rs`'s `which_command` (`:90`) is generic over the `Namespaces` role trait, but there is no `origin` or `which_variable` core there for either runtime to call. The two runtimes give different answers to the same script.

## Divergence

Verified against tclsh8.6.16/9.0.4 (identical):

```tcl
namespace eval src {namespace export p; proc p {} {return P}}
namespace eval dst {namespace import ::src::p}
namespace origin ::dst::p
# tclsh:        ::src::p
# runtime/rust: ::src::p
# tcl-vm:       ::dst::p

namespace eval foo {}
namespace eval foo {namespace origin set}
# tclsh:  ::set
# tcl-vm: ::foo::set

proc t {} {set loc 1; namespace which -variable loc}
# tclsh:  {} (empty)
# tcl-vm: ::loc
```

## Why it matters

`namespace origin` is the standard way to find where an imported command actually lives (introspection, debugging, tooling); tcl-vm answers with the *importing* namespace instead, the opposite of what callers rely on. `namespace which -variable` leaking proc locals means a variable-existence probe inside a proc can silently return a bogus qualified name for an unrelated local. Both are wrong on every script that imports commands or calls `namespace which -variable` from inside a proc.

## Relationship to open issues

#1412 covers the WASM runtime's rename/re-home bugs — the opposite runtime and a different subcommand. #1373 (tcl-vm gaps from SpecTcl benchmarking) may overlap in spirit, but this is a wrong *answer* from an implemented subcommand, not a missing one.

## Cleanup

Add `origin` (and a `which_variable`) to `tcl-cmd-core::namespace` alongside `which_command`, generic over the `Namespaces` role trait plus a `command_origin`/`namespace_var` accessor, and have both runtimes call it; the VM already holds everything needed (`resolve_command_fqn` + `imported_commands`).

**Scale:** medium — one shared crate (`tcl-cmd-core`) gains two new cores, and both runtime call sites switch over.

issues.title: Legacy `trace variable`/`vdelete`/`vinfo`: tcl-vm hand-rolls a permissive `rwua` parser beside the shared `parse_legacy_variable_ops`, runtime/rust omits the forms entirely, and neither matches the registry's TCL8X model
issues.body:
Found by the cross-surface centralisation audit following #1419's numeral-parser precedent (sibling of the #1371/#1400 legacy-duplication audit). Four surfaces implement three different behaviours for the same deprecated grammar.

## Implementation A (shared, correct)

`tcl_cmd_core::trace::parse_legacy_variable_ops` (`rust/tcl-cmd-core/src/trace.rs:107`) is the shared owner of the 8.x letter-ops grammar: strict validation against `rwua`, C's exact `bad operations "…": should be one or more of rwua` error text, flag-style dedup (repeats collapse, since C stores the selection as bit flags), and the fixed `rwua` reporting order. The registry consumes it correctly: `rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/trace.rs:561` validates the legacy op string through it, and `trace.rs:1144` gates the legacy `variable` subcommand to `DialectSet::TCL8X` ("removed in Tcl 9.0").

## Implementation B (private, divergent) and Implementation C (missing)

`tcl-vm`'s `legacy_variable` (`rust/tcl-vm/src/cmd_trace.rs:168`) re-derives the grammar as a `filter_map` over characters instead of calling the shared parser: an invalid letter is silently dropped rather than erroring, repeated letters are kept rather than deduped, and the input's own spelling order is preserved rather than canonicalised — so `trace remove variable`/`trace vdelete` exact-match removal fails against a registration spelled with the letters in a different order, something C's flag model treats as equal. The `"variable"`/`"vdelete"`/`"vinfo"` arms (`cmd_trace.rs:53`) are unconditional, offered at every dialect though C 9.0 removed them. `runtime/rust` implements none of the three legacy forms in any dialect: any of those words falls to the generic `bad option` branch (`runtime/rust/src/cmd_trace.rs:260`), even under the runtime's own 8.x emulation modes.

## Divergence

```tcl
trace variable x q cb
# tclsh 8.6:  error "bad operations \"q\": should be one or more of rwua"
# tcl-vm:      succeeds, installing a never-firing empty-ops trace
# runtime/rust: error "bad option \"variable\": must be add, info, or remove"
```

```tcl
trace variable x wr cb
trace remove variable x {read write} cb
trace info variable x
# tclsh:  empty (ops dedup and are spelling-insensitive)
# tcl-vm:  the trace survives -- stored ops [write, read] never exact-match [read, write]
```

## Why it matters

Legacy iRules and Tcl 8.x scripts using the single-letter trace form get three different outcomes across the engines: a silent install-with-no-effect on the VM for a typo'd op string, an outright "bad option" rejection on the WASM runtime even in 8.x emulation, and a trace that cannot be removed by an equivalent-but-differently-spelled op list.

## Relationship to open issues

No open issue touches `trace`'s legacy surface; #1377 (optimiser observability) and #1419's doc-notes are unrelated.

## Cleanup

Route the VM's `legacy_variable` through `parse_legacy_variable_ops` (error propagation plus the canonical op set), render `vinfo` from the canonical set as C's letter string, and gate the three legacy arms on the interp's dialect. Give `runtime/rust` the same thin adapter for its 8.x modes. Legacy forms are 8.4-8.6 only — the registry already has this right (`TCL8X`); `tcl-vm` offers them under every dialect and `runtime/rust` under none, despite carrying other 8.x fallbacks elsewhere.

**Scale:** small

issues.title: `namespace export -clear` never clears in tcl-vm and both runtimes ignore the registry's tclsh-pinned `max_leading_option_words: Some(1)` for `export`/`import`
issues.body:
Found by the cross-surface centralisation audit following #1419's numeral-parser precedent (sibling of the #1371/#1400 legacy-duplication audit). One registry-declared, tclsh-pinned fact about how many leading flag words `namespace export`/`import` consume is encoded three different ways at runtime, and two of the three are wrong.

## The registry's tclsh-pinned rule

`rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/namespace_.rs` declares, with the tclsh 8.6.14/9.0.4 probes written into the spec comment, that `namespace export` and `namespace import` consume **at most one leading** flag word — a second or trailing `-clear`/`-force` is an ordinary pattern. `export`'s entry sets `max_leading_option_words: Some(1)` (`:843`), with the comment above it citing `namespace export -clear -clear p` and `namespace export a -clear` against tclsh. `import`'s entry sets the same field (`:901`), pinning `namespace import ::src::p -force` → `no namespace specified in import pattern "-force"`. The analyser reads this field at `rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs:9121` — the only consumer of the declared fact.

## Three encodings, two wrong

`rust/tcl-vm/src/cmd_namespace.rs`'s `export` arm filters *every* word equal to `-clear` out of the pattern list (`.filter(|p| p != "-clear")`, `:198`) and calls `add_exports`, which only ever appends (`rust/tcl-vm/src/interp.rs:3007`, `add_exports`'s `extend_from_slice`) — nothing in the VM ever empties `ns_exports`, so `namespace export -clear` is a silent no-op that never clears. `-force` gets the identical at-any-position filter for `import` (`cmd_namespace.rs:207`: `if &*pat == "-force" { continue; }`). `runtime/rust/src/cmd_namespace.rs` consumes a flag at *any* position while `patterns` is still empty (`:326`: `if patterns.is_empty() && b == b"-clear"`, and `:366` the same shape for `-force`), so a second `-clear`/`-force` is swallowed instead of becoming a pattern.

## Divergence

Verified against tclsh8.6.16:

```tcl
namespace eval e1 {namespace export a b; namespace export -clear; namespace export}
# tclsh:  {}
# tcl-vm: a b   (still exported)

namespace export -clear -clear x; namespace export
# tclsh:        -clear x
# tcl-vm:       x
# runtime/rust: x

namespace import ::s3::q -force
# tclsh:         error: no namespace specified in import pattern "-force"
# tcl-vm:        silently imports q
# runtime/rust:  errors, but with the wrong sentence
```

## Why it matters

`namespace export -clear` is the documented way to reset a namespace's export list before rebuilding it; in tcl-vm it is a permanent no-op, so any script relying on it keeps exporting stale patterns. A second `-clear`/`-force` — an edge case, but one real Tcl treats as an ordinary pattern name — is silently swallowed by both runtimes instead of becoming an importable/exportable name, and `runtime/rust`'s import error text doesn't match tclsh's.

## Cleanup

Expose the registry's leading-option consumption as a small shared helper (`SubCommand::max_leading_option_words` plus the option table) that both runtimes call before pattern handling, and give the VM a real `clear_exports` so `-clear` is a state change rather than a word filter.

**Scale:** medium — touches two runtime crates plus a new shared helper, but the registry field and its semantics already exist.

issues.title: `TclPreventAliasLoop` implemented in tcl-vm but absent from runtime/rust: `interp alias {} a {} b; interp alias {} b {} a; a` installs fine and recurses natively without bound
issues.body:
Found by the cross-surface centralisation audit following #1419's numeral-parser precedent (sibling of the #1371/#1400 legacy-duplication audit). One engine ports C's cycle guard on alias creation; the other has no guard at all, and its trampoline recurses natively on a cycle.

## Implementation A (present, correct)

`tcl-vm` mirrors C's `TclPreventAliasLoop` on both alias creation and rename. `interp_alias_create` (`rust/tcl-vm/src/interp.rs:1676`) checks `self.alias_chain_loops(src, &src_key)` after installing the alias, and on a cycle it rolls the registration back and errors `cannot define or rename alias "…": would create a loop`. `alias_chain_loops` (`interp.rs:1698`) is the actual C-style chain walk, addressing cross-interp hops via stable `InterpId`s so it follows the alias graph across the whole interpreter tree. The rename path (`rust/tcl-vm/src/command.rs:521`) runs the same gate. `rust/tcl-vm/tests/cross_interp_alias_e2e.rs:148` pins the exact tclsh wording for an a→b/b→a cycle.

## Implementation B (missing)

`runtime/rust`'s `install_alias` (`runtime/rust/src/interp.rs:1448`) registers the `Command::Alias` redirect with no cycle check whatsoever. Its dispatch trampoline — `invoke` → `dispatch_alias` (`interp.rs:6436`) → `invoke` — is plain native recursion with no cycle or depth guard; `dispatch_alias` resolves the stored target and invokes it with nothing standing between a self-referential alias graph and the native call stack. The as-built doc's claim (`docs/design/runtime/rename-alias.md:198`) that alias-of-alias "recursion terminates when it resolves to something else" is false for a genuine two-alias cycle — it only holds when the chain eventually resolves to a non-alias command.

## Divergence

```tcl
interp alias {} a {} b
interp alias {} b {} a
# tclsh 8.6/9.0, tcl-vm: the second create errors
#   "cannot define or rename alias \"b\": would create a loop"
# runtime/rust: both installs succeed

a
# runtime/rust: recurses through invoke/dispatch_alias until native stack
#               exhaustion (wasm trap / abort)
```

`interp alias {} x {} x; x` (a self-alias) behaves the same way.

## Why it matters

A cyclic alias definition is a straightforward user mistake that C and the bytecode VM both reject at definition time with a clear error; on the WASM runtime the same mistake installs silently and only fails later, catastrophically, as an unbounded native recursion crash rather than a Tcl-level error the script could catch.

## Relationship to open issues

#1412 covers three different WASM-runtime faults (rename destroys an occupied destination, no proc re-homing, `interp` advertising unreachable subcommands); the missing alias-creation cycle guard is a different C guard with a different failure mode (native stack exhaustion), only noted as a VM-side extra in `rename-alias.md` §7.

## Cleanup

Port the create-then-walk-then-rollback guard into `runtime/rust`'s `install_alias` (and its rename path), reusing the VM's algorithm. As defence in depth, give `dispatch_alias` a nesting counter like the existing `CROSS_INTERP_DEPTH`. Add the cycle vectors to the runtime suite and fuzzer.

**Scale:** medium

issues.title: tcl-vm resolves qualified **variable** names with a hand-rolled `strip_prefix("::")`/`contains("::")` split, so `set ::a:::b` addresses a different variable from `set ::a::b`
issues.body:
Found by the cross-surface centralisation audit following #1419's numeral-parser precedent (sibling of the #1371/#1400 legacy-duplication audit). tcl-vm's variable-name path never canonicalises colon runs, unlike its own command-name path and unlike the WASM runtime's variable path.

## The canonical split (already used for commands)

tcl-vm routes command names through `canonical_cmd_key`/`qualifier_segments`, with a tclsh-pinned colon-run e2e suite (`rust/tcl-vm/tests/namespace_colon_runs_e2e.rs`) covering commands, namespaces, and import/forget patterns. `runtime/rust/src/namespace.rs`'s `var_home` (`:359-377`) applies the same discipline to *variables*: it splits with `tcl_syntax::naming::ends_with_separator` (`:366`) and `split_qualifier` (`qualifier_segments`), and `runtime/rust/src/vars.rs`'s `classify` (`:108`) routes every qualified variable through it.

## tcl-vm's hand-rolled variable split

`rust/tcl-vm/src/interp.rs`'s `locate_from` decides whether a name is "qualified" with `stripped.contains("::") || name.starts_with("::")` (`:4071`), having already stripped exactly one leading `::` (`:4070`: `let stripped = name.strip_prefix("::").unwrap_or(name);`) — and then uses the *raw remainder* as the global-frame key, with no run-collapsing. `ns_var_fallback` gates the same way, on a raw `name.contains("::")` (`:4524`). A colon run therefore survives into the key, minting a second, unreachable variable. `rust/tcl-vm/tests/namespace_colon_runs_e2e.rs:26` covers commands, namespaces, and import patterns — but has no variable case, so nothing catches this.

## Divergence

Verified against tclsh8.6.16/9.0.4 (identical):

```tcl
namespace eval a {variable b 1}
set ::a:::b 2
set ::a::b
# tclsh:        2
# runtime/rust: 2
# tcl-vm:       (unchanged) 1 — ::a:::b was keyed as the distinct entry "a:::b"
```

The same path also skips C's `can't set "::c::d": parent namespace doesn't exist` check, which real tclsh raises for a write into a non-existent namespace.

## Why it matters

`::a:::b` and `::a::b` name the same variable in real Tcl (and in the WASM runtime); in tcl-vm they silently become two different variables, so a script that reads back through the canonical spelling after writing through a colon-run spelling (or vice versa) sees a stale value instead of an error or the update. This is exactly the class of bug the command-name path already has a regression suite for.

## Cleanup

Route the VM's variable names through the same `canonical_cmd_key`/`qualifier_segments` seam the command path already uses (or better, a `tcl_cmd_core::namespace` var-home core shared with `runtime/rust`'s `var_home`), and add variable rows to `namespace_colon_runs_e2e.rs`.

**Scale:** small — one function's split logic, following a pattern already proven elsewhere in the same file.

issues.title: Safe-interp hidden-command table exists three times: `Traits::SAFE_INTERP_HIDDEN` in the registry (analyser W129 consumes it) plus byte-identical hand-copied 12-name `UNSAFE` consts in tcl-vm and runtime/rust that already miss `unload`
issues.body:
Found by the cross-surface centralisation audit following #1419's numeral-parser precedent (sibling of the #1371/#1400 legacy-duplication audit). The registry already owns which commands a safe interpreter hides; both engines hand-copy the set instead of reading it, and the copies have already drifted.

## Implementation A (shared, correct)

Which commands `interp create -safe` hides is a per-command fact the registry owns as `Traits::SAFE_INTERP_HIDDEN` (`rust/tcl-registry/src/traits.rs:819`), documented as mirroring C's `unsafeEnsembleCommands` row. The analyser's W129 safe-context gate consumes it generically — "the set membership is registry data; no command name appears here" — so the static-analysis side is correctly registry-driven.

## Implementation B (two byte-identical hand copies, already stale)

Both engines nevertheless hand-list the set as a local `UNSAFE` const, 12 names each with the same copied comment block: `rust/tcl-vm/src/interp.rs:2220` and `runtime/rust/src/interp.rs:5535`. Neither depends on anything forcing it to track the registry trait, even though both engines already link `tcl-registry`. The drift is already real: `rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/unload.rs:119` carries `Traits::SAFE_INTERP_HIDDEN` on `unload`, and a registry test (`rust/tcl-registry/src/registry.rs:3161`) asserts `unload` is in the safe-hidden set — but neither engine's `UNSAFE` const includes `unload`. This is masked today only because neither engine implements an `unload` command; the moment one gains a handler, a safe child interpreter will be able to call it. The `UNSAFE_PLATFORM` scrub lists (`interp.rs:2237` and `interp.rs:5556`) are likewise duplicated byte-for-byte, each including the other engine's backend keys.

## Divergence

This is currently a structural duplication rather than an observed runtime split (both consts happen to still agree on their 12 entries), but it is a latent divergence: the analyser reports `unload` as hidden in a safe interpreter (reading the registry trait correctly) while `make_safe` in either engine would leave it exposed the day `unload` is implemented, and editing one const without the other (e.g. adding `zipfs`) silently diverges safe-interpreter policy between engines with no test to catch it.

## Why it matters

A "safe" interpreter is a security boundary; a command the registry documents as unsafe but an engine's hand-copied list omits is exposed inside a sandbox meant to exclude it, and nothing in the current structure would catch the omission before a user does.

## Relationship to open issues

#1390 tracks hardcoded names in iRules/TclOO-unknown/auto_path/Tk checks — different call sites. #1403 is the `safe_on_uninit` field — a different trait entirely. This finding is specifically the `SAFE_INTERP_HIDDEN` encoding triplicated across analyser/VM/runtime.

## Cleanup

Both engines already link `tcl-registry`: derive the `make_safe` hide loop from the registry's `SAFE_INTERP_HIDDEN` set directly (skipping unregistered commands, as C's `hideUnsafeCommands` does), or at minimum add an xtask drift gate asserting each engine's const equals the trait set. Hoist the shared platform-scrub keys next to `tcl_platform::backend`'s key module. A registry-driven set can also carry dialect ranges (e.g. a 9.0-only entry) that a flat const cannot express.

**Scale:** small
