The argument's *compatibility text* for a quoted word is `${p} ${q}`, and `whole_var_reference` (`codegen/values.rs:65`) strips the outer `${`…`}` and returns `p} ${q` as the variable name. The emitted `tcl_codegen_var_get` fails, its null return is treated as a Tcl error, and `::top` stops silently.

The same string-shape heuristics gate `emit_var_get` (`name.contains('(')`) and the `AssignConst` direct assignment. All of them reparse an argument string, which `common-semantic-compiler.md` forbids; the leaf-invoke planner's `WordExpr` path already gets this word right.

Affected samples in the analysis tier: `t1-expr-control/11_while_loop`, `t2-values/20_lists`, `t2-values/24_regex`, `t4-scopes/41_upvar`.

## Fix shape

Retire `whole_var_reference` and the `contains('(')` gates from the WASM emitter; drive every direct operation from the structured `WordExpr` snapshot (phase P3 of the plan). Until then the `ChannelWrite` arm must decline any word that is not a single `WordExpr::Variable`.

issues.title: Replace non-injective flat command/namespace keys for colon-edge Tcl names
issues.body:
## Root cause

The shared constructed-name convention currently joins namespace segments and command tails with literal `::`. That encoding is not injective when legal Tcl segments begin or end with a lone colon. For example, these are distinct live command tokens in Tcl 9.0.4 but both render as `::a:::p`:

```tcl
namespace eval a: {proc p {} {return from-a-colon}}
namespace eval a  {proc :p {} {return from-colon-p}}
list [namespace eval a: {p}] [namespace eval a {:p}]
```

Nested literal-colon namespaces also expose unsafe string inversion: the constructed key for `a -> : -> p` is `::a:::::p`, and a written absolute spelling with the same bytes does not resolve because Tcl parses colon runs as separators.

## Required fix

- Give namespace and command identity a structured/token form (or an injective escaped internal key) below `tcl-syntax::naming`; do not infer ownership from rendered FQNs.
- Thread that identity through the compiler, registry consumers, TclVM namespace/command tables, procedure provenance, traces, aliases/imports, deletion, and LSP/workspace indexes.
- Keep Tcl display names and written-name parsing separate from internal identity.
- Add Tcl 9.0.4 differential coverage for `a:/p` versus `a/:p`, nested `a -> : -> p`, relative resolution, rename/import, trace ownership, and namespace deletion/recreation.
- Preserve dialect-aware parsing at ingress and centralize every consumer on the same owner.

Related token-lifetime work: #1751, #1753, #1755.

issues.title: Tracking: one Tcl parsing owner across tcl-lexer, the compiler, tcl-vm, and runtime/rust
issues.body:
## Where we are

The word-substitution owner landed on `claude/wasm-codegen-architecture-5exvpu` (lane `r10-word-parts`): `tcl_lexer::word_parts::decompose` splits a word or `subst` template into text runs, `$name`/`${name}`/`$arr(index)` references, `[script]` substitutions, and typed parse errors carrying C Tcl's exact messages, parameterised by `LexerConfig`. `runtime/rust` (`parse.rs`, `subst.rs`) and `tcl-vm` (`subst.rs`, `interp.rs`) now consume it; their private copies are deleted and `cargo xtask owner-resolution` has the row. Tokens already come from `tcl_lexer::Lexer`, backslashes/lists/numbers/booleans/expressions from `tcl-syntax`, and the dialect axis from `tcl-dialect`.

What still has more than one implementation:

| Surface | Copies today | Sub-issue |
|---|---|---|
| word components → `WordExpr` in the compiler | `tcl-compiler::segmenter` + `ir::CommandTokens::from_segmented` walk parts themselves | #1785 |
| command/word segmentation (command boundaries, `;`/newline/comment rules, `{*}`) | `tcl-compiler::segmenter` (owner per the contract), `runtime/rust::parse_script_with_config`, `tcl-vm` `command_end` | #1786 |
| parse-then-evaluate driver (C's per-command `Tcl_ParseCommand` model) | `runtime/rust` eval loop (per command), `tcl-vm` (whole-script up front, issue #1603) | #1787 |

Order: #1785 (after the `p3-native-lowering` lane lands, since it edits `tcl-compiler`), then #1786, then #1787.

## Done when

- every consumer (LSP, compiler, VM, runtime) reaches word components, command boundaries, and the evaluation-order model through one leaf-crate owner under `LexerConfig`;
- `docs/design/contracts/shared-utility-contracts-rust.md` names each owner and `cargo xtask owner-resolution` gates it;
- the tclsh-oracle sheets the `r10-word-parts` lane recorded (`rust/tcl-lexer/src/word_parts.rs` tests, `runtime/rust/tests/parser_gaps.rs`, `rust/tcl-vm/tests/word_parts_owner_e2e.rs`) pass unchanged through every consumer.

Related: #1646 (a bytecode-emitter defect that looked like a parsing one — R10 established the emitter pushes the raw `x\$y` literal for a quoted word inside a bracket word), #1586, #1576, #1603.

issues.title: TclVM variable observability ignores the compilation unit registry
issues.body:
## Root cause

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/var_observability.rs` resolves scope-alias transitions through `default_registry()` even when `CompilationUnit` already owns an exact registry/profile. Custom and SpecTcl-defined variable-cell alias transitions can therefore disappear from `top_level_extra_escaping`, allowing later slot/optimisation decisions to disagree with lowering and runtime dispatch.

## Fix direction

Thread the compilation unit’s exact registry into the shared observability scan and remove the hidden default-registry lookup. Keep transition interpretation in the registry-owned alias descriptor layer, not in command-name branches.

## Required coverage

- A custom registry alias transition changes top-level escape/observability facts.
- The same transition follows the resolved Tcl release/dialect profile.
- Default Tcl 9.0.4 behaviour remains unchanged.
- SpecTcl 1.x and 2.0 compatibility remains green.

issues.title: samples/optimiser: committed profile outputs predate the Rust optimiser
issues.body:
## What

The four committed profile outputs under `samples/optimiser/` were generated by
the retired Python optimiser and have never been regenerated. Re-running the
current Rust optimiser over `samples/optimiser/input.tcl` does not reproduce
them, so the directory documents behaviour the toolchain no longer has.

## Evidence

```sh
for p in readability standard full; do
    tcl opt --profile "$p" samples/optimiser/input.tcl \
        | diff "samples/optimiser/profile_$p.tcl" - | head
done
```

Roughly 20 / 52 / 72 diff lines respectively. The differences are behavioural,
not cosmetic:

| Committed output | Current `tcl opt` | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `incr count` | `set count [expr {$count + 1}]` | O114 no longer fires here |
| `if {${s} eq ""}` | `if {$s eq ""}` | brace-stripping differs |
| `return [expr {$r * $r}]` | `return [expr {$r ** 2}]` | different canonical form |
| — | `lassign {1 2 3} a b c` | new rewrite not in the goldens |
| — | trailing `# optimised: N rewrite(s)` summary block | new footer |

## Why this needs a decision rather than a golden refresh

`samples/optimiser/README.md` documents `readability` as including
`set x [expr {$x + N}]` → `incr x N` (O114), and the committed
`profile_readability.tcl` shows exactly that. The Rust optimiser is
deliberately more conservative: `optimise_incr_idioms` in
`rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/pattern_recognition.rs` gates O114 behind a
soundness check that needs the target proven `TclType::Int`
(see the `D5-O114 soundness gate` comment around line 349).

So regenerating the goldens would silently rewrite what the README claims each
profile does. Someone who owns the optimiser needs to decide which is intended:

1. **The gate is correct** — regenerate all four outputs and update the README's
   per-profile prose so it stops promising rewrites that no longer happen.
2. **The gate is too tight for this input** — `input.tcl`'s `set count 0; incr
   count` should be provably `Int`; if O114 is meant to fire there, the type
   fact is not reaching the gate and that is a separate optimiser bug.

## Already done

The stale *commands* are fixed in #1792 (the Docker native-CLI change): every
sample header and the README's "Regenerating samples" block now use `tcl opt`
instead of `uv run python ai/claude/tcl_ai.py optimize` and the retired
`server.` / `compiler.` / `shared.` module imports. Only the committed output
content is left alone, with a note in the README saying so.

## Done looks like

`samples/optimiser/` regenerates reproducibly from the current optimiser, and
`README.md`'s per-profile descriptions match what the committed outputs show.

issues.title: Centralize compiler frame reach and preserve exact composed eval, uplevel, and upvar distance
Key compiler effect summaries by stable procedure generation
issues.body:
## Root cause

`ModuleCommandBindings` can recover callable procedure bodies that are not present in `Module::procedures`, but upvar/global-write summaries only scan the single retained procedure map. Repeated definitions and moves also share one qualified-name target, so the parameter layout and effects of another live generation can be silently borrowed or missed.

## Required fix

- Publish the retained/recovered executable procedure-body inventory from the binding owner.
- Give callable procedure generations stable body identities, including parameter lists and execution namespaces.
- Build caller-frame and global-write summaries for every reachable generation.
- Resolve aliases/moves to generation identities and join only their actual targets.
- Fail closed for any terminal user target whose body generation is unavailable.

## Representative regressions

```tcl
namespace eval ::n [list proc writer {} {upvar 1 x y; ::set y 2}]
proc p {} {}
rename p old
proc p {} {upvar 1 x y; ::set y 2}
```

issues.title: Compiler scalar CFG ignores unresolved-command handler barrier traits
issues.body:
## Current status

Published in PR #2196 at 49ff9148f19abccd35d5e0eb5dcda5cb2f4ea2e4. Both required local gates passed, and fresh Codex review is requested. Deep CI found the native selection regression #2236, which is being fixed before merge. This issue remains open until the corrected PR merges.

## Report

## Root cause

A missing literal command can resolve terminally to the registry's `unknown` handler, so the binding lattice reports an enumerable target. The handler declares dynamic/external execution barrier traits and Tcl 9.0.4 `unknown` can auto-load a command and invoke it via `uplevel 1`, but the scalar CFG does not project those terminal traits into a value/frame barrier. SCCP can therefore retain local facts across an invocation that may mutate the frame.

## Required fix

Project registry-owned terminal barrier/evaluation traits through the closed command binding at each direct and embedded invocation. Use one generic synthetic effect boundary for builtins, aliases, and unresolved-handler fallback; do not special-case `unknown` by name. Add Tcl 9.0.4 differential coverage for an auto-loaded command reaching the caller frame.

issues.title: info consts enumerates aliases and misses namespace global fallback
issues.body:
## Problem

Both Rust Tcl engines derive `info consts` from resolved variable values instead of direct constant bindings. As a result, an `upvar`/`global` alias can be listed as a constant even though Tcl only reports the binding itself, and namespace-scope listings omit unshadowed global constants.

## Tcl 9.0.4 oracle

```tcl
const G 1
namespace eval N {const C 2}
proc p {} {
    const L 3
    global G
    upvar #0 ::N::C U
    list [lsort [info consts]] [info constant G] [info constant U]
}
list [namespace eval N {lsort [info consts]}] [p]
# => {C G} {L 1 1}
```

`G` and `U` resolve to constants inside the proc, but neither alias is a direct constant binding, so only `L` is enumerated there. Namespace `N` lists its own `C` plus unshadowed global `G`. Qualified patterns must preserve Tcl names byte-for-byte.

## Fix direction

Make direct frame/namespace constant-binding enumeration part of the shared Family-B runtime contract, and put namespace selection, global fallback, glob matching, and result construction in one byte-preserving `tcl-cmd-core` implementation used by both engines.

issues.title: native tclvm does not implement TclOO private instance variables
issues.body:
## Reproduction

```tcl
oo::class create C {
    private variable X
    constructor {} {const X 123}
    method value {} {list $X [info consts]}
}
set o [C new]
$o value
```

Tcl 9.0.4 returns `123 X`. Native `tclvm --tcl-version 9.0` fails the definition with `unknown definition command "variable"`. The standalone `runtime/rust` engine passes the corresponding Tcl 9.0.4 `var.test` cases.

## Root cause

The native TclOO `private` dispatcher forwards `variable` into the generic definition-command switch, which has no `variable` arm. Its class/object model also has no private-declaration set or per-declaring-class mangled storage mapping, so treating this as an ordinary public declaration would not be sufficient.

## Required fix

Port the typed private-variable model already present in `runtime/rust`: retain class/object private declarations, map method-frame aliases to declaring-provider-specific storage, and keep automatic bindings tagged as TclOO instance projections for shared `info consts` semantics. Validate at least upstream Tcl 9.0.4 `var.test` `var-29.3` and `var-29.6`, plus inheritance collisions from the TclOO suite.

issues.title: Rename refused as a namespace collision against a variable that is not in any document
issues.body:
## What happens

Reported from CLion 2026.2 against a project whose only Tcl file is:

```tcl
set a 1
incr a
puts "$a"
```

Renaming `a` to `b` is refused:

> cannot rename `::a`: `::b` is already declared in this workspace, and renaming
> would merge two distinct namespace variables into one cell.

There is no `b` anywhere in the file, and no other Tcl file in the project
(the rest is `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, `src/`, `target/`, `.tcl-lsp/`).

The refusal comes from the collision gate in
`Backend::cross_document_variable_rename` (`rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs`,
around the `is already declared in this workspace` message), which refuses when
either `index.variable_definitions_qualified(&new_cell, "")` or
`index.documents_aliasing_variable(&new_cell)` is non-empty.

## What does *not* reproduce it

Two e2e tests added on `claude/jetbrains-broken-xaldw6`
(`rust/tcl-lsp-server/tests/e2e/rename_safety.rs`), both passing:

- `a_global_variable_renames_when_the_target_cell_is_free` — open that exact
  buffer, rename `a` → `b`. Produces the expected three edits `b`, `b`, `$b`.
- `a_variable_renames_again_after_the_first_rename_was_undone` — open as `a`,
  `didChange` the whole buffer to `b`, `didChange` back to `a`, then rename.
  Still proceeds, so a stale *open-document* index is not the cause.

So the gate is correct for open-buffer state, and something else is putting
`::b` into the workspace index.

## Leading hypothesis

The workspace index is built by scanning files **on disk**, and the two tests
above only ever exercise in-memory documents. If the on-disk copy of `test.tcl`
still contains `b` — the rename was applied and saved, then undone in the editor
without saving — then the index legitimately holds `::b` while the live buffer
holds `a`, and the gate fires against a cell that exists in no current document.

That would make this a precedence question rather than an indexing bug: for a
file that is open, the open document's content should win over the on-disk copy
when the gate asks what cells are live. Worth confirming before fixing, since
the same precedence presumably affects every other workspace-index consumer.

Reproducing it needs a disk-backed workspace test where the on-disk text and the
open-buffer text disagree; I could not find an existing harness for that shape.

## Also worth a look while in here

The refusal renders in JetBrains as a single unwrapped line spanning the whole
IDE window (see the report's screenshot). These reasons are written as full
sentences and some are long — the alias one runs to about 300 characters — so
they want wrapping wherever the host shows them.

issues.title: TclVM unset codegen loses source-aware option and array-element semantics in nested and qualified forms
issues.body:
## Problem

Direct proc-local unset a(k) already lowers correctly, but the compiler loses two-part array-element semantics in several other contexts. Tcl 9.0.4 passes base name a and element k to traces; native tclvm often routes through a generic one-part call and passes a(k) as name1.

Confirmed divergent contexts on rust at 1044adae:

- set x [unset a(k)]
- catch {unset a(k)}, including statement and nested-result forms
- eval {unset a(k)}
- a direct qualified unset ::g(k), which should use a stack array-element opcode

The current lossy string hook also misclassifies braced, substituted, and escaped targets such as unset -nocomplain {a($k)}, unset -nocomplain a${tail}(k), and unset -nocomplain a\(k\). Dynamic option words require whole-call generic fallback. Missing-unset errorCode metadata is also lost.

## Root cause

The unset codegen hook receives stringified arguments. Registry resolution marks those raw spellings literal, while the emitter separately guesses options and variable shapes with prefix/string parsing. Catch/result compilation does not consistently dispatch the registered unset hook, and runtime-compiled non-proc bodies prohibit stack element specialization.

## Required fix

Create one source-aware, dialect-aware unset invocation plan from CommandTokens/WordExpr. Registry data owns option and target positions; compiler variable-word resolution classifies proven local scalar, local element, stack scalar, and stack element targets. If the complete option/target layout is not provable, lower the whole call generically. Make the same hook usable in statement, result, catch-body, and eval contexts, with result disposition explicit.

Emit array-element opcodes only for proven two-part targets. Centralize missing-unset completion metadata so array misses use TCL LOOKUP ELEMENT key and variable/scalar misses use TCL LOOKUP VARNAME base.

Cover direct, nested substitution, catch, eval, qualified, braced, escaped, and dynamic-option forms against Tcl 9.0.4.

issues.title: range_semantic_tokens_no_spurious_refresh_when_converged is flaky: its request census is not scoped to the round it asserts about
issues.body:
## What happens

`semantic_tokens_reference_client::range_semantic_tokens_no_spurious_refresh_when_converged`
(`rust/tcl-lsp-server/tests/e2e/semantic_tokens_reference_client.rs`, the
assertion at ~L1215) fails intermittently:

```
assertion `left == right` failed: no workspace/semanticTokens/refresh must fire
when the coarse and enriched viewports are identical — a spurious refresh
flickers every open document
  left: 1
 right: 0
```

Seen on CI in `lsp-e2e-partition (2/3)`
([run 34198379740](https://github.com/bitwisecook/tcl-lsp/actions/runs/34198379740/job/101971664465)).

## Measured rate — it is pre-existing

Same test, same machine, `cargo test -p tcl-lsp-server --test e2e
range_semantic_tokens_no_spurious_refresh_when_converged` in a loop:

| tree | runs | failures |
|---|---|---|
| `origin/rust` @ 46213fe | 42 | 1 |
| a branch adding one `await` to `Backend::dialect_for_open` | 25 | 2 |

Comparable rates, and the branch's change resolves the dialect *identically*
(it reads an empty map). So this is a pre-existing intermittent failure, not
something a change introduced — recording it because it will keep marking
unrelated PRs red, and because "flake" is not a root cause.

## Why it fails

The test makes two different assertions, and only the first is race-free.

**The primary one is scoped correctly.** It reads the
`semantic_tokens.range_convergence.settled` log line for *this* round and
requires `refresh=false`. That line is emitted by the path that made the
decision, so it cannot race. In the CI failure above it passed — the log line
reads `refresh=false, outcome=compared-equal`.

**The census after it is not scoped at all:**

```rust
let refreshes = lsp
    .server_requests()
    .into_iter()
    .skip(req_since)
    .filter(|r| r.get("method").and_then(|m| m.as_str())
        == Some("workspace/semanticTokens/refresh"))
    .count();
assert_eq!(refreshes, 0, …);
```

It counts every `workspace/semanticTokens/refresh` that reached the client
since `req_since`, **from any source**. The refresh push is deliberately
workspace-scoped and debounced (`SEMANTIC_TOKENS_REFRESH_DEBOUNCE`), and the
`semanticTokens/full` convergence path has its own settled marker and its own
refresh — the doc comment on `log_full_convergence_settled` says as much:

> an observer needs a message-passing signal that the coarse-vs-enriched
> decision for *this* request has been made, rather than a fixed sleep or a
> wall-clock race against the debounced `workspace/semanticTokens/refresh`
> that only *sometimes* follows it.

The census is exactly the wall-clock race that comment warns about, one layer
up: a legitimately-emitted workspace refresh belonging to another round lands
inside the window and is counted against this one.

## Suggested fix

The census is a useful independent guard, so scope it rather than delete it.
Options, roughly in order of preference:

1. Take the census from the settled marker's own timestamp rather than
   `req_since`, so it covers only the interval after this round decided.
2. Have the refresh push carry (or log) the URI and round that asked for it,
   and filter the census on that — the settled line already distinguishes
   `served-enriched` / `compared-equal` / `refresh-suppressed`, so the
   vocabulary exists.
3. Failing either, assert the census only when no other convergence round
   settled in the window, and record the skip rather than passing silently.

Whatever the shape, the test should keep failing for the defect it was written
for (a *spurious* refresh on an equal comparison) and stop failing for a
refresh that another round correctly asked for.

## Notes

- Both `lsp-e2e-partition (2/3)` and the aggregate `lsp-e2e` job report it.
- The retry loop above the assertion already handles `outcome=cancelled` by
  consuming the refresh and re-requesting; this is the case it does not cover.

issues.title: clay::define declares no class to the analyser, so nothing in a clay-based file navigates
issues.body:
## What happens

`AnalysisResult::all_classes` is **empty** for a file whose classes are defined
with `::clay::define`. Measured over the corpus in `tmp/`:

| file | definer | classes recorded |
|---|---|---|
| `tcllib-2.0/modules/virtchannel_base/cat.tcl` | `oo::class create` | 1 (`::tcl::chan::cat::implementation`) |
| `tcllib-2.0/modules/httpd/httpd.tcl` | `::clay::define` | **0** |

`httpd.tcl` defines three classes this way (`::httpd::mime` at L45,
`::httpd::reply` at L319, `::httpd::server` at L734), each with a full body of
`method` declarations.

## Consequence

Everything that hangs off `all_classes` is inert for such a file: go-to-definition
and Find References on a method, Rename, Code Lens counts, Call Hierarchy, and
the method-dispatch provider walk. `method connect {sock ip port}` at
`httpd.tcl:773` has no references at all, including its own declaration.

This is not a callback-prefix gap. The registry-driven prefix walk works — it
resolves `after $delay [namespace code [list my Post $c]]` in `cat.tcl`
correctly, which is the same shape `httpd.tcl` uses at L1011/L1014
(`socket -server [namespace code [list my connect]]`). There is simply no class
for it to resolve *into*.

## Where it comes from

Found while adding a corpus-gated test for #1703 / #1704 over the real tcllib
files both issues cite. `cat.tcl` passes; `httpd.tcl` is unreachable for this
reason, so the test is scoped to `cat.tcl` with a comment pointing here.

clay is a `dialect`-style metaclass system: `::clay::define` is produced by
`::clay::dialect::create`, which is the same machinery #1571 / #1652 / #1655
analyse for its factory prefix. Those issues are about proving the *factory*;
this is the consumer end — even once the factory is proven, the definer family
has to be modelled for the class body to be walked.

Per the registry invariant, a new class system is "a `DefinitionBodyGrammar`
plus a `DefinerFamily` arm, not walker code"
([tcloo-implementation.md](docs/design/contracts/tcloo-implementation.md)), so
the shape of the fix is known even if the evidence work is not.

## Worth settling first

- Whether clay is in scope at all, or whether the honest answer is that a
  third-party metaclass system needs its definer declared by a SpecTcl pack
  rather than shipped in the registry.
- Whether the same hole exists for the other definer-producing systems in the
  corpus (`tool::define`, `oo::dialect`-derived definers generally). A sweep
  over `docs/CORPUS.md`'s catalogued sources would say.

## Done looks like

- A file using a supported definer family records its classes, and method
  navigation works in it.
- A corpus-gated test over `httpd.tcl` asserting `method connect` reaches its
  `socket -server [namespace code [list my connect]]` call sites — the
  assertion #1703's acceptance criteria wanted and that is currently
  unreachable.

issues.title: Command identity realm misses namespace-local shadows
issues.body:
## What

`document_realm_bindings_with_config` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/realm.rs:443`) builds `CommandBindingRealm` from a single **top-level** segmentation, so a `proc` declared inside a `namespace eval` body never becomes a binding fact. A bare call in that namespace still resolves to the global builtin, and every consumer of the realm inherits the error.

## Reproduction

Both of these are wrong under a `tcl8.4` target. The call resolves to the namespace-local proc, so neither diagnostic should fire.

```tcl
namespace eval n { proc format {args} {}
format %b 5 }              ;# W138 fires — pre-existing

namespace eval n { proc binary {args} {}
binary format q 1.0 }      ;# W202 fires
```

The top-level equivalent behaves correctly in both cases, because the realm does record that transition:

```tcl
proc format {args} {}
format %b 5                ;# clean
```

## Why it matters beyond diagnostics

`CommandBindingRealm::resolve` is the shared answer to "what command is this head, really". Its consumers include the version-gate diagnostics (`W138`, and `W200`/`W202` as of #2029), semantic tokens, inlay hints and hover. A namespace-local shadow currently gets the builtin's treatment in all of them: builtin colouring, builtin parameter hints, builtin hover text, and builtin argument diagnostics.

## Suggested shape

Fix it once in the realm rather than per consumer:

- Recurse into `namespace eval` bodies when collecting binding facts, recording the qualified name.
- Give `resolve` the caller's scope, so a bare head consults the enclosing namespace chain before the global table, matching Tcl's own lookup.
- Cover the new behaviour in each consumer: a namespace-shadowed builtin should get no version-gate diagnostic, no builtin semantic token, no builtin inlay hints, and no builtin hover.

A gate-local namespace check is the wrong fix. It would give one consumer a better identity model than the rest, which is the divergence pattern that produced the `binary` grammar drift #2029 removed.

## Provenance

Found by Codex review on [#2029](https://github.com/bitwisecook/tcl-lsp/pull/2029#discussion_r3969565822) against the new `W202` gate, then confirmed to predate it and to affect `W138` identically. Deliberately not fixed in that PR: the fix belongs to the realm and touches every identity consumer, which is well outside a binary-field-grammar change.

issues.title: Three tests assert less than their names promise (`irules_alias_dialect_accepted`, entry-protocol lowering, `empty_source_returns_empty_chain`)
O129 never folds `[self class]` in the spelling anyone actually writes
issues.body:
## What

The `TclOO` frame-constant fold fires only when *both* the outer command head and `self` are written fully qualified. The spelling real code uses never folds.

Observed at `rust` d88ed01 via `tcl opt --profile full`:

```tcl
oo::class create ::ticklecharts::C {
    method render {} { puts [self class] }
}
```
→ no rewrite.

```tcl
oo::class create ::A {
    method m {} { ::puts [::oo::Helpers::self class] }
}
```
→ `O129  Fold constant builtin command substitution`.

Every existing test for this fold uses the second spelling, which is why the gap is not visible in the suite.

## Two independent blockers

Probing `scan_module_command_mutations` on d88ed01:

| body | `has_runtime_selected_frames` | `trusts_proc_binding("::A")` | `trusts("self")` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `puts [self class]` | true | false | false |
| `::puts [self class]` | true | false | false |
| `::puts [::oo::Helpers::self class]` | false | true | true |

Note row 2: qualifying only the outer head changes nothing. The `[self …]` substitution alone trips both mechanisms.

**1. Frame opacity.** `oo_frame_for` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/propagation.rs:1000`) returns `None` when `has_runtime_selected_frames()` is true (gate at `:1008`), which it is for any body naming a command relatively. Added by #2042 — before that the same abstention came via the module-wide `dynamic` flag, so this is not a regression, just a relocation of the existing rule.

**2. Embedded-substitution opacity.** `apply_embedded_transitions` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/command_binding.rs:1843`) calls `mark_opaque_binding_mutation()` when `namespace.for_head(head_name)` returns `None` (`:1862`) — i.e. an embedded `[...]` whose head has no nameable namespace in a runtime-selected frame. That sets `dynamic`, so `trusts` and `trusts_proc_binding` answer false module-wide. Untouched by #2042.

Either alone is sufficient to block the fold, so both need addressing.

## Why this is not simply a bug to fix

The first blocker encodes a deliberate decision, pinned by three tests in `rust/tcl-compiler/tests/optimiser_codegen_residual.rs`:

- `runtime_selected_my_abstains_from_the_entire_method_body` (`:1058`)
- `an_instance_variable_never_propagates_inside_a_method_body` (`:1167`)
- `runtime_selected_my_abstains_when_the_target_can_reach_its_caller_frame` (`:1213`)

They assert that a body reaching any command relatively must abstain from **every** deep fact, "including the independent frame constant", because a receiver-local command can shadow the head. They cite the miscompiles behind #1096 / #1097.

While preparing #2042 I tried narrowing that rule so the natural spelling would fold. All three tests failed. I read them as specification rather than stale expectations, reverted, and scoped #2042 to the blast radius instead — so the frame stays exactly as opaque as it was. That judgement is the thing worth re-examining here, and it is a design call rather than a defect.

## The question to settle

May the lexical `TclOO` fallback justify the frame constant specifically?

The argument that it may: `[self class]` reads no variable, and for an object-local command to shadow `self`, something must *create* one. Within the module's closed world every such creation is a command-binding effect, which #2042's predicate already detects and answers with module-wide distrust.

The argument that it may not: the closed world is an assumption, not a proof. `namespace eval [expr {...}] {proc self ...}` or any construction the scan cannot resolve defeats it, and the pinned tests exist because that reasoning has produced miscompiles before.

I did not want to resolve that unilaterally inside a bug fix, which is why it is here rather than in #2042.

## If it is worth doing

1. Decide the question above. If the answer is no, close this and add a comment at `oo_frame_for` recording that the natural spelling is deliberately not folded, so it is not re-opened.
2. If yes, narrow the frame rule to permit only frame constants (never variable propagation), keeping the three pinned tests passing for the propagation cases they actually guard.
3. Separately narrow `apply_embedded_transitions` so an embedded head that declares no command-binding transition does not mark the domain opaque — the same shape as #2042's `declares_command_binding_effect`, applied to the second analysis.
4. Add tests in the *unqualified* spelling, which is the coverage gap that hid this.

Owner docs if it lands: `docs/design/contracts/command-binding-and-aliasing.md` (the "Frame opacity is scoped, name opacity is not" bullet added by #2042) and `docs/kcs/codes/kcs-optimisation-o129-builtin-command-substitution-folding.md`. The O129 note currently says nothing about `[self class]`; a section for it was removed from that note while #2016 was open, which is consistent with the behaviour as it stands.

## Impact

Missed optimisation only — the compiler abstains, which is the safe direction. No wrong code is produced today. The cost is that a fold the codebase implements and documents machinery for never fires on real input, and that the difference between the two spellings is invisible to anyone reading the tests.

## How this was found

While fixing #2016 (O107 emptying `TclOO` method bodies). The reported symptom was a method body deleted entirely; tracing why the frame fold did not compensate turned up first the module-wide trust blast radius (fixed in #2042) and then this.

## Related

- #2016 — O107 emptying complexity-guarded bodies
- #2042 — scoping runtime-selected frame opacity, which relocated blocker 1 and left blocker 2 alone
- #1096, #1097 — the miscompiles the pinned tests cite

issues.title: `MathFuncSpec` carries no result classification, so `type_infer.rs` keeps a second name-keyed table of the same functions
issues.body:
## What happens

`tcl_syntax::expr::mathfunc::MathFuncSpec` declares a function's name, the release it arrived in (`MathFuncSince`), its arity and its boolean-operand rule, but not what it returns. `expr_call_type` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/type_infer.rs:436` therefore classifies results by matching function names a second time, and the two tables can disagree when a function is added to one.

## What is expected

A `result_class` on `MathFuncSpec` (integer, double, same-as-argument, boolean, list-dependent), read by `type_infer.rs` in place of its own match, so the expression owner declares the result type once. The evaluation contract in `docs/design/compiler/value-evaluation.md` names this field and the retirement of `expr_call_type`.

## Where

- `rust/tcl-syntax/src/expr/mathfunc.rs` (`MathFuncSpec`).
- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/type_infer.rs` (`expr_call_type`).

issues.title: O100 specialises a callee to its single call site: `upvar 1 $name v` becomes `upvar 1 n v`
issues.body:
## What happens

```tcl
proc bump {name} {
  upvar 1 $name v
  incr v
}
set n 1
bump n
puts $n
```

Observed at `rust` 3b5eba8a, `tcl opt --profile full`:

```tcl
proc bump {name} {
  upvar 1 n v
  incr v
}
set n 1
bump n
puts $n
# O100  Propagate constant into command argument
```

Call-site seeding propagates the one call's argument into the callee and rewrites the callee's source. The rewritten proc is correct for this program and wrong for any other caller: `bump m` now increments `n`. The rewrite is sound only under a closed-call-set assumption (every call to `bump` is in this unit and passes `n`), and that assumption is not stated in the finding, not checked at the source edit, and not true for a proc that a `source`d file, a `namespace import`, an `interp alias` or an event handler can also call.

## What is expected

Either the seeded run informs the *call site* only (fold `[bump n]`'s effects where they are provable) and never rewrites the callee body, or the callee rewrite is gated on a proof that the unit is the proc's whole call set and that the proc is not reachable by name from outside it, and the finding says so. `docs/design/compiler/interprocedural-call-site-seeding.md` states the contract the seeding run is meant to keep; the proc-level transfer summaries in `docs/design/compiler/value-transfers.md` keep a `Name` parameter's binding per call site for this reason.

## Where

- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/propagation.rs` (`evaluate_proc_with_constants`, `seed_params_from_args`, the O100 rewrite over a callee body).
- `docs/design/compiler/interprocedural-call-site-seeding.md`.

issues.title: A `try` statement erases the definiteness of names bound before it: W210 after `try … finally`, and O109 deletes the `finally` body's store
issues.body:
## What happens

```tcl
proc p {} {
  set f 0
  try {error boom} finally {set f 1}
  return $f
}
catch {p} m
puts $m
```

Observed at `rust` 3b5eba8a:

```
$ tcl diag e4.tcl
e4.tcl:2:7: hint    W220     Assignment to 'f' is never read
e4.tcl:4:10: warning W210     Variable 'f' is read before it is set
$ tcl opt e4.tcl --profile full
  try {error boom} finally {}
# O109  Eliminate dead store
# O107  Eliminate unreachable dead code
# O100  Fold return of constant variable
```

`f` is bound at line 2 on every path, and `finally` runs on every path, so the W210 is a false positive and the W220 is wrong (the `return $f` reads it). The optimiser then deletes `set f 1` inside `finally` as a dead store and empties the body as unreachable. The program's observable output is unchanged only because the error propagates past the `return`; the same shape without the `error` returns the wrong value. `catch {for {set i 0} {$i < 2} {incr i} {}}; if {$i == 2} …` reports W210 for `i` at the `catch` line for the same reason.

## What is expected

A `try` or `catch` body neither kills nor hides the definitions that reach it: a name bound before the statement stays bound after it on every completion path, a `finally` body is reachable on every path, and a store inside it is live when the name is read after the statement. `docs/design/compiler/value-transfers.md` § `catch`, `try`, and completion gives the completion-path outcomes; until then the lowering of `try` must not present the statement as a definition barrier.

## Where

- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/cfg_builder/cfg_lower.rs` (`lower_try`, `lower_try_dispatch`, `push_try_handler_exception_edges`, `emit_opaque_catch`).
- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs` (W210, W220) and `optimiser/elimination.rs` (O107, O109).

issues.title: A proc materialised from a `subst -nocommands` factory has no span: its W214 is anchored at line 1, column 1
issues.body:
## What happens

```tcl
proc Configure {name default d} {
  proc $name {x} [subst -nocommands {return $default}]
}
Configure port 8080 {the port}
puts [port ignored]
```

Observed at `rust` 3b5eba8a:

```
$ tcl diag e6.tcl
e6.tcl:1:1: hint    W214     Parameter 'x' of proc '::port' is unused
e6.tcl:1:30: hint    W214     Parameter 'd' of proc '::Configure' is unused
e6.tcl:5:7: hint    W123     Unknown command 'port'
```

`::port` is the child the factory materialises at compile time (`specialise_factories.rs` extracts the template through the registry's substitution answer). It exists nowhere in the source, so its diagnostic is anchored at the file's first character, and the W123 on the call says the analyser does not know the proc the lowering created.

## What is expected

A materialised child carries the span of the factory call that produced it, so a diagnostic about it points at `proc $name {x} […]` inside `Configure` or at the `Configure port …` call, and the analyser learns the created command so the call is not unknown. The template-word plan in `docs/design/compiler/value-transfers.md` gives the materialisation its provenance.

## Where

- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/specialise_factories.rs` (`register_synthesised`, `extract_subst_nocommands_template`).
- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/usage.rs` (W214's span source) and the analyser's proc registration.

issues.title: The `expr`-trust gate misses a fully-qualified `proc ::n::expr`, so expression rewrites fire inside a namespace that shadows `expr`
issues.body:
Raised by Codex as a P1 on #2158 and verified. It is real, but it is **pre-existing and independent of that PR** — both `set` and `return` bodies have it, and `set` has had it all along.

## What happens

`ctx.command_mutations.trusts("expr")` gates O101, O110, O113, O115 and O129. It answers a flat, module-wide question about the name `expr`. A `proc` that shadows `expr` *for one namespace*, written fully qualified, does not register:

```tcl
proc ::n::expr {s} { return $s }
proc ::n::f {r} { return [expr {$r ** 2}] }
```

Inside `::n::f`, the unqualified `expr` resolves to `::n::expr` first, which returns its argument verbatim — so the value is the string `$r ** 2`, not a number. The optimiser nevertheless rewrites, measured via `optimise_raw_for_profile` under `tcl8.6`:

| source | result |
|---|---|
| `proc ::n::expr` + `return [expr {$r ** 2}]` | `O110` → `return [expr {$r * $r}]` |
| `proc ::n::expr` + `set v [expr {$r ** 2}]` | `O110` → `set v [expr {$r * $r}]` |
| `namespace eval ::n { proc expr … }`, either shape | **declines** — correctly |
| `interp alias {} myexpr {} expr`, either shape | rewrites (aliasing *to* `expr` does not shadow it) |

So the gate is not vacuous: the `namespace eval` spelling **is** caught. What escapes is the fully-qualified definition, and it escapes for both statement shapes equally.

## Why it is not #2158's bug

#2158 extends the `expr_simplify` family from `set` bodies to `return` bodies (#1962). The `set` row above is on `rust` today and predates it. The PR widens the exposure by one statement shape; it does not create the hole.

Narrowing only the new `return` path was considered and rejected: it would leave `set` wrong, and it would break the agreement property that PR exists to establish and pins with a test.

## What is expected

Trust needs to be namespace-sensitive rather than a flat global answer. `ModuleCommandMutations` already reasons about namespaces for a related case — `opaque_namespaces` and `import_shadowed` exist precisely so `namespace import ::lib::*` into `::app` does not distrust `::lib::helper` — so the shape is there. What is missing is that defining `::n::expr` must make unqualified `expr` untrustworthy *for bodies whose resolution namespace is `::n`*, while leaving it trusted elsewhere.

`trusts(&self, name: &str) -> bool` cannot express that, since the answer now depends on the caller's namespace.

## A second angle, from the original report

`Statement::Return` carries a `command_binding` naming the command the nested substitution actually resolved to. Consulting it would catch this case at the `return` site specifically. Worth noting the limitation, though: `Statement::AssignExpr` has no equivalent binding to consult, so that route fixes one shape and not the other — which is why the namespace-sensitive trust answer above looks like the real fix rather than a per-site patch.

## Where

- `ModuleCommandMutations::trusts` and the surrounding scan, `rust/tcl-compiler/src/command_binding.rs`.
- Consumers: `expr_simplify::{try_rewrite_assign_expr, try_rewrite_expr, try_rewrite_return_expr}`, `propagation::try_fold_return_terminator`, and the O129 builtin fold.

## Verification notes

All four rows above were measured against the real optimiser through the `optimise_raw_for_profile` helper, on a temporary probe since removed — not read off the source. I have not checked whether the same fully-qualified spelling escapes the gate for commands other than `expr`; the machinery is shared, so it probably does, but that is untested.

issues.title: O100 and O103 disagree about a shadowed builtin in one statement: `set v [llength {a b c}]; return $v` becomes `set v 99; return 3`
issues.body:
A clean miscompile of a **valid, runnable** program, and the two halves of
the rewrite contradict each other.

## What happens

```tcl
namespace eval ::n { proc llength {l} { return 99 } }
proc ::n::g {} { set v [llength {a b c}]; return $v }
```

`::n::g` returns **99** on tclsh 8.6.18 and 9.0.4 — the namespace-local
`llength` shadows the builtin.

The optimiser emits `O100` + `O103` and rewrites the body to:

```tcl
proc ::n::g {} { set v 99; return 3 }
```

So `::n::g` now returns **3**. The value is wrong, and the statement is
self-contradictory: `set v 99` immediately followed by `return 3` where
the source says `return $v`.

## Why this is not #2159

#2159 is the trust gate failing to *notice* a shadow. Here the shadow is
noticed and handled correctly by one pass: **O103 folds the call through
the shadowing proc and gets 99**, which is right. A second pass — O100,
copy propagation — independently replaces `$v` with the **builtin's**
answer, 3. Two passes hold two different answers for the same call in the
same statement, and the later one wins the return.

Not namespace-specific. A plain global shadow does the same thing:

```tcl
proc llength {l} { return 99 }
namespace eval ::n {}
proc ::n::g {} { set v [llength {a b c}]; return $v }
```

→ `proc ::n::g {} { set v 99; return 3 }`, same codes `["O100", "O103"]`.

## Measured

Through `opt_codes` / `optimised` under `tcl8.6` in the optimiser coverage
harness, against `tclsh8.6` / `tclsh9.0` for the truth. Probe removed
after measuring.

| program | tclsh | optimiser |
|---|---|---|
| namespace-eval shadow | `99` | `set v 99; return 3` |
| global shadow | `99` | `set v 99; return 3` |
| no shadow (control) | `3` | `set v 3; return 3` ✓ |

The control confirms the shape folds legitimately when nothing shadows,
so the rows above are not vacuous.

## Where

- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/propagation.rs` — O100's copy
  propagation, and O103's interprocedural fold.

Suspicion, not verified: O100 sources `$v`'s value from a builtin-fold
fact computed before or independently of O103's resolution of the call,
so the two never reconcile. Whichever is right, they must not both be
consulted for one statement.

issues.title: A computed `rename` still miscompiles a shadowed builtin — and O102 proves the names in the same run without feeding them back
issues.body:
The residual left by #2164's fix. It is a miscompile of a **valid,
runnable** program, measured, not hypothetical.

## Reproduction

```tcl
set a llength
set b mylen
proc mylen {l} { return 99 }
rename $a {}
rename $b $a
proc g {} { set v [llength {a b c}]; return $v }
puts [g]
```

tclsh 8.6.18 and 9.0.4 both print **99**. The optimiser emits
`["O100", "O102", "O109"]` and rewrites the body to `return 3`.

## Why #2164's fix does not cover it

That fix gated the shared value lattice on
`ModuleCommandMutations::observed_binding_is_the_builtin` — the
**named-subject** half of `trusts`: no shadowing `proc`, no `rename` or
alias naming the command, no opaque import.

It deliberately does **not** consult the `dynamic` "unbounded top" axis,
because a single unresolved command head sets `dynamic` (`foo bar` alone
makes `trusts("list")` false), so gating the lattice on the whole of
`trusts` would withdraw every builtin fold from any file naming a command
the registry does not know. That trade is recorded in #2164.

A computed `rename` raises `dynamic` **without naming a subject**, so it
falls in the gap: the lattice folds `[llength {a b c}]` to 3 and O100
publishes it.

## The sharper half: the optimiser proves the names itself

The rewritten source this run produces is:

```tcl
proc mylen {l} { return 99 }
rename llength {}
rename mylen llength
proc g {} { set v [llength {a b c}]; return 3 }
```

O102 constant-propagated `$a` and `$b` in the same pass, so the output
**literally reads `rename llength {}`** — the information needed to
distrust `llength` was derived by the optimiser itself and never fed back
into the trust gate. The command-mutation scan runs once, before
propagation, and nothing re-asks it afterwards.

That suggests a fix narrower than "narrow the `dynamic`
over-approximation": re-run (or incrementally update) the mutation scan
after constant propagation resolves a computed `rename`/`interp alias`
operand, and re-gate. A command whose rename target the optimiser has
just proved is no longer a dynamic unknown.

## Why it is not simply "make `dynamic` gate the lattice"

That is the other available fix and it is a real option, but it costs the
coverage #2164 measured: every builtin fold in any file mentioning an
unresolved command, plus a live analyser false-positive test
(`fp_obj_19_created_names_via_list_foreach_no_w307`, where `C create c1`
raises `dynamic`). Worth weighing against the narrower approach above.

## Status

Pre-existing rather than a regression — before #2164 the lattice had no
trust gate at all and got this wrong too, along with the literal shadow
cases that are now fixed. Filed so the remaining hole is on the record
with a concrete repro rather than living only in a commit message.

## Where

- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/sccp.rs` — `try_fold_cmd_subst`, `FoldTrust`.
- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/command_binding.rs` —
  `observed_binding_is_the_builtin`, the `dynamic` axis, and
  `scan_module_command_mutations`, which runs before propagation.
- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/propagation.rs` — O102, which resolves
  the operands.

issues.title: `info consts` lists a TclOO instance projection the method body actually references, where C stops listing it
issues.body:
`info consts` inside a method enumerates an automatic TclOO instance-variable projection even when the method body **references** that variable. C stops listing it once the body does.

Measured on tclsh 9.0.4 and 9.1b0 (identical) against `tclvm --tcl-version 9.0`.

## The divergence

```tcl
oo::class create N { variable pub; constructor {} {const pub 7}; method m {} {list [info consts]} }
oo::class create R { variable pub; constructor {} {const pub 7}; method m {} {list $pub [info consts]} }
oo::class create I { variable pub; constructor {} {const pub 7}; method m {} {list [info exists pub] [info consts]} }
oo::class create S { variable pub; constructor {} {const pub 7}; method m {} {set q $pub; list [info consts]} }
```

| method body | C | `tclvm` |
|---|---|---|
| never mentions `pub` | `pub` | `pub` ✅ |
| reads `$pub` | `{}` | **`pub`** |
| `info exists pub` | `{}` | **`pub`** |
| `set q $pub` | `{}` | **`pub`** |

So the discriminator is whether the body *references* the declared variable, not whether the storage is constant. Referencing it gives the method a compiled local slot for that name, and C's enumeration then does not report it; the projection is still live, since `$pub` reads 7 and `info constant pub` answers 1 in the same frame.

## Where it is

`Vm::const_names` (`rust/tcl-vm/src/interp.rs`) reports a link whenever its origin is `FrameLinkOrigin::TclOoInstance` and the target is constant:

```rust
Local::Link(target) => {
    cell.link_origin() == FrameLinkOrigin::TclOoInstance
        && self.const_vars.contains(target)
}
```

That condition has no term for whether the body compiled a reference to the name, so all four rows above answer the same way.

## Not the whole story — the current behaviour is right for the common case

The listing rule is genuinely two-sided, and `info_consts_includes_only_tcloo_instance_links` already pins the half we get right: a projection the body does **not** reference *is* listed, unlike an ordinary `upvar`/`global` alias, which never is. Upstream `var.test` var-29.3 and var-29.6 depend on that too — their `checkList` is a separate method that does not touch `X`, which is exactly why they expect `X`.

So this is not "stop reporting TclOO links". It is the missing second term: report the projection **unless** this activation has a compiled local slot for that name.

## Worth checking while fixing

- Whether the rule is really "body references the name" or "the name has a compiled LVT slot in this method's bytecode" — they coincide in every case above, and the second is what C's `TclInfoConstsCmd` can actually see.
- The same question for `info vars`, which reports `pub` in every row above on both engines, so it is not affected — useful as a control.

## Not a regression

Pre-existing, and independent of TIP 500: every row above uses a plain `variable`, no `private`. Found while implementing #1933, whose repro (`list $X [info consts]`) references `X` and so lands on the wrong row — which is also why that issue's stated expectation of `123 X` does not match tclsh, which gives `123 {}`.

## Related

- #1933 — TclOO private instance variables, where this surfaced
- `rust/tcl-vm/tests/cmd_info_prefix_e2e.rs::info_consts_includes_only_tcloo_instance_links` — pins the half that is correct

issues.title: tcltest parity sweep omits 68 upstream Tcl 9 test files, including portable core suites
issues.body:
Audited rust 2118dc20392d0550f29132e86988d14e191acf38 against the full Tcl 9.0.4 release tree.

rust/xtask/src/tcltest_sweep.rs selects 101 hardcoded TIERS stems; upstream tests/ contains 169 .test files. The default sweep therefore never attempts 68 files. Portable omissions include binary, encoding, env, init, package, tcltest, tm, utf, utfext, util, autoMkindex, and pkgMkIndex. Several are already described as core in docs/design/runtime/tcl-test-tiers.md.

Make the upstream directory inventory authoritative or add a completeness gate that accounts for every .test file. Classify remaining suites explicitly, allowing only justified platform, unavailable host-capability, and C-only internal-probe exclusions. Unsupported portable VM semantics must remain visible failures. Retain the real upstream init.tcl and tcltest.tcl; both vendored files currently match the downloaded originals byte-for-byte.

The C and VM can legitimately report different skip counts for backend-specific capabilities; identical skip counts are not an acceptance criterion. The current overlay has no effect on native C for the existing 101 stems, so that is not the reported defect.

Acceptance: omitted core suites are attempted; every upstream file is accounted for; unknown newly added files fail the inventory gate or run automatically; exclusions carry narrow, documented reasons; a measured C/VM result records failures and timeouts honestly.

Found during the requested TclVM parity audit, using a GPT-5.6 Luna subagent.

issues.title: tclvm: a qualified interp alias under a new parent namespace is not dispatchable
issues.body:
Found while tracing #2188 with real Tcl 9 package.tcl, whose final statement creates `::pkg::create` using interp alias.

Reduced witness:
```tcl
interp alias {} ::fresh::alias {} list
puts [list [namespace exists ::fresh] [namespace which -command ::fresh::alias] [catch {::fresh::alias value} result] $result]
```
C Tcl 9.0.4 returns `1 ::fresh::alias 0 value`. The baseline VM returns `1 {} 1 {invalid command name "::fresh::alias"}`. Thus namespace existence alone is insufficient: the alias is not reachable through ordinary resolution/dispatch after its qualified parent is created implicitly.

Fix the generic alias destination namespace/command identity registration seam, preserving namespace incarnations and alias ownership. Do not special-case pkg::create. Cover a fresh parent, nested parent, existing namespace, namespace which and actual invocation against C9.

Taking this together with the child-startup portion of #2188, as a separate named defect. The standard-library source must remain unchanged.

issues.title: `catch` does not write an array-element result variable
issues.body:
Found while reviewing #2207's `catch` inlining, but **pre-existing and unrelated to it** — reproduces identically on `3215695`, before any of that work.

## What happens

An array element as `catch`'s result variable is never written:

```tcl
catch {set x ok} a(key)
puts "a=[info exists a] akey=[info exists a(key)]"
```

| | |
|---|---|
| tclsh 9.0.4 | `a=1 akey=1` (and `$a(key)` is `ok`) |
| `tclvm` | `a=0 akey=0` |

Same at the top level and inside a procedure, and the same on `3215695`, so it is the opaque `catch` path rather than anything to do with inlining.

## Why it is worth a separate issue

#2207's inline path had its own, *different* wrong answer here (`a=1 akey=0` — it wrote a scalar `a`, because lowering normalises `a(key)` to `a`). That is fixed by keeping non-literal destinations on the opaque path, which is where this issue starts: the opaque path does not write the element either.

So `catch {…} a(key)` is wrong today, was wrong before #2207, and is still wrong after it — just consistently rather than in two ways.

## Scope

Worth checking whether the options variable (`catch {…} m a(key)`) and the same shapes on `try`'s handler variables have the same gap, and whether a qualified destination (`catch {…} ::ns::v`) is written correctly.

issues.title: `existStk` re-resolves an already-resolved braced variable name, so `info exists {{zz}}` answers 0
issues.body:
Found while extending `info exists` inlining for #2207, but **pre-existing** — it reproduces without that change.

## What happens

A braced variable name reaches `existStk` already resolved, and comes back wrong:

```tcl
set {{zz}} V
set e [info exists {{zz}}]
puts $e
```

| | |
|---|---|
| tclsh 9.0.4 | `1` |
| `tclvm` | `0` |

`set {{zz}} V` creates a variable literally named `{zz}` (the outer braces are the word's quoting). `[set {{zz}}]` reads it back correctly and `info vars *zz*` lists it, so the variable exists — only the `info exists` answer is wrong.

## Where

`emit_inline_info_exists` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/codegen/cmd_subst.rs`) takes the compiled-local form when it has a slot, and otherwise falls back to `push_lit(name)` + `existStk`. The `existStk` path is the wrong one: the name it is handed is already resolved and must not be substituted or brace-stripped again, which is the same rule `variable_name_resolution_e2e`'s vectors pin for the *name* half generally ("a resolved name is never substituted again").

It shows up outside a procedure because there is no local table there, so every `info exists` takes the stack form.

## How #2207 relates

That change inlines `info exists` in statement position too. Routing more callers through `existStk` would have spread this, and it broke the pinned name-resolution vectors until the inline form was gated to the compiled-local path only (which is also what C does — it inlines where it has a slot). So #2207 works around this rather than fixing it, and the gate can be relaxed once this is fixed.

## Scope

Worth checking the sibling stack forms for the same handling — `ARRAY_EXISTS_STK`, `STORE_STK`, `LOAD_STK` — against a braced name, since the resolved-name rule is shared.
