issues.title: tcl-vm: the `Namespace` and `UnknownHandling` guard domains move on fewer events than the runtime's, and `namespace unknown` never invalidates
issues.body:
## What happens

The two lookup guard domains are moved by different events in the two runtimes, and both move on fewer events than their documentation promises.

Measured with a probe that issues a `Namespace | UnknownHandling` token in each runtime and checks it after each event:

| Event | `runtime/rust` | `tcl-vm` |
|---|---|---|
| `namespace path` | stales | stales |
| `namespace delete` | stales | keeps |
| `namespace export` | stales | keeps |
| `namespace unknown h` | stales | keeps |
| `namespace eval ns {}` (creation) | keeps | keeps |
| `namespace import` / `namespace forget` | keeps | keeps |
| `proc unknown args {…}` / `rename unknown {}` | keeps | keeps |

In the VM, `ns_unknown_set` (`rust/tcl-vm/src/interp.rs` ~5620) neither bumps the command epoch nor calls `invalidate_lookup_guards`; the four `invalidate_lookup_guards` sites (~4497, ~4905, ~5092, ~5569) cover `namespace path` only. In the runtime, the eight `invalidate_command_environment` sites cover the first four rows.

The doc comments on `GuardDomain` in `rust/tcl-runtime-api/src/guard.rs` (~46–51) describe `Namespace` as covering namespace membership and `UnknownHandling` as covering namespace and interpreter unknown-command handling, and `rust/tcl-vm/src/backend_registry.rs` (~256–263, `guard_domain()`) maps `DispatchDependencyDomain::UnknownHandling` and `NamespaceLookup` onto these domains, so the ABI promises invalidations neither runtime performs.

## Why it matters

Today the only issuer of a guard token in each runtime is `prepare_command_guard`, which also requires an attested command identity that is re-resolved live, so no compiled fast path currently depends on these domains alone. A future guard family that relies on `Namespace` or `UnknownHandling` by itself would stay valid across the events above.

## Reproduction (test-shaped)

```rust
let t = vm.prepare_command_guard("guarded", ID,
    GuardDomains::one(GuardDomain::Namespace).with(GuardDomain::UnknownHandling))?;
eval("namespace eval ns {}; namespace delete ns; proc unknown args {return 0}");
assert!(!vm.check_command_guard(t, "guarded")); // fails in the VM on every event; in the runtime on the last
```

## Proposed fix

Decide the contract and make both runtimes follow it: give the VM the runtime's lookup events (namespace creation and deletion, `namespace export`, `namespace forget`, `namespace unknown`) through `invalidate_lookup_guards`, move `UnknownHandling` in both runtimes when the `unknown` command is bound, renamed or deleted, and then state in the three `GuardDomain` doc comments exactly which events move each domain.

issues.title: Flaky e2e test under load: `workspace_symbol_waits_out_the_startup_scan` (tcl-lsp-server document_symbols)
issues.body:
`rust/tcl-lsp-server/tests/e2e/document_symbols.rs` (~678) `workspace_symbol_waits_out_the_startup_scan` failed once while the machine was under heavy parallel build load, with

```
the on-disk fixture's proc must be found on the first query: []
```

and passed on a rerun alone. The test's premise is that the first `workspace/symbol` query is answered only after the startup scan has indexed the on-disk fixture; under load the query appears to be answered before the scan reaches the file, so either the wait is time-based rather than event-based, or the scan can report completion before the fixture is indexed. Worth making the wait deterministic (block on the scan's completion signal, or poll the query until the fixture appears with a generous deadline) rather than relying on timing.

issues.title: W220 false positive: an assignment read only through a computed array key is reported as never read
issues.body:
## What happens

```tcl
array set a {x 1}
set k x
puts $a($k)
```

`tcl diag --dialect tcl8.6` reports W220 "Assignment to 'k' is never read" on `set k x`, although `$k` is read inside the array element reference `$a($k)`.

## Expected

No W220: a variable substituted inside an array element's key is a read of that variable. The read-tracking that feeds W220 does not descend into the key part of an array element reference.

Found while reviewing the switch selection work on the compiler branch; it reproduces on the current tree independently of that work.

issues.title: W220 false positive: a global assignment read by a procedure through `upvar` is reported as never read
issues.body:
## What happens

```tcl
proc p {} {
    upvar 1 go go
    while {$go} { set go 0 }
}
set go 1
p
```

`tcl diag --dialect tcl8.6` reports W220 "Assignment to 'go' is never read" on the top-level `set go 1`, although `p` reads it through `upvar 1 go go` and the call `p` follows the assignment.

## Expected

No W220. A top-level assignment that a called procedure reads through `upvar` (or `global`, or a `::`-qualified name) is read; the W220 read-tracking should treat a call to a procedure whose body aliases the caller's variable as a read of it, or decline the finding when the variable escapes into such a procedure.

Found while reviewing the switch selection work on the compiler branch; it reproduces on the current tree independently of that work.

issues.title: runtime/rust: `namespace forget` of a command imported from the global namespace removes nothing
SSA treats `::name` and `name` as different places at the top level: wrong I230/O112 fold, false W210 and W211
issues.body:
## What happens

At the top level a plain variable name and its `::`-qualified spelling are the same global, but the SSA name interner (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/ssa.rs`, `nonlocal_names_and_defsites` and the interner it feeds) keeps them as two places, so a write through one spelling is invisible to a read through the other.

```tcl
set go 1
if {[gets stdin] eq "q"} { set ::go 0 }
if {$go} {puts a} else {puts b}
```

`tcl diag --dialect tcl8.6` reports I230 (`$go` always true) and `tcl opt --profile full` rewrites the last line to `puts a`; tclsh prints `b` on input `q`.

Related false positives from the same split: `set ::g 5; foo; if {$g} …` draws W210 (read before set), and `set g 5; …; puts $::g` draws W211 (set but never used).

## Expected

At the top level (and in `namespace eval ::` bodies) `name` and `::name` resolve to one place, so writes and reads through either spelling meet in the lattice and in the read/write tracking. Inside a procedure the plain name stays the local unless bound by `global`/`variable`/`upvar`.

Found during the slice 6 review of the value-transfer work; it reproduces on the current tree independently of that work.

issues.title: A same-frame `upvar 0` alias write is not a write of its target: false I230 and W241
issues.body:
## What happens

```tcl
proc p {} {
    set go 1
    upvar 0 go alias
    set alias 0
    if {$go} {puts a} else {puts b}
}
p
```

`tcl diag --dialect tcl8.6` reports I230 (`$go` always true); tclsh prints `b`. The loop form

```tcl
set go 1
if {[gets stdin] eq "q"} { upvar 0 go alias; set alias 0 }
while {$go} {puts x}
```

draws W241 (provably infinite) although it terminates on input `q`.

## Cause

`upvar 0 target alias` creates an alias in the same frame; the alias-tracking that feeds the value lattice handles `upvar` to outer frames and `global`, but a level-0 alias's writes are not mapped back onto the target, so the lattice keeps the target's old constant.

## Expected

A write through a same-frame alias is a write of the aliased place (or the aliased place is marked externally mutable from the `upvar 0` onward), so the condition is not folded and the loop verdict stays undecided.

Found during the slice 6 review of the value-transfer work; it reproduces on the current tree independently of that work.

issues.title: O109 deletes a store that a `vwait` or a deferred script still reads: `vwait`'s operand counts as a kill, and callback reads are not tracked
issues.body:
Two related dead-store miscompiles in the optimiser; both rewrites change the program's output.

## 1. `vwait`'s operand is a kill

`rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/vwait.rs` ~260 tags `vwait`'s operand `VarWrite` (deliberately, so a never-set variable draws W210), and O109 (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/elimination.rs`) reads that role as a kill of the previous store.

```tcl
set x 5
after 100 {incr x}
vwait x
puts $x
```

tclsh prints `6`; after `tcl opt --profile full` deletes `set x 5`, the program prints `1`.

## 2. Callback reads are not tracked

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/deferred_writes.rs` records the writes a deferred script makes, but not its reads, so O109 sees no use of a store that only a callback reads.

```tcl
set x 5
after 0 {puts $x}
update
set x 6
puts $x
```

tclsh 8.4–9.1 print `5` then `6`; after O109 deletes `set x 5` the `after` script raises `can't read "x"`. The trace analogue (`trace add variable y write {puts $x ;#}`) is handled.

## Expected

`vwait`'s operand is a read-and-wait, not a write (W210 can be kept through a dedicated role or a separate check), and a store read by a deferred script, or by a `vwait`ed callback, is live until that script can no longer run.

Found during the slice 6 review of the value-transfer work; both reproduce on the current tree independently of that work.

issues.title: runtime/rust: `upvar 1` from a procedure called inside `namespace eval` cannot read the namespace-eval frame's variable
issues.body:
## What happens

```tcl
namespace eval ns {
    set x world
    proc up {vn} {upvar 1 $vn v; return $v}
    puts [up x]
}
```

tclsh 8.4.20, 8.6.18 and 9.0.4, and `tclvm`, print `world`; `runtime/rust` raises `can't read "v": no such variable` at every release.

## Where

`runtime/rust/src/cmd_var.rs` ~282: `upvar` links a `VarHome::Frame` into the `namespace eval` frame, where the caller's variable `x` lives as a namespace variable (`::ns::x`), so the link resolves to a frame slot that does not exist instead of to the namespace variable the frame would resolve `x` to.

## Expected

`upvar 1 x v` from a procedure called by a `namespace eval` body resolves `x` the way the body itself would (its namespace variable), as Tcl does.

Found by the differential fuzzer over the `tclvm`/`runtime-rust` pair (15 of 24 findings in one campaign are this defect; seeds in the 7210000, 7310000 and 7410000 ranges); it reproduces on the current tree.

issues.title: Writes inside a `catch` body nested in a command substitution are invisible to the value lattice: wrong I230 and false W210
issues.body:
## What happens

A `catch` whose body writes a variable is handled as an opaque statement when it stands on its own, but when the `catch` sits inside a `[…]` substitution its body's writes are not stated, so the lattice keeps the old value.

```tcl
set g 5
set rc [catch {set g 0}]
if {$g} {puts a} else {puts b}
```

`tcl diag --dialect tcl8.6` reports I230 (`$g` always true) and the optimiser folds the `if`; tclsh prints `b`.

The same root gives a false W210 (read before set):

```tcl
proc p {f} {
    set rc [catch {set fd [open $f]} err]
    if {$rc} {return}
    puts [read $fd]
}
```

`fd` is written inside the nested `catch` body, yet `read $fd` draws W210.

A computed `catch $s` inside a condition in a procedure has the same gap (no unseen-call marker or barrier is emitted for it): `proc q {s} {set g 5; if {[catch $s]} {puts err}; if {$g} {puts a} else {puts b}}` draws I230.

## Where

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/ir_helpers.rs` `walk_braced_expr_words` descends `Expr` words only, and `rust/tcl-compiler/src/cfg_builder/mod.rs` `embedded_subst_extras` / `command_reaches_unseen` do not apply the opaque-script walk (`opaque_script_effects`) to a `catch` found inside a substitution.

## Expected

A `catch` (or `try`) body inside a substitution contributes the same may-definitions, caller-frame barrier and unseen-call marker as a top-level opaque `catch`; a computed `catch $s` in a condition is an unseen call.

Found while reworking the opaque-statement effects on the compiler branch; it reproduces on the current tree independently of that work.

issues.title: A computed command head inside a command substitution is not resolved: `puts [$e configure]` with `$e` a known widget path
issues.body:
## What happens

```tcl
set e [ttk::entry .e]
puts [$e configure]
```

When a computed head (`$e`) appears as the command of a nested substitution, the analyser does not resolve it through the variable's known value the way it resolves a computed head at statement level: the unseen-call marker the substitution emits precedes the host statement, so the resolution that would classify `$e` as a widget path (a typed receiver) never runs for the nested command, and the call is treated as an unseen call with the widest effect. At statement level (`$e configure -text x`) the same head resolves.

## Where

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/cfg_builder/mod.rs`: `embedded_subst_extras` places the marker ahead of the host, and `call_is_unseen` has no receiver class, so a head whose value is a known widget path (or any typed receiver) is an unseen call at the top level even when the statement-level path would resolve it.

## Expected

A computed head inside a substitution resolves through the same receiver classification as a statement-level computed head, so a known widget path is a widget command (precision), and the marker is placed so that classification runs first.

Found while reworking the opaque-statement effects on the compiler branch; it reproduces on the current tree independently of that work.

issues.title: A `-command` callback passed through `{*}$options` is invisible to the deferred-script scan
issues.body:
## What happens

The deferred-script scan records the variables a callback script writes so the value lattice never refines them (an `after`, `bind` or `-command` script can run later). It asks only the commands whose registry descriptor marks a script word (`DEFERS_BODY`) and reads the word at the declared position, so a callback that arrives through argument expansion is never seen:

```tcl
set options [list -text Go -command {set done 1}]
set done 0
button .b {*}$options
while {!$done} {update}
```

The `-command` script writes `done`, but the scan sees no script word on the `button` call, so the lattice keeps `done` at 0 and the loop draws W241 (provably infinite).

## Where

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/deferred_writes.rs`: the scan reads declared script positions only; an expansion word (`{*}…`) on a command that can take a `-command` option is not treated as a callback it cannot read.

## Expected

An expansion word on a command whose descriptor admits a deferred-script option is a callback the scan cannot read, so it declines (every variable may be written), as a computed callback word already does.

Found while reworking the deferred-script rule on the compiler branch; it reproduces on the current tree independently of that work.

issues.title: Interprocedural summary records a global read through `[set ::g]` but not through `$::g`, so a body reading a global is judged pure
issues.body:
## What happens

The procedure summary in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/interprocedural.rs` records a read of a global through the command form (`[set ::g]`) as an effect, but a read through variable substitution (`$::g`, `$::ns::v`) is recorded as nothing. A body that depends on global state therefore summarises as pure:

```
infer_from_body("x", "return $::seen", "tcl9.0").pure == true   // no side_effects row
```

`infer_from_body` is the Studio's proposal path, so a command whose body reads a global would be proposed as a pure, constant-foldable implementation; the registry's whitelist scan that derives implementations refuses qualified variables on its own, which is why this did not surface as a wrong fold.

## Expected

A qualified or `global`/`variable`-bound read in a body is a read of external state in the summary (a `Variable` read effect on the global), the same as the command form, so `pure` is false and the Studio proposes nothing it cannot prove.

Found while building the reference-body derivation on the consumer-contracts branch; it reproduces on the current tree independently of that work.

issues.title: W210 false positive: a read inside a loop after a call the module cannot see is reported as read before set
issues.body:
## What happens

```tcl
foo
while {1} {
    puts $g
    set g 1
}
```

With `foo` defined elsewhere (a sourced file that sets `::g`), `tcl diag` reports W210 "Variable 'g' is read before it is set" on `puts $g`. A read of a never-assigned top-level name directly after unseen code is no longer reported (the unseen call may have defined it), but inside the loop the read is of the loop's merge point (a φ over the entry and the back edge), not of the entry version, so the suppression that looks for an unseen call ahead of a version-0 read does not apply.

## Expected

No W210: the entry operand of the loop's merge is the version the unseen call may have defined, so a read of the merge inherits the suppression (the check should follow the φ's entry operand back to the unseen-call record instead of requiring a version-0 read).

## Where

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/helpers.rs`, the W210 suppression that walks the `UnseenCall` marker sites (`UndefSuppression::unseen_call_before`) and `rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs`'s W210 walk.

Found while landing the slice 9 review follow-ups on the compiler branch; it reproduces on the current tree.

issues.title: An assignment's target word that substitutes a command is in no definition, so O126 deletes the whole statement
issues.body:
## What happens

The statement walk scans an `AssignValue`'s value word only. When the target word substitutes a command, the writes that substitution makes are stated nowhere, and dead-store elimination removes the statement with them.

```tcl
proc p {} {
    set i 0
    set a([incr i]) 5
    if {$i == 0} {return zero} else {return nonzero}
}
puts [p]
```

| Where | Result |
|---|---|
| tclsh | `nonzero` |
| after `tcl opt` | `zero` |

O126 deletes `set a([incr i]) 5` whole, `incr i` included, so `i` keeps its initial value and the `if` folds the other way. The same happens with `set a([incr i]) [incr j]` and with an `expr` host, so it is independent of the value-transfer work on the branch where it was found.

## Expected

A target word that substitutes is walked like a value word: its substitutions' writes are definitions, and a statement whose target word writes a variable is not dead.

Found while measuring the nested `catch` evaluation on the value-transfer branch; it reproduces on the current tree.

issues.title: tclvm: variable errors carry no C Tcl `-errorcode` (`NONE` where C Tcl says `TCL LOOKUP VARNAME`, `TCL READ VARNAME`, `TCL WRITE VARNAME`)
issues.body:
## What happens

The VM raises its variable errors with the right message but without C Tcl's error code, so `catch … m o` shows `-errorcode NONE` where C Tcl 8.6 and 9.0 give a `TCL …` code.

```tcl
catch {set nosuch} m o
dict get $o -errorcode
```

| Where | `-errorcode` |
|---|---|
| tclsh 8.6.18, 9.0.4 | `TCL LOOKUP VARNAME nosuch` (a read of an absent variable is `TCL READ VARNAME`, a bad write `TCL WRITE VARNAME`) |
| tclvm | `NONE` |

`unset` differs the other way: the VM uses `TCL UNSET VARNAME` where C Tcl reports `TCL LOOKUP VARNAME` (or `TCL LOOKUP ELEMENT` for an array element).

About 52 sites build these messages. The gap is visible from plain scripts, and it is also what a C extension sees through `Tcl_GetVar2Ex` / `Tcl_ObjSetVar2` with `TCL_LEAVE_ERR_MSG`: the extension host tests on the value-transfer branch pin nine such divergences against answers captured from tclsh 9.0.

## Expected

Each variable error carries the code C Tcl gives it, so `catch`'s options dictionary and `errorCode` agree with tclsh.

issues.title: runtime/rust: "invalid command name" carries `-errorcode NONE` where C Tcl gives `TCL LOOKUP COMMAND name`
issues.body:
## What happens

The WASM runtime (`runtime/rust`) raises the right message for an unknown command but no error code.

```tcl
catch {nosuch} m o
dict get $o -errorcode
```

| Where | `-errorcode` |
|---|---|
| tclsh 8.6.18, 9.0.4 | `TCL LOOKUP COMMAND nosuch` |
| runtime/rust | `NONE` |

A C extension sees the same through the C API: a `Tcl_EvalObjEx` that fails on an unknown command reports no code to its caller.

## Expected

The lookup failure carries C Tcl's `TCL LOOKUP COMMAND <name>` code, so `catch`'s options dictionary and `errorCode` agree with tclsh.

Found while growing the runtime's C API to a real extension's surface on the value-transfer branch; the tclvm engine's equivalent gap for variable errors is #2342.

issues.title: O109 deletes a scalar store that a later element store on the same name depends on: `set y 0; set y(c) 3` stops raising
issues.body:
## Program

```tcl
set y 0; set y(c) 3; puts [array exists y]
```

| | result |
|---|---|
| tclsh 8.6, 9.0, 9.1 | error `can't set "y(c)": variable isn't array` |
| after `tcl opt --profile full` | prints `1` |

The optimised source is

```tcl
; set y(c) 3; puts [array exists y]
```

with the rewrites `O109 Eliminate dead store` and `O102 Forward literal load of 'y(c)' from its single reaching definition`. The program is clean with `--disable O109`. The same happens with the two stores inside a `catch` body, where the message reaches the catch variable.

## Why it is wrong

`set y 0` has no read of `$y`, so the dead-store pass removes it. But the next statement, `set y(c) 3`, depends on the variable's kind: with `y` a scalar the element store is an error, and with `y` unbound it creates the array. The store is live through the kind it gives the variable, not through its value. A store whose variable later takes an element store (or `array set`, `array exists`, `info exists y(c)`, `upvar` into an element) is not dead.

This is the same family as #2346 (a removed store whose substituted value raises): a dead-store pass that counts only value reads.

issues.title: An iRules `when` handler's binding walk runs in `::when` while its binding sites are recorded in `::`, so every command in the handler looks unbound
issues.body:
## Program

```tcl
when HTTP_REQUEST {
    set x 1
    HTTP::header insert X 1
}
```

under the f5-irules dialect.

## What happens

The CFG builder takes the handler's command namespace from the qualified name `::when::HTTP_REQUEST`, so the binding walk for the body runs in `::when`. The binding sites for the body's commands are recorded in `::`. `command_binding_site_is_exact` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/command_binding.rs`) therefore fails for every site in the handler, `has_opaque_domain` rises, and every command in every `when` body is treated as a call to code the module cannot see. The IRULE1201 and IRULE5002 controls and the iRules I230 case show the loss once a pass reads the opacity.

## Expected

The walk and the recorded sites in one namespace, with no opacity for a handler body whose commands are the dialect's own.

## Where

`command_binding_site_is_exact` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/command_binding.rs`, and the CFG builder's `command_namespace` for `::when::` handlers. The branch's unseen-call marker does not read `has_opaque_domain`, so the iRules diagnostics keep working there; the defect is in the binding walk's namespace, on `rust`.

issues.title: A procedure's global-write summary misses a plain write inside its `namespace eval ::` body, so a caller's read of that global is folded
issues.body:
## Program

```tcl
set done 0
proc p {} {namespace eval :: {set done 1}}
p
if {$done eq 0} {puts zero} else {puts changed}
```

| | prints |
|---|---|
| tclsh 8.6, 9.0, 9.1 | `changed` |
| after `tcl opt --profile full` | `zero` |

The one rewrite is `O112 Eliminate constant if (condition is always true)`, and `tcl diag` reports `I230 Condition '$done eq 0' is always true; the alternate branch is unreachable` on line 4. The same happens when the body sits in a callback's lambda: `set done 0; after 10 {apply {{} {namespace eval :: {set done 1}}}}; after 50; update; if {$done eq 0} {puts zero} else {puts changed}` prints `changed` under tclsh and `zero` after `tcl opt`.

## Why it is wrong

A `namespace eval ::` body runs in the global namespace, so its plain `set done 1` writes the global `done`. The procedure's global-write summary (`collect_write_targets` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/cfg_builder/global_write_info.rs`) walks the `namespace eval` body with the procedure's own `global`/`variable` flag state, reads the write as a local of `p`, and leaves `done` out of the summary; the call to `p` then preserves the caller's constant and the branch folds. The body's namespace, `::` here or any named namespace whose variables the caller can read, decides which variables a write inside it reaches, and the summary should read the body under that namespace rather than under the procedure's frame.

issues.title: A `::name` write in the top-level body does not alias the plain `name`, so O102, O109 and O100 fold the stale value
issues.body:
## Program

```tcl
set z a
set ::z c
set w $z
puts $w
```

| | prints |
|---|---|
| tclsh 8.4.20, 8.5.19, 8.6.18, 9.0.4, 9.1.0 | `c` |
| after `tcl opt --profile full` | `a` |

The optimised source is `set z a; set ::z c; puts a`: O102 forwards `z`'s literal into the read, O109 removes `set w`, O100 inlines `w`.

## Why it is wrong

At the global frame `::z` and `z` are one variable, so the qualified write changes what `$z` reads. The escaping set (`escaping_names` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/sccp.rs`, over `var_observability::analyse_var_observability`) has no entry for a name written through its qualified spelling in the same body, so the top-level `z` is treated as a plain local and the qualified write is never a definition of it. The same gap reaches the predicate refinement on `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42`: `set z [expr {[clock seconds] > 0 ? "a" : "b"}]; if {$z eq "a"} {set ::z c; set w $z; puts $w}` prints `c` under every release and `a` after `tcl opt` there. A qualified spelling of a global-frame name should resolve to the same place as the plain name, in the same body and in `namespace eval` bodies for their own namespace's names.

issues.title: W210 is silent on a read after `unset` inside an `info exists` guard
issues.body:
## Program

```tcl
proc p {} {
    set x 1
    if {[info exists x]} {
        unset x
        puts $x
    }
}
p
```

tclsh 8.4 to 9.1: `can't read "x": no such variable` (exit 1). `tcl diag` reports `I230 Condition '[info exists x]' is always true` and nothing on the read.

## Why it is wrong

The read on line 5 follows an `unset` of the same variable, so it is unbound on every path, and the existence rung has an `Unbound` fact for the version after the `unset`. `emit_read_before_set_diagnostics` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs`) exempts the read because the `info exists` guard dominates it, by name, before the rung's fact for that version is consulted. The guard proves the version it tested, not a later version the body unbinds; the exemption should apply to the guarded version only, and the rung's `Unbound` fact for a later version should win.

issues.title: The W210 KCS note promises `info vars` and `catch {set _ $X}` idiom narrowing that the analyser does not do
W210 never reports an array element read once any element of the array is set
issues.body:
## Program

```tcl
proc p {} {
    set a(k) 1
    if {[info exists a(k)]} { puts $a(j) }
}
catch {p} m; puts $m
```

tclsh 8.4 to 9.1 print `can't read "a(j)": no such element in array`. `tcl diag` reports nothing.

## Why it is wrong

W210 keys the array as a whole, so once any element is set no element read is a read-before-set, and `a(j)`, which no path sets, is read without a report. The existence rung already distinguishes elements from the array (an `info exists a(k)` guard proves `a(k)` and `a`, not `a(j)`); W210 should key a literal element read by its element where the rung has an element fact, and fall back to the array only for a computed element.

issues.title: W210 fires on the short-circuited read inside an `info exists` guard's own condition, and its per-variable dedupe then hides a real unguarded read
W210 reports `array size`, `array names` and `array get` on a possibly unset array as a read before set; tclsh returns 0 or the empty list
issues.body:
`array size`, `array names` and `array get` do not raise when their array does not exist: tclsh 8.4 through 9.1 return `0`, the empty list and the empty list. W210 treats each as a value read of the array and reports "read before it is set".

## Repro

`puts [array size a]` alone:

```text
w210-array-size.tcl:1:1: warning W210     Variable 'a' is read before it is set
```

tclsh 8.4, 8.5, 8.6, 9.0 and 9.1 all print `0`.

A may-set array in a procedure:

```tcl
proc p {c} {
    if {$c} {set a(k) 1}
    puts [array size a]
    puts [array names a]
}
p 1
p 0
```

```text
w210-array-size-proc.tcl:3:5: warning W210     Variable 'a' is read before it is set
```

tclsh 8.4 through 9.1 print `1`, `k`, `0` and an empty line.

`puts [array exists a]` followed by `puts [array get a]`: W210 at line 2 (the `array get`), none at line 1. tclsh prints `0` and an empty line.

## Where

`existence_query_vars` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs` exempts only `info exists` and `array exists` (`IntrinsicId::InfoExists | IntrinsicId::ArrayExists`) from W210's value-read classification, so the `size`, `names` and `get` members of the `array` command (`rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/array_.rs`) are still counted as reads that would raise. `array statistics` and `array startsearch` do raise on a missing array, so they are correctly reads.

Found while landing the value-transfer work on `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42`; the report is the same on the branch and before it. Not fixed there.

issues.title: A `foreach` with a `::`-qualified binder is lowered as an opaque call whose body writes are invisible, so O109 and O100 fold a stale value (miscompile)
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
set i 0
foreach ::x {1 2} { incr i $::x }
puts $i
```

tclsh 8.4 through 9.1 print `3`.

`tcl opt --profile full` under every dialect:

```tcl
foreach ::x {1 2} { incr i $::x }
puts 0
```

O109 deletes `set i 0` and O100 inlines `puts 0`; the optimised program prints `0`.

## Where

`lower_foreach_dispatch` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/cfg_builder/mod.rs` (`has_qualified_vars`) keeps a `foreach` with a qualified binder as a `Statement::Call` whose definitions do not include the body's writes; `tcl explore --show cfg` shows one block, `call foreach ::x 1 2 incr i $::x`. The body's writes, `incr i` here, must be recorded as may-definitions of the call as an opaque body's are, or the loop lowered with the qualified binder as a write to the qualified name.

Not #2370 (a `::name` write against a plain `name`). Found by the adversarial review of the value-transfer loop work on `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42`; the lowering predates it and is untouched by it. Not fixed there.

issues.title: O103 folds a builtin's call through a same-named `proc` defined later in the file, where the earlier call ran the builtin (miscompile)
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
proc p {} { set x [string range foobar 0 2]; return $x }
puts [p]
proc string {args} { return SHADOW }
puts [p]
```

tclsh 8.4.20 through 9.1.0 print `foo` then `SHADOW`. `tcl opt --profile full` (identical under every dialect) rewrites `p`'s body to `set x SHADOW; return $x`, so the program prints `SHADOW` twice.

The whole-module trust rightly stops the lattice from evaluating `string range` as the builtin once a `proc string` exists, but `try_o103_proc_fold` then folds the substitution through the user procedure's summary (`const('SHADOW')`, three literal words, `args` accepts them) without regard to order. A procedure's own call before its definition is not folded (`puts [p]` before `proc p` stays), so the builtin-to-procedure transition is the gap. `redefined_procedures` gates only a procedure defined twice and `trusts_proc_binding` only `rename` and `interp alias`. With the shadow defined first, both calls print `SHADOW` and the fold is right.

Not #2217 (a shadowed `expr` evaluated as the builtin).

## Where

`try_o103_proc_fold` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/propagation.rs`: the fold needs the call to be dominated by the procedure's definition, as a call of the procedure itself already is.

Found by the slice 7a review on `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42`; pre-existing on the summary path (the literal `return SHADOW` folded this way before the slice).

issues.title: O109 deletes a top-level store read by a procedure through `global` when the name is later `unset` (miscompile)
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
proc b6 {} { global g; return $g }
set g 6
set r [b6]; puts "<$r>"
set g 123
set r [b6]; puts "<$r>"
unset g
```

tclsh 8.4.20 through 9.1.0 print `<6>` then `<123>`. `tcl opt --profile full` (every dialect) deletes `set g 6` as O109 "Eliminate dead store", and the rewritten program raises `can't read "g": no such variable` (exit 1) under every release.

Without the trailing `unset g`, or with `puts [b6]` in place of `set r [b6]`, the store is kept. In the larger program this was reduced from, every store of `g` before reads through `global g`, `$::g`, `[set ::g]`, `upvar #0 g v` and `info exists ::g` was deleted.

The procedure's summary is the same before and after slice 7a (no constant, no passthrough), so the decision is the dead-store elimination's. Related to #2297 by mechanism (a read through the procedure missed), but this one is a miscompile; not #2350, #2308, #2231, #2261 or #2370.

## Where

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/elimination.rs` (O109): a store to a global the module's procedures read through `global` is live at every call of such a procedure, whatever follows.

Found by the slice 7a review on `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42`; pre-existing.

issues.title: The purity scan takes a `foreach` over a qualified variable as pure, so O103 folds the call and drops the global write (miscompile)
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
proc p {} {foreach ::x {1} {}; return 2}
puts [p]
puts $::x
```

tclsh 8.4.20 through 9.1.0 print `2` then `1`. `tcl opt --profile full` (every dialect) folds `[p]` to `2` on O103's summary path, so the call is gone and with it the loop's write to `::x`, and the rewritten program raises `can't read "::x": no such variable` (exit 1) under every release.

## Where

The purity scan behind O103's summaries (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/interprocedural.rs`): the CFG keeps a `foreach` (and `lmap`) over a qualified loop variable as a plain `Call` holding its list and body words, and the scan reads that call as pure although the loop binds a global on every iteration. The same shape with a local loop variable is lowered into blocks and is read correctly. A `foreach` whose variable is qualified, or any binder the registry declares as writing a non-local place, should make the procedure impure (or the write should be counted among the globals the summary reports).

Found while redoing the slice 7a review's N2 on `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42`; pre-existing (the scan predates the slice). The related return-fold miss on the same shape (`foreach ::x {1} {return 1}; return 2` folded to 2) is the lane's own gap in #2393's rule and is closed by the slice's nits commit.

issues.title: A procedure that calls one defined later in the file has no transfer summary, so mutual recursion never summarises
issues.body:
## Precision limit (sound, no miscompile)

A procedure's transfer summary (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/interprocedural/transfer.rs`) says what a call to it does to its caller's places; the caller's lattice applies it, and without one the call widens every place it may write. A procedure has no summary when it reaches code the module cannot see, and the flow graph marks a call to a procedure the file defines *later* as exactly that: the source-order timeline gives the call the unseen-call marker (`SyntheticMarker::UnseenCall`), because at the point of the caller's definition the callee is not yet bound.

```tcl
proc twice {name} {upvar 1 $name w; bump w; bump w}
proc bump {name} {upvar 1 $name v; incr v}
proc c {} {set x 0; twice x; return $x}
```

`twice` has no summary here, where with `bump` defined first it has one and the caller's place is bound afterwards. Mutual recursion therefore never summarises, while a procedure that calls itself does. The answer is sound: the call keeps the widening every call to unseen code has, and only precision is lost.

## Why it was left

The marker is the flow graph's source-order rule for every caller, not the summary's. A procedure body runs after the whole file in the ordinary case, so reading a forward call as a call to the procedure the file defines is a change to that rule, with its own witnesses (a caller invoked at top level before the callee's `proc` really does call unseen code). Recorded under "Open — a procedure that calls one defined after it has no transfer summary" in `docs/design/compiler/precision-limitations.md`.

## What a fix needs

- A rule that distinguishes a forward call inside a procedure body (the body runs later, the callee is ordinarily bound by then) from a forward call at top level (genuinely unseen at that point), with witnesses for both.
- The summary composition over strongly connected sets already handles cycles (a cycle that does not settle answers may-bound), so once forward calls inside bodies resolve, mutual recursion summarises through the existing path.

issues.title: A module that rebinds any builtin has no transfer summaries for any of its procedures
issues.body:
## Precision limit (sound, no miscompile)

A module that rebinds a builtin, whether by a `proc` named like one, a `rename` or an alias onto one, or a rebinding whose subject the scan cannot name, has no transfer summaries at all (`ModuleCommandMutations::rebinds_builtins`, consulted by the summary build in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/interprocedural/transfer.rs`). Every call to a procedure of such a module keeps the widening a call to unseen code has.

```tcl
proc incr {args} {puts "shadowed"; return 0}
proc bump {name} {upvar 1 $name v; set v [expr {$v + 1}]}
proc c {} {set x 0; bump x; return $x}
```

Here `bump` has no summary, although it never calls the module's `incr`, so `x` is unknown after `bump x` in `c`'s lattice.

## Why it was left

The flow graph lowers a builtin to a typed statement (`set`, `incr`, `expr`) with no call in it, so a call to the module's replacement there is invisible to the summary's call walk, which could then miss a frame the replacement reaches. Telling which typed statements a rebinding actually moves is the lowering's question, answered per command; the conservative rule holds until a rebinding module motivates the precise one. Recorded under "Open — a module that rebinds any builtin summarises no procedure" in `docs/design/compiler/precision-limitations.md`.

## What a fix needs

- Per-command knowledge of which typed statements a given rebinding moves (`RebindingSubjects` already names the subjects the scan can see), so that only procedures whose bodies lower one of the rebound commands lose their summary, or so that such a lowered statement is treated as a call to the replacement in the summary's walk.
- Witnesses for a rebinding the scan cannot name (the subject computed), which must keep the module-wide conservative answer.

issues.title: A callee's write through a `::`-qualified `upvar` name argument, or a caller's `upvar #0` alias passed as one, is not a global write: the top level forwards and deletes the stale store (miscompile)
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
proc bump {name {by 1}} {upvar 1 $name v; incr v $by}
set g 1
proc c {} {bump ::g; return $::g}
puts [c]
puts $g
```

tclsh 8.4.20, 8.5.19, 8.6.18, 9.0.4 and 9.1.0 print `2` then `2`.

`tcl opt --profile full` (every dialect) leaves `puts [c]` and rewrites the last line to `puts 1`, with `set g 1` deleted (`# O102 Forward literal load of 'g'`, `# O109 Eliminate dead store`). Under 8.4 the optimised program then raises inside `bump`, since `incr` of an absent variable is an error there.

The same happens with `c` called as a statement, with `bump ::g` at the top level (`puts 1` for `2`), through a second procedure (`proc twice {name} {upvar 1 $name w; bump w; bump w}` called as `twice ::g`: `puts 1` for `3`), and with the caller's own alias passed as the name: `proc c {} {upvar #0 g x; bump x}`.

`global g; bump g` in the caller, and `bump ::ns::g` of a `namespace eval` variable, are right.

## Where

The CFG builder's global-write collection (`GlobalWriteInfo`, `rust/tcl-compiler/src/cfg_builder`) records no write made through a callee's link to a qualified or aliased place, so the top level's lattice never sees `c` write `::g`, and the forward and the dead-store deletion follow. The procedure transfer summary of `interprocedural/transfer.rs` inherits the gap in its `globals` (`component_outer_writes`).

Identical under the binary built from `e355162ca`, before the proc-level transfer summaries. Related: #2370 (a top-level `::name` write not aliasing `name`), #2367 (a global-write summary missing a write inside `namespace eval ::`).

issues.title: O126 removes a bare write to a `::`-qualified `variable`'s tail as an unused assignment, and W211 reports it (miscompile)
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
proc init2 {} {variable ::cfg2; set cfg2 2}
init2
puts $cfg2
```

tclsh 8.4.20 to 9.1.0 print `2`.

`tcl opt --profile full` gives `proc init2 {} {variable ::cfg2; }` (`# O126 Remove unused variable assignment`), and the optimised program raises `can't read "cfg2": no such variable`. `tcl diag` reports `W211 Variable 'cfg2' is set but never used` at the assignment.

## Where

`variable ::cfg2` links the local `cfg2` to the global, so the bare `set cfg2 2` writes `::cfg2`. The read-before-set side already knows the tail (`collect_qualified_variable_alias_tails` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/helpers.rs`); O126 (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/`) and the W211 analyser do not consult it, so the write looks like a dead local store.

Identical under the binary built from `e355162ca`.

issues.title: iRules: a `sharedvar` variable's writes are deleted as unused or dead stores, with false W211 and W220 (miscompile)
W220 false positive: a caller's local is reported never read when a callee writes a same-named namespace variable through `variable`
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
namespace eval ns {
    variable n 0
    proc inc {} {variable n; incr n}
}
proc q {} {set n 1; ns::inc; return $n}
puts [q]
```

tclsh 8.4.20 to 9.1.0 print `1`: `ns::inc` increments `::ns::n`, not `q`'s local.

`tcl diag` reports `W220 Assignment to 'n' is never read` at `set n 1`. `tcl opt` leaves the program unchanged (O109 does not fire), so only the report is wrong.

## Where

The CFG builder widens the `ns::inc` call's definitions with the callee's outer write `n` (`global_write_procs`, `rust/tcl-compiler/src/cfg_builder`) without knowing whether the caller's `n` is linked to that outer place, so the caller's own store looks overwritten before its read. A `variable` write in the callee targets the callee's namespace, which a plain local of the caller never is.

Identical under the binary built from `e355162ca`.

issues.title: O109 deletes the store feeding a procedure call's `upvar` name argument inside an `if` or `elseif` condition, and W220 reports it never read (miscompile)
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
proc bump {name {by 1}} {upvar 1 $name v; incr v $by}
set n 1
if {[bump n] == 2} {puts yes} else {puts no}
puts $n
```

tclsh 8.4.20 to 9.1.0 print `yes` then `2`.

`tcl opt --profile full` (every dialect) deletes `set n 1` (`# O109 Eliminate dead store`), and the optimised program prints `no` then `1`. `tcl diag` reports `W220 Assignment to 'n' is never read` at the store.

The same without the `else`, in a procedure body, with two calls in the condition (both stores go), through a second procedure (`twice n`), and through a `[catch {bump n} msg]` header (`set n foo; if {[catch {bump n} msg]} {puts err}; puts $n`: the store is deleted and `puts foo` forwarded, so the optimised program prints `foo` where tclsh prints `err` then `foo`). `while` and `for` headers keep the store (the loop's φ reads it), as does a nested `[incr n]` in the condition.

## Where

The SSA (`tcl explore --show ssa`) has the `<cond>` statement with `defs {n#2}` and `uses {}`: no form of a call records the callee's read of the place a name argument names (`bump n` and `set r [bump n]` show `uses {}` too). The statement and value-word forms survive only because `collect_rmw_hidden_reads` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/elimination.rs`) credits them with a hidden read, and that scan never covers a `Branch` condition. The fix is to record the name argument as a read on the call and on the condition's dispatch (the callee's `VarRead` trait, or the transfer summary's `Name` role), which makes the SSA right for all three forms instead of papering over two of them. #2297 (W220 on a top-level store read by a procedure through `upvar`) rests on the same missing read.

Identical under the binary built from `e355162ca`. In a generated sweep of 1470 programs (21 callee bodies over `upvar 1 $name v`, 5 place states, 7 call shapes, under tcl8.4, tcl8.6 and tcl9.0 against their own tclsh), every one of the 227 differing rows was this shape.

issues.title: An `upvar` name parameter's default names a caller place that no definition records: O102 forwards and O100 folds across the call (miscompile)
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
proc bumpd {{name n}} {upvar 1 $name v; incr v}
set n 1
bumpd
puts $n
proc p {} {set n 1; bumpd; return $n}
puts [p]
```

tclsh 8.4.20 to 9.1.0 print `2` then `2`: a call with no argument links `v` to the caller's `n` through the parameter's default.

`tcl opt --profile full` prints `1` then `1` (`# O102 Forward literal load of 'n'`, `# O100 Fold return of constant variable`).

## Where

The CFG builder's call-by-name definitions come from the call's words (`param_targets`), never from a parameter's default, so the call `bumpd` defines nothing in the caller and the store before it is forwarded across it. `parameter_values` already computes the default an omitted argument binds; the builder's `upvar_invalidated` needs to give the default's place a definition.

Identical under the binary built from `e355162ca`, before the proc-level transfer summaries, which build on this gap (their fix names the default's place as the call's linked place).

issues.title: `tcl explore` and `tcl diag` panic (index out of bounds in `ssa.rs`) on a module with a procedure named `top`
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
set g 1
proc top {} {}
```

```
$ tcl explore --source $'set g 1\nproc top {} {}' --show interproc --text --no-colour
thread '<unnamed>' panicked at rust/tcl-compiler/src/ssa.rs:351:24:
index out of bounds: the len is 0 but the index is 0
```

exit 101. `tcl diag` on the same source panics the same way (exit 101); `tcl opt --profile full` is fine (the program is left as written). Renaming the procedure to `top2` makes both commands succeed. tclsh 8.6.18 and 9.0.4 run the program without complaint.

## Where

The backtrace goes through `taint::apply_module_variable_traces` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/taint.rs:2758` and `:2846`) into `SsaFunction::var_name` (`ssa.rs:351`). The top-level unit is itself named `::top`, so the module's variable traces for the top level are applied to the procedure of the same name, whose SSA has no such version.

A diagnostics run that panics is a total loss of diagnostics for the file in the language server, so this is worse than its shape suggests. Identical under the binary built from `e355162ca` and under the current head of `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42`.

issues.title: tcllib `struct::set` and `struct::list` mutators declare no variable write, so `tcl opt` folds the stale value after them (miscompile)
A `proc` replacing an ensemble implementation (`::tcl::dict::size`) does not stop the O129 fold of `dict size` or its qualified spelling (miscompile)
issues.body:
## Program

```tcl
proc ::tcl::dict::size {d} {return 7}
puts [::tcl::dict::size {a 1}]
```

and the ensemble spelling, `puts [dict size {a 1}]`, after the same `proc`.

| | prints |
|---|---|
| tclsh 8.5.19, 8.6.18, 9.0.4, 9.1.0 | `7` (both spellings) |
| after `tcl opt --profile full --dialect tcl8.6` (also `tcl9.0` and the auto dialect) | `1` (both spellings) |

The optimised source is `puts 1` with `O129 Fold constant builtin command substitution`. (tclsh 8.4.20 raises `can't create procedure "::tcl::dict::size": unknown namespace` on the definition; that is a separate defect, filed beside this one.)

## Why it is wrong

`dict` is an ensemble whose subcommands map to `::tcl::dict::<name>`; a `proc` of that name replaces the implementation, so both `dict size` and `::tcl::dict::size` run the procedure from then on. A `proc dict` stops the fold (#1585), but a procedure declared on the implementation spelling is not read as shadowing the builtin: the qualified spelling resolves through the registry's default binding to the builtin's callback, and the ensemble spelling never consults the implementation command's binding. The declared-surface check that stops a fold should cover the implementation spellings of every ensemble the registry models that way, in both directions.

Found by the value-transfer review on `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42` at fb005d9c5; the base binary at 4872a52c7 folds identically.

issues.title: A `proc` whose namespace does not exist is taken as defined, where every tclsh raises `unknown namespace`
issues.body:
## Program

```tcl
proc ip::version {a} {return shadowed}
puts [ip::version 1.2.3.4]
```

| | result |
|---|---|
| tclsh 8.4.20, 8.5.19, 8.6.18, 9.0.4, 9.1.0 | error `can't create procedure "ip::version": unknown namespace` |
| after `tcl opt --profile full` (every dialect) | prints `shadowed` |

The optimised source is `proc ip::version {a} {return shadowed}; puts shadowed` with `O103 Fold pure-proc call to '::ip::version' to its constant return`.

## Why it is wrong

`proc` creates the command in the namespace its qualified name names and raises when that namespace does not exist, so the program never reaches the `puts`. The compiler registers the procedure as `::ip::version` without reading whether `::ip` exists at the statement. A `namespace eval ip {}` before it, or a `package require` whose package creates the namespace, makes the program valid; without one the definition is a raise, not a standing definition, and a definition whose namespace is created conditionally is at most may-defined. The same reading reaches `proc base32::encode {x} {...}` without `package require base32`, where tclsh raises the same error.

Found by the value-transfer review on `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42` at fb005d9c5; the base binary at 4872a52c7 behaves identically.

issues.title: Use structured payloads for all diagnostics and eliminate message parsing in consumers
issues.body:
Diagnostic consumers currently recover semantic data from human-facing messages and suggested edits. For example, the W123 consumers in `rust/tcl-lsp-db/src/lib.rs` and `rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs` extract the first single-quoted token, and W120 refinement extracts a package from a quick fix. A valid command containing an apostrophe can be truncated; changing wording, localization, quoting or an edit can change resolution and suppression.

Require structured diagnostics throughout the repository. Messages are rendered presentation. Consumers must use the diagnostic code, typed payload and independently retained source facts.

Related: #2286 (shared Tcl naming).

## Required contract

- One shared diagnostic envelope owns stable code/kind, severity, source location, typed semantic payload, related locations and fixes. Family-specific payload types retain the information their consumers need without duplicating semantic owners.
- Producers populate structured subjects and operands from the actual parsed/resolved source facts, Registry descriptors and dialect-aware naming interfaces. Retain byte identity, source channel, lookup purpose, provenance and temporal context where relevant; a display string cannot substitute for them.
- Rendering derives messages and fix descriptions from that structure. A rendered message, description or replacement edit is never an input to resolution, classification, suppression, navigation, availability, code actions or aggregation.
- CLI, LSP, database, MCP, WASM, reports and editor adapters preserve the structure needed by their consumers. Version serialized diagnostic payloads when required; derive all representations from the shared owner.
- Missing structured data remains explicitly unknown. Consumers must not reconstruct it from presentation or silently assign a guessed source identity.
- Preserve native Tcl/Jim guest-error message and errorCode/errorInfo compatibility under their actual dialect/version policy. Typed internal error information and source facts remain available to tooling; an engine-provided string alone does not establish a semantic payload.

## Repository-wide work

1. Inventory every diagnostic producer, diagnostic type and consumer across syntax, Registry, compiler/analyser, compiler checks, runtime/VM, package/workspace/database, server, F5 dialects, SpecTcl and tool/editor/report adapters.
2. Audit consumer reads of `message`, fix descriptions and `new_text`: identify regexes, delimiter scans, prefixes/substrings and other attempts to recover semantic fields. Distinguish display/search functions from decisions about program behavior.
3. Specify the shared envelope, typed family payloads and accessors. Reuse existing source/name/lookup owners; document ownership, currency and dialect requirements.
4. Migrate all producers and consumers, including W120/W123, cross-file refinement, recovery, deduplication, filtering, fixes and serialized adapters. Remove obsolete text parsers and parallel payload representations.
5. Add a maintained audit/drift check that rejects new semantic parsing of diagnostic presentation. Any presentation-only use is documented and constrained to that purpose.
6. Document the current contract and examples for implementers, including how a new diagnostic family declares its payload and how consumers handle missing or unsupported facts.

## Acceptance and proof

- Every diagnostic family has a defined structured payload contract, including an explicit no-additional-payload case where appropriate.
- Every semantic consumer uses that structure. No diagnostic decision depends on reparsing messages, fix descriptions or replacement text.
- Tests demonstrate that changing wording, quotes, localization, suggested fixes or message formatting leaves semantic decisions unchanged when the structured payload is unchanged.
- Separate controls show that identical messages with different structured subjects retain different outcomes, and that absent payloads do not manufacture identity.
- Exercise command/package/variable names containing quotes, whitespace, escapes, non-ASCII characters and native opaque bytes where the source/API supports them; cover qualified, aliased, renamed and temporal subjects.
- Round-trip tests verify structured payloads at serialization boundaries, along with source locations, codes and related information.
- Where behavior depends on Tcl/Jim/F5 semantics, tests cite narrowly scoped proof records and actual supported provider/version evidence. Rust payload-preservation tests are identified as implementation contracts.
- Required repository gates pass. Documentation describes only the current interfaces and behavior.

issues.title: W210 is silent on a read after a `foreach` over an empty list, although I230 already decides `[info exists x]` false there
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
proc p {} {
    foreach x {} {}
    if {[info exists x]} { puts yes }
    puts $x
}
foreach y {} {}
puts $y
```

Every tclsh from 8.4.20 to 9.1.0 raises `can't read "y": no such variable` (and the same for `x` when `p` is called): a `foreach` over an empty list never binds its variable.

`tcl diag` reports I230 "Condition '[info exists x]' is always false" — the existence fact holds `x` unbound after the zero-iteration loop — but no W210 on `puts $x`, nor on the top-level `puts $y`.

## Expected

W210 at both reads, from the same existence fact I230 decides the guard from. `docs/design/compiler/value-transfers-migration.md`'s W210 row states that W210 reads the existence fact.

## Where

`analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs`'s undef trace: the zero-iteration `foreach` is not a definition-free path for its loop variable in the trace, although the existence rung already holds the variable unbound there.

Pre-existing: the read was not reported at `6d214350b` either. Found by the final review of `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42` (the bounded-loop worked example); not fixed there.

issues.title: O100 folds `return ${a b}` to `return 3}`: the replacement span stops before the braced variable reference's closing `}` (invalid optimised program)
issues.body:
## Repro

```tcl
proc p {} {set {a b} 3; return ${a b}}
puts [p]
```

Every tclsh from 8.4.20 to 9.1.0 prints `3`. `tcl opt` (any dialect) rewrites the procedure to `proc p {} {set {a b} 3; return 3}}`: one `}` too many, so the optimised program raises `extra characters after close-brace` before any output.

## Where

`try_fold_return_terminator` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/propagation.rs` reports O100 with the statement span it inherited; for a `${…}` variable reference the segmenter's `widen_word_end` (`segmenter.rs`) returns the inner token's end when `group_closer()` is absent, so the reported range `[24,36)` stops before the closing `}` of `${a b}` and the replacement `return 3` leaves it behind. `tcl explore --json` shows the range.

Not #2391 (a braced literal word treated as a substitution) and not #2340 (text lost from a composite return word): this return word is one valid variable substitution.

Pre-existing: the merge base `6d214350b` produces the same invalid procedure (its O100 report is identical; only the later O103 fold of `[p]` is new). Found by the pre-PR review of `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42`; not fixed there.

issues.title: W220 false positive: `set s abc` is "never read" when its only read is inside a nested `[expr {[string length $s] * 2}]` in an `if` condition
issues.body:
## What happens

```tcl
proc q {} {
    set s abc
    if {[expr {[string length $s] * 2}] == 6} { return yes }
    return no
}
```

`tcl diag` reports W220 "Assignment to 's' is never read" on `set s abc`, although the nested `[string length $s]` reads it. The optimiser keeps the store (no O109), so this is a false diagnostic, not a miscompile. Without the nested `[expr]` (`if {[string length $s] * 2 == 6}`) there is no W220.

## Where

The dead-store fact W220 and O109 share: the fused `[expr {…}]` in the condition records no use of `s` (the same cause as the nested-call decline in #2454). Whether the merge base `6d214350b` shows the same W220 has not been checked.

Found on `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42` while restating its design pages; not fixed there.
